entries.title: An agent inside After Effects: editable teaching graphics, with a bridge to verify
entries.summary: The saved demonstration points toward agents building editable After Effects projects. Adobe’s automation foundations support that direction, but the particular connector and its reported speed remain unverified.
entries.reason: An agent interface to an established motion application can support editable production workflows and reuse native tools; a short demonstration does not establish the connector’s breadth or the claimed timings.
entries.html:
The useful part is the editable project

Carlos Santana’s July 13 bookmark describes two linked experiments: asking GPT-5.6 Sol to build an MCP connection for After Effects, then asking it to animate a ChatGPT-style interface inside that application. The post reports six minutes for the connection and two minutes for the animation. Those are the creator’s timings, not independently reproduced measurements. The captured evidence does not identify a public repository, a tool catalogue, or a repeatable installation procedure. Its value is a concrete demonstration claim about bringing an agent into a mature creative application. Saved demonstration

For a teacher producing explanation videos, the interesting deliverable would be an After Effects project containing understandable layers, text, timing, and reusable compositions. A flattened video can be watched; an editable project can be corrected after discovering that a label is wrong, a sentence needs longer on screen, or a course has changed its visual identity. An agent that helps build this structure could remove tedious setup while leaving familiar controls for human revision. That is a more durable ambition than reproducing the particular chat interface shown in the announcement.

The bookmark does not establish that its connector can operate every After Effects feature. Nor does a successful interface animation establish reliability on tracked footage, complex expressions, third-party effects, or long projects. This report therefore separates the saved demonstration from Adobe’s documented automation foundations and from proposed workflows. The practical question is which small, inspectable set of operations would make an agent useful in your own production process.

A bridge, an application, and a motion plan

MCP supplies a common way for an AI application to communicate with servers exposing tools and other context. The host manages a client connection; the server provides capabilities that the agent can discover and invoke. The protocol does not itself know how to animate a rectangle or save an After Effects project. A connector must translate a tool request into operations the target application understands, then return useful results or errors. MCP architecture

Adobe already documents application scripting through ExtendScript, a JavaScript-related language associated with JSX files. Scripts can automate operations such as rearranging layers or replacing text. File writing and network access are separately controlled in After Effects preferences. These documented foundations make a custom bridge technically plausible, but they do not tell us which mechanism Santana used or whether his implementation has been shared. Adobe scripting documentation

There is also a current Adobe UXP status development surface. Adobe’s Adobe host API reference reference lists objects for projects, compositions, layers, properties, text, shapes, and render queues, while the Adobe UXP status landing documentation describes an evolving beta. Version requirements matter: this current documentation should not be retroactively treated as the implementation behind a July demonstration. A developer considering a new connector should first identify the installed After Effects version and the Adobe host API reference family actually available to it. Adobe host API reference Adobe UXP status

A useful connector design would distinguish observation from editing. Observation might report the active composition, dimensions, frame rate, layer identifiers, and selected properties. Editing might create a named text layer or apply specified keyframes to a known layer. Saving and rendering deserve explicit operations because they affect files and production time. These are proposed interface boundaries, not a verified inventory of the bookmarked server. They make errors easier to diagnose: an unavailable font is a different problem from a disconnected bridge or an incorrectly targeted composition.

For an average coder, the first implementation goal should be a short round trip. Read the composition, create one clearly named shape, change one property, read it back, and inspect the result in the application. This establishes that requests reach the intended document and that returned state corresponds to actual changes. A connector that only reports success without returning object identity or observable state is much harder to trust across twenty subsequent edits.

Translate intentions into visible decisions

Prompts such as “make this professional” leave the important decisions unresolved. A better brief identifies audience, reading order, output size, duration, visual vocabulary, and what must remain editable. For example, a twelve-second vocabulary introduction might contain one headword, one short example, a highlighted suffix, and a final still suitable for pausing. The motion should direct attention through those elements in order. Decorative movement should have to justify the time it occupies.

Keyframes describe values at particular times; interpolation determines the values between them. Adobe distinguishes temporal interpolation, which controls change over time, from spatial interpolation, which controls a motion path. This distinction explains why an object can follow the correct route yet feel poorly timed, or have pleasant acceleration while curving away from its intended alignment. A request to change the path should not accidentally rewrite the reading rhythm. Adobe interpolation guide

In the vocabulary example, the headword could appear first, the suffix highlight second, and the example sentence third. The final state should hold long enough for an actual reading task. Specify approximate beat boundaries, then review them with the intended narration. If the learner must simultaneously decode unfamiliar text and follow a traveling label, simplify the movement. The measure of success is whether the instructional relationship becomes easier to see.

Layer names are part of the interface between you and the agent. Names such as “sentence-example,” “suffix-highlight,” and “term-title” carry intent; dozens of anonymous rectangles do not. Ask the agent to report which layers implement each beat and which properties it changed. That small discipline makes later requests precise: shorten the highlight entrance, lengthen the final hold, or replace the example without rebuilding the composition. It also lets a human editor recover the project when an agent session ends.

Separate semantic content from animation decisions. Keep the vocabulary spelling, translation, example sentence, and source reference in a small reviewed content record. Keep fonts, spacing, and timing in a template specification. If the translation changes, you should not need to reinterpret the whole motion brief. If the animation changes, the content should remain traceable. This separation is particularly useful when generating multiple language versions whose line lengths differ substantially.

Three educational projects worth trying

A sentence that reveals its structure

Start with one Latin sentence whose grammatical analysis you have already checked. Decide whether the lesson concerns subject and verb agreement, noun endings, or word order. Do not attempt to explain all three at once. Prepare separate text layers for the relevant words and a consistent visual cue for the chosen relationship. The agent’s job is to arrange and animate that approved explanation, not to silently invent grammatical analysis while building graphics.

A useful sequence begins with the intact sentence, highlights the two related endings, and then introduces a short explanatory label. Keep the full sentence visible throughout, so the highlighting does not remove context. Finish with the same sentence unhighlighted and a question for the learner. This creates a miniature retrieval exercise rather than a continuous performance of answers. Produce a second version with the final answer withheld for classroom use.

Review the animation at three levels. First, check the text and accents against the approved content. Second, pause at each explanatory beat and check that the spatial relationship is unmistakable. Third, play the whole sequence at classroom projection size. A perfect close-up in the editor can become unreadable from the back of a room. These are proposed acceptance criteria; no version of this exercise was produced during this research.

A reusable evidence chart

After Effects can import data formats including JSON, CSV, and TSV and use expressions to connect data with properties. Adobe documents JSON as imported footage whose values can drive animation. That gives a credible foundation for reusable charts, although support in an application does not guarantee exposure through an arbitrary MCP connector. Adobe data-driven animation guide

For a reading lesson, use a small, synthetic dataset showing how different groups interpreted a paragraph. Keep the chart’s axis and scale fixed while bars appear in sequence. Ask the agent to display values and sample sizes from the same data record used for geometry. This prevents a common authoring error in which a visible number changes while the bar still reflects the previous value. Label synthetic examples clearly, and preserve real survey sources when using actual classroom research.

Build one chart manually or with tightly supervised assistance before attempting a batch. Include a zero value, a very long category label, and the largest expected value in the first review. These cases reveal whether the template survives variation. Then produce alternate lesson versions from the same approved layout. A useful batch report would list which data record produced each composition and where text overflow or unusual values required human attention.

An app walkthrough with meaningful emphasis

A short tutorial for your own learning app is a particularly good match for the saved interface demonstration. Begin from screenshots or a controlled recording of the actual application. Identify the action being taught: choosing a lesson, revealing a hint, or reviewing a mistaken answer. Use motion to connect the action with its consequence. Avoid adding attractive interface elements that do not exist in the real product.

Create a storyboard with four states: the starting screen, the action target, the resulting feedback, and the next step. Ask for editable labels and highlights around the real assets. Preserve the original screenshot separately so that a redesigned screen can be substituted later. Review the final video against the current app; a visually polished walkthrough that teaches an obsolete menu path is still a failed instructional asset.

This workflow can also expose product problems. If the explanation needs three arrows and a long narration to describe a basic action, the underlying interface may need revision. Treat the animation exercise as a usability review: what did the agent need to call attention to, and why was that information not obvious in the application itself? The useful output may include a shorter video and a clearer app.

Make the second video cheaper to produce

Adobe’s Essential Properties allow selected properties of a nested composition to be adjusted from its containing composition. Different instances can use different values while retaining a shared underlying composition. This is a documented mechanism for reusable designs, and it provides a better long-term target than repeatedly asking an agent to recreate the same title card from scratch. Adobe Essential Properties guide

For a course series, define a title, subtitle, accent color, lesson number, and optional illustration as explicit controls. Choose which values may vary and which should remain fixed. A consistent baseline and text size can be more useful than unlimited stylistic freedom. The agent can then help populate instances, inspect exceptional cases, and explain how to revise the master. Whether it can directly create those controls depends on the connector’s actual tool coverage.

Consider two kinds of reuse separately. Content reuse means replacing approved text or data in an existing motion design. Structural reuse means applying the same rhythm to a different arrangement of content. The first is usually easier to validate. The second may require design judgment: a two-word title and a twelve-word title do not necessarily deserve identical entrance timing. Establish limits for the template rather than pretending every input will fit.

A practical first library might contain only three compositions: a title, a two-column comparison, and a labeled diagram. Give each one a short usage note explaining appropriate content length, the intended final hold, and the controls that can be edited safely. This small library creates a shared language for future requests. “Use the comparison composition with these two examples” is more actionable than another broad request for a polished educational video.

Keep a record of the agent’s changes alongside the project version. It need not be elaborate: composition name, changed content, changed timing, imported assets, and known issues are enough. If a later edit breaks an expression or loses a font, that record helps distinguish an inherited problem from the newest change. A useful assistant should leave you with a recoverable project, not dependence on its memory of the conversation.

A successful tool call is only the start of review

Application state, appearance, motion, and export are different kinds of correctness. State review asks whether the intended layers and keyframes exist. Appearance review asks whether text fits and objects align. Motion review asks whether entrances, holds, and exits support comprehension. Export review asks whether the delivered file has the right dimensions, duration, transparency, and sound. Passing one category does not imply passing the others.

Adobe distinguishes rendering frames from encoding or otherwise exporting them. Its Render Queue and output modules provide controls over the resulting files; a preview inside the application is not the same artifact as the final encoded movie. An agent may successfully enqueue a composition without completing a render, and a rendered file may still be the wrong deliverable. Require precise language about which stage has actually completed. Adobe rendering and export guide

For a first connector evaluation, use a disposable copy of a small project. Ask for one localized change and compare before and after. Then test a revision request against the same layer, a missing asset, and an unsupported operation. The point is to learn how the bridge behaves under ordinary production friction. Does it explain the limitation, leave a partial result, or claim success? Recovery quality often matters more than the most impressive clean demonstration.

Keep the target composition explicit whenever several are open. Avoid commands that depend solely on whichever panel happened to be active. Save versions at meaningful milestones: approved layout, approved timing, and approved final output. For an agent-accessible workflow, identifiers and paths are as important as visual instructions. The clearest creative brief can still produce the wrong result if a tool edits the wrong composition.

Expect some manual work. The bookmark offers no evidence about font discovery, expression debugging, effect compatibility, color management, or render recovery. Those are not reasons to reject the idea; they are the boundaries that determine whether it fits your project. Start with native text and simple shapes, then add complexity when the bridge has demonstrated that it can inspect and revise what it creates.

Define a useful pilot before building a bridge

A sensible pilot has a baseline, a bounded task, and a revision. Make a simple title and diagram through your normal process, recording the steps that feel repetitive. Then ask an agent-assisted workflow to produce the same approved content. Compare the resulting projects by how easily you can correct them, not only by how quickly the first preview appears. Include your own review time in the comparison.

The revision should be deliberately ordinary: change the title to a longer phrase, move the final explanation two seconds later, and replace the accent color across the composition. Check whether the agent changes the correct objects without disturbing unrelated work. A system that handles this revision well is beginning to demonstrate production value. A system that rebuilds everything may still be useful for experiments, but it has a different maintenance cost.

Keep the pilot’s learning objective narrow. For example, the diagram might explain how a browser request reaches a server and returns a response. Approve the three labels and arrow directions first. Ask the agent to show one direction at a time, hold the completed diagram, and provide a still frame for the accompanying handout. This produces two useful teaching assets from one reviewed composition while keeping the factual content easy to audit.

After the pilot, choose the next improvement from observed friction: clearer layer inspection, better text fitting, or more predictable timing updates. Building every imaginable tool before testing this small loop would make it harder to identify which capability actually saves work.

A strong direction, with the connector still unverified

The score of eight reflects the significance of connecting an agent to an established, editable motion workflow. The strongest near-term applications are repeated educational graphics, concise interface walkthroughs, and controlled template variations. A teacher who already uses After Effects could gain more from reliable assistance with these tasks than from an ambitious promise of autonomous filmmaking.

The next useful evidence would be a public connector description, a list of supported operations, a reproducible project, and demonstrations of revision and failure recovery. Until then, the saved post is an interesting creator report supported by a plausible application automation foundation. Use it to shape a small evaluation project, and judge that project by editability, instructional clarity, and dependable revision rather than the reported number of minutes.

entries.title: GPT-5.6 prompting: keep the useful contract, test the stronger claims
entries.summary: The saved guide promotes outcome-driven work, durable rules, and independent verification. Its strongest practical lessons survive scrutiny, while fixed agent counts, broad performance claims, and historical cost anecdotes need qualification.
entries.reason: Model-specific prompting guidance can improve development efficiency, but the article’s concrete recommendations and claimed advantages must be checked against official documentation and reproducible tasks.
entries.html:
A useful working contract wrapped in extravagant claims

Miraqle's July 9 article argues that GPT-5.6 should receive a clear destination, durable rules, and a measurable quality bar rather than exhaustive step-by-step direction. The expanded original also advocates independent review, persistent goals, model routing, browser work, progress visibility, and reuse of earlier projects. Its central practical idea is to define what acceptable completion looks like.

That idea deserves attention from a teacher building apps or educational content. A request to improve a grammar exercise is difficult to judge. A request to explain wrong answers accurately, preserve retry behavior, and demonstrate the resulting interaction creates a much clearer collaboration. The benefit comes from the task definition and review process; it does not require accepting the article's promotional framing.

Several stronger assertions remain unverified here: the scale of early reviews, a claimed comparative grader-gaming record, a numerical rate of off-script behavior, and a fixed four-agent interpretation of Sol Ultra. The article's anecdotes and claims about progress boards do not establish universal product behavior. This report uses current official documentation for model identity and supported mechanisms, while treating the proposed workflow as something to evaluate.

Keep the requested model and its settings precise

The official GPT-5.6 Sol page identifies gpt-5.6-sol and says the gpt-5.6 alias routes to it. Documented API reasoning levels are none, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. Product-interface labels should not be assumed to map to a particular API setting or agent count without checking that surface.

The current page lists Sol at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, with promotional pricing available at least through November 21, 2026. This differs from the article's historical $5 and $30 figures. Long-context and cache-write conditions also affect charges. A claim that an overnight run costs less than a familiar everyday purchase is not a usable estimate without the workload.

The family also includes GPT-5.6 Terra, positioned for an intelligence-cost balance, and GPT-5.6 Luna, positioned for cost-sensitive volume. These are documented options, but assigning each a job title does not prove which is economical for your task. Compare accepted outputs, latency, retries, and review effort under the same requirements.

Describe the outcome while preserving necessary procedure

A proposed development brief is: revise the English tense exercise so each incorrect answer receives a short explanation tied to the sentence context; keep existing question identifiers and learner progress; provide a reviewable change and demonstrate representative correct, incorrect, and retry interactions. This leaves room to inspect the implementation without leaving the educational behavior vague.

Sometimes a procedure is necessary. A school may require a particular review sequence, an importer may depend on a fixed file format, or a migration may need a documented rollback step. Giving those instructions is not automatically inferior prompting. The useful distinction is between constraints that protect the result and unnecessary micromanagement of ordinary implementation choices.

Ask the agent to identify missing information that would materially change the outcome. If two answer interpretations are valid, that deserves teacher input. If the agent can choose between equivalent internal helper names, it can proceed. This keeps your attention on decisions that affect learners or future maintenance.

The official prompting guide emphasizes explicit instructions and evaluation across model versions. It does not establish a universal rule that withholding procedural guidance makes GPT-5.6 better. Treat the brief as a hypothesis about effective collaboration and refine it from observed failures.

Use rules that protect the product without forcing everything through a model

A blanket prohibition on hard-coded special cases can be counterproductive. Some behavior should be deterministic: validating required fields, enforcing ownership, checking question identifiers, and rejecting malformed exercise data. Asking a model to reason afresh about these rules can introduce unnecessary variability. Reserve model judgment for the parts that benefit from it, such as proposing natural examples or identifying ambiguity.

For a language app, a practical rule set could require preservation of stable identifiers, separation of student-facing material from answer keys, and explicit review of new external dependencies. Explain why each rule exists. A rule tied to a real maintenance concern is easier to apply than a slogan about keeping the stack boring.

Rules should also remain revisable by the person responsible for the project. If the current task intentionally changes an old convention, surface the conflict and resolve it. Do not design a workflow in which an obsolete instruction silently defeats the user's current objective.

The Structured Outputs documentation describes schema-constrained responses for supported models and distinguishes output structure from tool calling. For an exercise generator, a schema can require fields such as question, options, and explanation. It cannot establish that the explanation is pedagogically sound. Structural checks and content review solve different problems.

Make independent review specific enough to be useful

A separate review pass can help, but another model with fresh context is not an oracle. It may share blind spots with the builder or misunderstand the same requirement. Give the reviewer the actual artifact, the original brief, and the evidence needed to assess it. Avoid asking merely whether the work looks good.

For the tense exercise, ask the reviewer to identify questions with more than one defensible answer, explanations that contradict the sentence, and feedback that reveals an unrelated answer. Require concrete examples and locations. A teacher can then assess the findings instead of trying to interpret a numerical quality score with no rationale.

Combine this with deterministic checks where appropriate. Verify that every question has an identifier and that the answer key refers to existing options. Inspect the rendered learner interaction separately. A valid data file can still display confusingly, and a clear screen can still contain a wrong answer.

OpenAI's evaluation guidance recommends task-specific criteria and calibration against human judgment. The useful principle is to evaluate the actual behavior and retain representative failures. It does not support treating a fresh model's approval as sufficient evidence of correctness.

Use a goal when the next step depends on the result

The Codex goals cookbook documents persistent objectives with lifecycle controls and evidence-based completion. This is a host capability, not a property that every GPT-5.6 API request automatically acquires.

A suitable proposed goal might migrate a selected exercise unit to a new format while preserving accepted answers. The agent can inspect the data, convert it, check differences, and resolve failures iteratively. Completion should require the migrated unit and a readable comparison, with unresolved content decisions identified.

By contrast, correcting a label does not need an elaborate continuation loop. The extra machinery can make a small task harder to supervise. Choose persistence when the work genuinely requires discovery and iteration, and make its scope narrow enough that success is recognizable.

Keep a practical limit on investigation. If the reference behavior cannot be established or necessary inputs are missing, the useful output is a clear account of what was attempted and what decision remains. An agent should not manufacture certainty merely because a long-running objective encourages continued activity.

Measure the value of routing instead of assuming it

For a proposed lesson-production pipeline, begin by separating tasks. Extracting a known set of fields from a well-formed brief is different from resolving a subtle translation ambiguity. Drafting a scene list differs from checking whether a grammar explanation is correct. These distinctions create candidates for different models or deterministic code.

Evaluate each candidate on representative inputs, including awkward cases. A cheaper model may be suitable for formatting but create extra review work on ambiguous language. A stronger model may improve a difficult explanation while adding no value to a simple identifier check. The relevant comparison is the cost of an accepted result.

Record retries and human correction effort. If an inexpensive first pass fails frequently and requires a second model call, its apparent saving may disappear. Conversely, using the most capable setting for every small operation can spend resources without improving the lesson.

Keep routing explicit in the application design. A model can recommend which task is difficult, but your system still needs a dependable policy for choosing a path and handling failure. Start with a simple arrangement you can measure before adding a complicated network of agents and graders.

Reuse prior work as context, with provenance

Previous lessons, app repositories, and production notes can make a new task easier to specify. Supply a successful worksheet as a quality reference and explain which properties should carry over: clarity of directions, answer-key detail, or print layout. Identify what should change, such as topic, learner level, and vocabulary.

Calling this archive a private training set can be misleading. Providing examples or session logs as context does not itself update the model's weights. It supplies information for the current workflow. That distinction matters when deciding what is retained, what must be supplied again, and what evidence supports a claimed improvement.

Curate the archive rather than feeding it indiscriminately. Old logs may contain abandoned approaches, temporary credentials, or instructions that no longer apply. A short decision record explaining what worked and why can be more useful than an unfiltered transcript.

For video work, preserve the approved script, scene plan, captions, and correction notes together. A later project can reuse the production pattern while checking new factual claims independently. Reuse should reduce repeated setup; it should not turn a previous project's mistakes into a permanent house style.

A concrete quality bar for an educational video

Suppose the task is to prepare a three-minute explanation of the difference between literal and natural translation. A vague quality bar asks for an engaging video. A useful one requires two paired examples, an explanation of what meaning is preserved, and a final exercise whose answer is supported by the preceding explanation.

Supply the source sentences and approved interpretations. Ask GPT-5.6 to produce a narration draft, on-screen text, and scene notes. Require each scene to identify the teaching point it serves. The model can choose the order and propose transitions, while the content requirements remain stable.

Review the script for meaning before reviewing production choices. If the translation example is misleading, changing the animation will not fix it. Then inspect whether the on-screen text competes with the narration and whether the final exercise introduces an unexplained distinction. Actual duration must be assessed from the spoken and rendered result, not inferred solely from a requested time limit.

A separate reviewer could compare the package against these criteria and identify specific gaps. A human teacher would still decide whether the explanation fits the class. This example makes the article's strongest principle practical: define evidence that corresponds to the intended learning outcome, rather than relying on a model's own impression of polish.

A practical experiment beats a universal prompting doctrine

Choose one educational task and compare your existing brief with an outcome-focused version. Keep the input material and acceptance criteria fixed. Track correctness, unnecessary changes, unresolved assumptions, and the time needed to review the result. Include a difficult example so the comparison reveals more than success on a friendly demonstration. No such experiment was performed for this report.

The 7/10 score reflects useful advice about completion criteria, reusable context, and review, tempered by unsupported superlatives and overly absolute rules. GPT-5.6 remains the subject here; newer model guidance should not be silently substituted as proof of its behavior. The durable lesson is to make the work contract concrete, retain deterministic safeguards, and let evidence determine how much autonomy and complexity the workflow deserves.

entries.title: Codex inside Claude Code: independent review, focused rescue, and a careful handoff
entries.summary: OpenAI’s plugin exposes distinct paths for reviewing Claude Code work, delegating a problem, and moving a conversation into Codex. Its strongest use is a bounded second opinion with traceable evidence and clear ownership of changes.
entries.reason: A defined integration between development agents can make independent review and task delegation easier to reproduce; its actual interface, prerequisites and permission model need checking.
entries.html:
A small bookmark pointing to a substantial integration

The saved reply from Shubham Saboo is essentially a repository pointer. Its GitHub card identifies openai/codex-plugin-cc as a way to use Codex from Claude Code for code review or task delegation. It does not contain a benchmark, an installation diary, or evidence that two agents automatically outperform one. The report therefore follows the actual implementation rather than expanding that short link into a performance claim.

The official OpenAI repository contains a Claude Code plugin, command definitions, runtime scripts, and tests. Its practical attraction is reducing the friction of getting another agent involved while remaining in an existing coding workflow. A teacher building an app can ask one system to implement a feature and another to inspect a defined change, without manually repackaging every request into a separate chat.

The important distinction is between review, delegation, and transfer. Review produces findings about work. Delegation asks Codex to investigate or carry out a bounded task. Transfer creates a continuation point in Codex. Those operations have different purposes and different consequences, so a useful workflow chooses one deliberately instead of treating the plugin as a generic button for more intelligence.

The integration uses the local Codex runtime

The current README describes a wrapper around the installed Codex CLI and app server, using the same local authentication and configuration. It works in the same repository checkout and machine environment. It is not a separate hosted coding service hidden behind Claude Code, and the wrapper does not make Codex usage disappear into the Claude subscription.

That architecture is useful because the second agent can work with the actual project state. It also means configuration and context deserve attention. The repository explains that project-level Codex configuration depends on project trust. A developer should understand the installed environment before assuming that a plugin invocation has the same model, permissions, or network access as another session.

OpenAI’s app-server approval documentation describes requests for command execution, file changes, and other permissions, with the client returning a decision. This is a general protocol capability, not proof that every plugin operation presents every possible approval interaction. The narrower evidence in this repository matters: the companion implementation explicitly selects read-only operation for adversarial review and chooses task sandbox mode according to whether writes were requested.

No plugin was installed or executed for this report. The account, model, and operating-system combinations available to a reader should be checked against current requirements at the time of use. The useful architectural conclusion is that this is a real integration around an existing agent runtime, with the responsibilities of that runtime still present.

Choose the right review question

The normal review command definition is explicit about review-only behavior. It supports reviewing relevant working-tree changes or a branch comparison and has foreground and background options. It does not accept arbitrary focus text or staged-only and unstaged-only scopes. These details matter because a plausible-looking command can ask for a capability the implementation does not provide.

The separate adversarial-review command can take a focus. Its purpose is to question the chosen approach and its assumptions, not merely look harder for coding defects. For an educational app, that difference is valuable. A feature can be correctly implemented while embodying the wrong learning model.

/codex:review --wait
/codex:adversarial-review --wait Focus on whether revealing a hint can wrongly preserve full credit.

These examples illustrate documented command forms; they were not run here. The first asks for an ordinary review of the selected local work. The second uses the command that supports custom focus. Before either, establish what change is being reviewed. A finding about yesterday’s code is not evidence about a revised implementation, even if it appears in the same conversation.

Require findings to be actionable: the scenario that triggers the problem, the affected behavior, and enough location information to inspect it. A vague warning that the code could be cleaner is less valuable than a reproducible case where a student receives an incorrect score. Review quality is about useful evidence, not the length or severity of the report.

Workflow one: review a language-practice feature

Suppose Claude Code adds an exercise that asks students to choose the correct Latin ending. The intended behavior is simple to describe but easy to mishandle: a first correct attempt earns full credit; a hint changes the attempt category; retrying after an incorrect answer should not erase the history; and moving to the next question should not retain the previous selection.

Before implementation, write those rules in a small acceptance note with examples. Keep the note independent of the code so both agents can inspect the same product contract. Otherwise the reviewer may infer the intended behavior from the implementation and approve an internally consistent mistake. A second model is not an independent authority on your grading policy.

After Claude completes the feature, pause changes to the affected files and request a normal review. Inspect each reported issue against a concrete student action. If Codex identifies stale state after navigation, reproduce that transition or ask for a focused check. If it proposes a different scoring philosophy, decide whether that is a defect or a product suggestion. The teacher owns that distinction.

Next, use an adversarial review if the feature’s design itself deserves challenge. Ask whether the activity rewards memorizing button position, whether hints accidentally reveal every answer, or whether a feedback animation interrupts reading. These are different questions from whether a callback references the correct variable. They can reveal weaknesses that a purely local diff review may miss.

Route accepted findings back to the implementation owner with a narrow request. Change one behavior, preserve the other rules, and verify the triggering scenario again. The output should be a small corrected diff and evidence that the actual problem is resolved. Avoid accepting a broad rewrite simply because it arrives with confident reasoning.

Workflow two: delegate a difficult failure

The rescue command forwards a task through a dedicated Codex subagent. Its definition distinguishes fresh and resumed work and supports foreground or background execution. It also keeps the user’s request central instead of asking the forwarding subagent to conduct its own investigation first. The practical effect is a clearer handoff to Codex, rather than a chain of loosely summarized interpretations.

A good rescue task includes the symptom, a minimal reproduction, the expected behavior, what has already been tried, and the files or subsystem likely involved. For example: after editing an answer twice, the preview shows the previous explanation; the saved lesson data is correct; restarting the preview clears the problem; investigate the update path before proposing a change. That gives the second agent a problem to solve rather than a request to express confidence.

Begin with investigation when the failure is poorly understood. Ask for a causal account supported by the relevant code and a proposed small repair. If you explicitly authorize a fix, define the scope and require the agent to report what it changed and what it checked. The companion’s distinction between read-only and write-enabled task execution is useful, but a clear task boundary remains necessary.

Do not let two agents modify the same fragile area simultaneously. While Codex investigates the preview update path, Claude can work on an unrelated content task or wait for the result. Shared files are a coordination issue even when both agents have good intentions. A passing check can become stale as soon as another worker changes its inputs.

The best rescue result is not merely a patch. It explains why the symptom occurred, which assumption was wrong, and what evidence would reveal a regression. That explanation helps an average coder understand the project and decide whether the repair is proportionate. If the problem remains uncertain, an honest narrowed hypothesis is more useful than a large speculative rewrite.

Workflow three: inspect a content-production pipeline

The same approach applies to a website that generates narrated lesson videos. Suppose Claude adds a pipeline from a lesson record to a script, caption file, and rendered sequence. A normal review can inspect data handling and failure paths. An adversarial review can ask whether the design preserves source attribution, distinguishes draft from approved content, and handles revisions without mismatching narration and captions.

Create a tiny fixture with one title, two source-backed claims, and one deliberately uncertain statement. Ask the reviewer to trace those items through the pipeline. Does the uncertain statement become a confident narration line? Does a source link survive into the lesson page? If a script is edited after captions are generated, does the system flag that the captions may be stale?

Those questions turn editorial quality into inspectable data relationships. They do not ask the reviewer to certify the historical or scientific truth of every claim. A factual source review remains a separate task. The coding review checks whether the software preserves the evidence and approval distinctions you intended.

For visual output, inspect actual frames and playback where appropriate. Code review alone cannot establish that a subtitle fits the frame, that a chart is readable, or that a transition gives students enough time to process the explanation. The plugin is a route to an additional agent, not a replacement for the evidence required by the medium.

A useful completion record names the fixture, the checks performed, the output reviewed, and any unresolved limitation. This makes later work safer because the next session can distinguish a verified production step from a plausible but untested plan.

Transfer preserves a continuation, not perfect understanding

The transfer command is designed to create a resumable Codex thread from the current Claude Code session and retain the resulting session identifier. The README describes an importer and transcript-location constraints. A continuation mechanism reduces copying, but it should not be treated as proof that every tool event, implicit assumption, or external state has become equally meaningful to the receiving agent.

Before a substantial handoff, prepare a short state note: the goal, the current implementation, decisions already made, checks completed, known failures, and the next concrete action. Include file references rather than relying solely on conversational memory. A receiving agent can inspect those files and reconcile the note with the actual checkout.

For example, transfer a nearly completed vocabulary app with a note that content import works, duplicate detection remains unresolved, and deployment has not been authorized. Ask Codex first to confirm the current state and identify any mismatch. This costs a little time but avoids a common failure in agent handoffs: continuing confidently from an outdated description.

Use transfer when you want to continue ownership in another environment. Use rescue when you want a bounded contribution while retaining the existing workflow. Use review when you want findings before deciding whether to change anything. Choosing the smaller operation often makes the result easier to understand and supervise.

Background work needs a stable target and a stopping rule

The README documents status, result, and cancellation commands for background jobs. The broker source also contains explicit handling for a busy shared runtime and for interruption requests. This is evidence of operational coordination in the implementation, not a promise that arbitrary parallel tasks can run without contention.

For a long review, record the target state and avoid changing that state until the review has enough context. If you continue unrelated work, keep ownership clear. When the result arrives, compare it with the current code before applying suggestions. A finding may already be fixed, or a later change may invalidate the reviewer’s assumptions.

Set a stopping rule for investigation. A useful task might end after producing a reproducible cause, a bounded patch, and one relevant verification step. An open-ended request to keep improving the application has no natural boundary and can consume attention as well as usage. The plugin makes delegation convenient; it does not decide what amount of work is worth doing.

The optional review gate deserves particular restraint. The repository warns that a stop-triggered review can lead to a long Claude/Codex loop and rapidly consume limits. Treat it as an actively monitored workflow choice, not a default quality guarantee. Repeated reviewer disagreement may indicate an ambiguous requirement rather than a defect that another automatic iteration will resolve.

Measure whether the second opinion earns its place

Try the integration on a small set of changes that matter to the product: scoring logic, content import, navigation state, and a production export. For each, record the findings accepted, false alarms, actual defects reproduced, and time spent resolving disagreement. Compare that with your usual workflow. Do not use raw finding count as the success metric; an excessively noisy reviewer can make the overall process worse.

Include known edge cases in the evaluation, but do not secretly modify real student data to create them. Use fixtures or a local sample project. Ask whether the review catches meaningful issues and whether its explanations help you understand them. A tool that produces fewer but clearer findings may be more useful for an average coder than one that emits a comprehensive-looking list of speculative risks.

Watch for correlated mistakes. Both agents may misunderstand the same vague brief, rely on the same incomplete documentation, or miss the same absent test. Different model families can offer different perspectives, but agreement is not a proof of correctness. External evidence—an actual behavior check, a source document, or a domain expert’s decision—remains decisive.

Keep the simplest alternative in view: a focused second session with a clear task and the relevant project files. The plugin is especially valuable when switching and packaging context are recurring costs. If you need another opinion only occasionally, its additional moving parts may be less important than learning to write a precise review brief.

Turn disagreement into a small decision record

Two agents can disagree productively if the disagreement is made specific. Imagine Codex flags the quiz engine’s local progress storage as unreliable, while Claude says it is appropriate for a no-account classroom activity. Neither statement settles the question. Write down the product requirement: progress only needs to survive a page refresh on the same device during one lesson, or progress must follow the learner across devices for a term. The implementation should be judged against that requirement.

A compact decision record can contain the finding, the concrete failure scenario, the requirement it threatens, and the chosen response. Mark the outcome as accepted, rejected with a reason, or unresolved pending evidence. This prevents the same ambiguous concern from returning in every review and makes it easier to distinguish a genuine regression from an intentional tradeoff.

For an accepted defect, ask for the smallest meaningful change and the evidence that would disprove the fix. If progress disappears only when the browser tab is closed before a delayed save, a useful check exercises that timing. A test that merely confirms the save function exists would mirror the implementation without addressing the user’s failure. The reviewer should help connect the code to observable behavior.

For a rejected suggestion, preserve the reason without turning it into a permanent prohibition. A server database may be unnecessary for this small activity and appropriate for a future product. The record should say why the current scope does not require it, rather than instructing all future agents never to use a server. This keeps review from accumulating accidental architecture rules.

An unresolved finding needs a named next step. Perhaps the content owner must decide whether an accented form should count as equivalent, or a developer must reproduce a failure on the intended device. Repeating the review with a more forceful prompt will not supply missing domain evidence. The plugin is most useful when it reveals the precise decision that remains, then lets the right person or check resolve it.

Keep this record beside the change rather than burying it in a long chat. When a later session resumes the work, it can see both the code and the reasons for its boundaries. That is a practical way to turn an additional model’s opinion into durable project knowledge without treating either agent as infallible.

Why the integration earns eight points

The eight-point score reflects a concrete, inspectable bridge between established coding workflows, with distinct interfaces for review, rescue, and continuation. For educational software, that can make disciplined second opinions easier to request at the moments where mistakes matter. The score does not imply a measured productivity increase or universal compatibility. Its value rises when the task has clear acceptance criteria, a stable review target, and a human owner who can distinguish implementation defects from unsettled teaching decisions. It falls when two agents merely exchange confident prose without producing evidence.

entries.title: Cinematic websites with coding agents: directing media without losing the lesson
entries.summary: Four tutorial bookmarks point toward visually ambitious websites across GPT and Claude models. Inspected demonstration posters and the creator’s current written lessons reveal useful production choices, while the original videos’ complete steps and speed claims remain unverified.
entries.reason: The tutorial may provide useful composition and implementation techniques for educational sites; the recorded workflow needs inspection before extracting specific steps or judging reproducibility.
entries.html:
Four invitations to build a cinematic website

The four saved posts capture a recurring promise: an AI coding assistant can turn an ambitious visual idea into an animated website quickly. Viktor Oddy’s July 10 bookmark advertises a twenty-one-minute tutorial using GPT-5.6 Sol. His June 16 post points to an eleven-minute GPT-5.5 and Codex walkthrough. Both celebrate the visual possibilities, but neither short announcement provides enough detail to establish production time, reliability, or a comparison between models.

Oddy’s June 10 post promotes a twelve-minute animated-site tutorial, opening with a reference to Claude Mythos before naming Fable 5 in the tutorial description. Preserve that ambiguity rather than treating the two names as interchangeable. The fourth bookmark, FHILY’s June 11 post, contrasts Opus 4.8 with Fable 5 and promotes a twelve-minute introduction to making 3D sites without prior design or coding experience. It is another saved endorsement, not an independent technical evaluation.

The models are identifiable in primary material. OpenAI’s documentation identifies GPT-5.6 Sol and its text-output, image-input capabilities; Anthropic’s pages document Opus 4.8 and the Fable family. Model identity does not establish which assets were generated by which tool in a particular video. The useful question is how to divide a cinematic page into content, imagery, motion, and behavior that a human can review.

What the saved demonstrations actually show

Two original video posters were inspected. The July poster shows a local page preview with a fantastical house above clouds, large pale typography, and an assistant conversation alongside it. The visible conversation includes a request to make displayed business numbers more realistic. That is a valuable caution: plausible-looking marketing figures are still unsupported unless the project owner supplies evidence. A school resource should not inherit invented completion rates, testimonials, or achievement claims merely because a template expects them.

The June poster shows a metallic figure behind oversized typography and a request to move a text block upward. It illustrates a concrete revision expressed in spatial terms. It also displays an assistant’s build-status message, which is evidence of what the interface reported, not an independently repeated test. Both images are posters containing actual demonstration screens; neither proves the animation’s timing, responsiveness, or finished navigation.

The complete spoken walkthroughs were not retrieved through the permitted research tools. A creator-owned YouTube upload matching the GPT-5.5 tutorial was located, and Oddy’s current MotionSites Academy provides written lessons and associated videos. The analysis below uses those later written materials where identified. It does not present them as transcripts of the four saved clips. This distinction keeps the article useful without filling gaps in the evidence with invented steps.

Cinematic is a presentation goal, not a rendering format

A page can look three-dimensional while displaying a flat video. It can also render an actual three-dimensional scene, or combine ordinary text with layered images and modest transforms. These approaches offer different controls. A video gives the creator precise visual composition but only a predetermined sequence. A live scene can change viewpoint or respond to object selection, but it requires geometry, materials, lighting, and rendering logic. The Three.js fundamentals describe those scene-building components.

Choose the method by the learner’s action. If visitors only need to see an object turn, a short clip or a sequence of stills may be sufficient. If they need to inspect a hidden face, compare two configurations, or manipulate a part, actual geometry may earn its complexity. If the goal is reading, a static image with clear annotations may outperform either. These are design judgments to test in context, not measured rankings of the techniques.

For an average coder, the useful division is between a document layer and a visual layer. The document contains headings, evidence, links, controls, and explanations. The visual layer supplies the scene. Keep the document useful when the visual is absent or paused. That arrangement makes it possible to improve the visual independently, while the central information and reading order remain understandable.

The model’s role is to translate a sufficiently clear specification into implementation and help revise it. The owner still decides what the page should communicate, supplies factual material, and judges whether an effect has a purpose. A dramatic preview lowers the difficulty of imagining a result; it does not remove the need for those decisions.

Inspecting the creator’s written video method

The current MotionSites scroll-animation lesson describes choosing a visual direction, preparing a background video, and specifying the page in detail. Its included NovaAI prompt separates editable text from the background, defines a fixed visual layer, maps page progress to media position, and provides poster, video, and canvas states. It also includes narrow-screen layout rules and focused revision examples. This is concrete author-supplied material, although it is a later lesson rather than a verified transcript of the July bookmark.

The important design insight is separation of responsibilities. A background should carry atmosphere or a planned visual explanation. Navigation and factual copy should remain editable page content. A progress signal should control motion predictably. Loading behavior should have a visible fallback. These responsibilities can be discussed and tested individually; asking for a “premium cinematic page” leaves all of them unspecified.

The same lesson’s detailed prompt proposes a cache of sampled frames. That is an implementation proposal, not a guarantee of smoother behavior on every device. Assuming ninety uncompressed RGBA frames at 960 by 540 pixels, the raw pixel data alone would be about 178 MiB. This is an illustrative calculation, not a measurement of the lesson’s implementation; actual memory depends on storage and browser behavior. It explains why a seemingly small media choice deserves a deliberate budget.

Inspecting the separate geometry method

A second current MotionSites lesson takes a different route: produce multiple views of an object, pass them to an image-to-3D tool, export a GLB, and use a coding assistant to integrate it with Three.js and scrolling. It proposes relatively modest texture sizes and a staged layout. Its claims about agency-equivalent output or completing work in an afternoon remain promotional; they were not tested for this report.

Multiple generated views are useful design inputs, but they are not measurements. For a fictional object, inconsistencies can be artistic problems. For a museum object or scientific apparatus, they can become factual errors: the back may be invented, the scale may drift, or a mechanism may be impossible. Use measured or documented reference material when the lesson depends on physical truth, and label interpretive reconstructions clearly.

The lesson suggests tone mapping as a remedy for dark renders. That is too narrow as a universal diagnosis. Three.js’s color-management documentation distinguishes input, working, and output color spaces. In a real project, examine the lights, environment, materials, texture interpretation, exposure, and output processing before treating one setting as a cure. Ask the assistant to explain the visible cause and make one reversible change at a time.

A sensible first geometry task is one object, one deliberate camera view, and one meaningful selection. Add a clear reset before adding scrolling choreography. This gives the coder a tractable system to inspect and avoids confusing a camera problem with a document-layout problem.

Storyboard an explanation before generating its assets

Begin a teaching page with three sentences: what the learner sees, what changes, and what that change explains. For a proposed page about an inscription, the first state shows the complete object, the second highlights a short abbreviation, and the third places the expansion beside the original marks. The movement has a job: it directs attention from object to evidence to interpretation. No flying camera or particle system is necessary to make that sequence feel deliberate.

Write a small state table. Each row contains the learner’s question, the evidence visible, the explanatory text, the intended transition, and the static alternative. Attach source identifiers to the evidence before requesting image generation. If a generated background is only atmospheric, label it as such in the project notes and avoid placing it where a reader might mistake it for a documentary photograph.

Then define the layout at the start, middle, and end of the sequence. Decide where text can sit without covering the relevant object. Supply an actual long heading and the real explanatory paragraph. Ask for a still layout first. If the page does not communicate at rest, animation is unlikely to repair the underlying information hierarchy.

Only then choose the visual asset. A photograph may need a crop; a diagram may need two labelled states; a model may need a documented camera path. Ask the assistant to list what must be generated, what can be drawn with code, and what should remain ordinary text. That inventory helps prevent unnecessary media generation and makes the production work reviewable.

Build one complete section before expanding

An initial implementation should contain one heading, one visual, one explanation, and one real action. For an educational exhibition, the action might open the first object record. For a video companion, it might jump to the transcript. For a course introduction, it might launch a sample activity. Make that destination work before expanding the page into pricing, testimonials, statistics, and other sections suggested by commercial templates.

A useful original brief is: “Build a public introduction to this lesson using the supplied text and evidence. Start with one complete section. Keep the explanation readable before media loads. The visual may illustrate the concept, but it must not contain essential text. Add a static alternative and a clear route to the first activity. Report missing assets and unverified claims.” This is a proposed brief, not one extracted from a saved video.

After the first section works, revise one dimension at a time. Change the type scale without changing the copy. Adjust the crop without altering scroll timing. Reposition the explanation without replacing the background. These narrow changes make causes visible and keep an assistant from treating every correction as permission to redesign the whole page.

Preserve a working copy before adding motion. If the animation fails, you should still have a useful page and a clear description of the new failure. For an average coder, this is an effective learning structure: a sequence of understandable changes is easier to maintain than a large output whose parts were never examined.

Scrolling should remain a reading action

Scroll-linked media maps a reader’s movement through the document to a visual state. The browser’s currentTime property can move a video to a specified playback position, but seeking is different from ordinary continuous playback. The media must load and decode; the reader may reverse direction or move quickly. An implementation therefore needs to handle unavailable frames and changing scroll positions without hiding the explanation.

For a lesson, tie progress to the relevant section rather than assuming the entire page has a fixed length. Adding a source note or enlarging text should not make the illustrated event occur beside the wrong paragraph. Give each meaningful state a descriptive label, and provide a way to reach it without performing a precise scrolling gesture. A learner should be able to revisit the evidence after reading the conclusion.

Phone layouts require composition decisions, not merely smaller dimensions. Object-fit can preserve a media element’s proportions while filling or fitting its box; filling can crop important content. Check where the subject ends up in portrait orientation. If essential marks disappear, use a different crop or a dedicated mobile composition instead of shrinking the labels until they fit.

For an English close-reading page, consider a simpler alternative: a stationary passage with a sequence of highlighted phrases controlled by buttons. It can still feel carefully directed while allowing the learner to control the pace. Cinematic presentation is most useful when it supports the explanation’s rhythm rather than imposing a performance on the reader.

A concrete English lesson: how a narrator directs attention

A useful first content experiment is a short page about narrative viewpoint. Supply a teacher-written paragraph describing a room, then a second paragraph describing the same room from another character’s perspective. The visual scene should stay substantially unchanged while selected details gain emphasis. This makes the design itself demonstrate the distinction between a shared setting and a narrator’s selective attention.

Ask the assistant to build two clearly labelled states with a direct switch between them. Keep both passages available as ordinary text, and provide a comparison view that highlights wording changes. The imagery can be a simple illustration with three selectable objects; a generated cinematic background is optional. If used, it should not add objects or events that contradict either passage.

The learner’s task is to identify which details each narrator notices and explain what those choices imply. Feedback should refer to the supplied text, not infer a single correct emotional interpretation from the image. A teacher can review several acceptable responses before implementation. If the page includes an automated exercise, constrain it to a checkable question, such as locating a phrase, while leaving interpretation open for discussion.

For a narrated companion video, show the first passage, hold the same room, and change the emphasis with the second passage. Keep a readable still at the key comparison. The coding work becomes concrete: preserve the scene, switch the annotations, update the active label, and support a reset. This is a proposed teaching design, not an example claimed to appear in the bookmarked tutorials.

Budget for the visual before it becomes the page

Specify what should happen before the main asset arrives. A representative poster can establish composition; the heading and route to the activity should already work. MDN’s video reference documents poster images, playback controls, loading hints, and inline presentation. These are building blocks, not a promise that every device will behave identically. Verify the intended combination in the actual deployment context.

Google’s video-performance guidance explains why format, compression, and loading choices affect the experience. For a classroom project, begin with a concrete constraint: the visual must not prevent the explanation from becoming usable. Record asset sizes and observe a slow connection. Compare the initial load with a repeat visit so cached media does not disguise the first-time experience.

For live geometry, consider texture size, scene complexity, and the amount of work performed every frame. Do not assume that a short source file is cheap to render, or that an attractive desktop preview predicts mobile behavior. Ask the assistant to identify the most expensive visual operation and offer a simpler fallback. Then compare that fallback on the devices you expect learners to use.

Keep performance claims local and concrete. “The activity remained usable on this tested phone with this asset” is more informative than an unmeasured promise of smoothness. No frame rates, loading times, device comparisons, or production costs were measured for this report. The proposed budget is a way to generate that evidence during a real build.

Make the directed experience optional

Motion should not be the only route to the lesson. The reduced-motion media feature lets a page respond to the user’s preference. Design that version deliberately: show the meaningful states, preserve the evidence and explanation, and remove unnecessary camera movement. Simply making a long transition slightly slower may leave the same obstacle in place.

For sustained automatic movement alongside other content, consult the applicable W3C pause, stop, and hide guidance. Learner-controlled movement, automatic loops, and narrated media need different decisions. An explicit pause should not trap keyboard focus. A static reading mode should still contain the information needed to answer the activity.

Test a reader’s journey with the pointer unavailable. Can they reach the controls, identify the active state, and move on? Increase text size and see whether a pinned scene covers the explanation. If a teacher projects the page, can someone at the back identify the relevant detail? These are practical review questions, not a claim that passing a short checklist establishes complete accessibility.

When turning the page into a narrated video, create captions and a transcript as part of the editorial plan. A browser demonstration recording may contain tiny interface text or rapid movement that worked only for its author. Reframe it around the learner’s question, and retain a companion page where evidence can be examined at an individual pace.

What a useful handoff contains

A finished prototype should include more than a preview link. Keep the supplied content, asset origins, model and tool choices, the final brief, and a short account of revisions. Separate verified statements from placeholder material. Remove invented business numbers and replace demonstration testimonials before sharing a real educational service. In the inspected July poster, the request for realistic-looking figures shows exactly why this editorial pass matters.

Ask another person to complete three tasks: explain what the page teaches, reach the first activity, and find the supporting source. Record confusion in their words. Then review the visual sequence at rest, during loading, and after a change in screen size. These checks are more closely connected to a useful site than the advertised duration of the tutorial.

The catalogue score is nine: a base of six plus three additional saved mentions. That reflects repeated interest in a broadly useful creation workflow, not four independent confirmations of speed or quality. The strongest transferable practices are precise visual references, separation of content from media, incremental construction, and review of real learner tasks. The unresolved part is the full content and reproducibility of the four original recordings. The current written lessons support a concrete starting method; only building and testing a particular page can establish whether its cinematic treatment serves its audience.
