entries.title: Lottie Creator MCP: from a prompt to an editable learning-app animation
entries.summary: Creator’s documented agent tools can build and revise Lottie scenes, themes, and interactions. The strongest educational uses are small, purposeful assets whose exported behavior is checked in the actual learning app.
entries.reason: Native animation tools can give agents an editable output suited to application interfaces, but production readiness depends on supported features, export fidelity and playback validation.
entries.html:
Two bookmarks, two useful pieces of evidence

The first saved post, published by Nattu on June 10, presents a one-prompt animation demonstration using LottieFiles Creator MCP and an assistant identified as Fable 5. It describes the output as a real Lottie animation suitable for production. The second independently saved post is a documentation reply announcing availability and compatibility with Claude and many other agents. Together they preserve both the visual promise and the route toward trying the workflow. Saved animation demonstration Saved documentation reply

The practical attraction is clear: an agent can work inside an animation editor and leave an editable asset for an application. That differs from asking a video model for a clip. A developer can potentially revise the shape, timing, color, and interaction after generation. For a teacher building quizzes or explanatory websites, the most useful outputs may be small feedback animations and controllable diagrams rather than elaborate promotional sequences.

The original posts remain announcement evidence. Their named model, first-prompt success, production-readiness claim, and compatibility count are not independent benchmarks. Current documentation provides much stronger support for the existence and scope of Creator’s agent connection. The report below uses that documentation to describe the workflow, while proposed classroom and app projects are original examples that were not built during this research.

Choose the connection that edits the animation

The local Creator MCP bridge connects an assistant to an open Creator browser tab. The current guide requires Node.js 18 or newer, an MCP-compatible client, and local MCP enabled in Creator. It documents scene inspection, shapes and text, styling, keyframes, imported assets, themes, and state-machine editing. Feature access follows the workspace and plan. These are documented capabilities, not a guarantee that every model will use them correctly. Creator MCP documentation

LottieFiles also has a hosted MCP for workspace and account data. Its developer portal explicitly distinguishes that service from the local Creator connection. Confusing the two could leave you with an assistant that can find an animation in your workspace but cannot modify its layers. Decide whether the task concerns asset management or authoring before choosing a connection. LottieFiles developer portal

The current Creator guide additionally describes WebMCP as another route for compatible browser assistants, without the local bridge. It says the Creator editing capabilities are shared across these interfaces. This is useful current context, but it should not be silently substituted for the local MCP setup described by the saved June posts. Keep the interface, client, and application version in any reproducible evaluation notes.

A good first interaction is observational. Ask the assistant to describe the current scene’s dimensions, duration, layers, and major animated properties. Compare that description with the editor. Then ask for one small revision to a named layer. This establishes a connection to the intended document and gives you a baseline for later changes. A complex prompt issued before this check makes connection problems harder to distinguish from design problems.

For an average coder, the important mental model is an editor with callable operations. The agent still needs to plan the sequence of operations, choose sensible values, and inspect what it has made. The existence of a tool for adding a keyframe does not determine which keyframe will communicate the right idea. Treat the assistant as a collaborator working on the same scene, with a brief and a review cycle.

What the resulting file contains

Lottie JSON describes animation elements and motion as structured data. The dotLottie format packages animation data with supporting assets and features such as themes and state machines in a compressed container. A compatible player interprets that data at runtime. This means the deliverable can retain properties that a video would have already flattened into pixels, but the chosen file format and player must support the intended behavior. Lottie format guide

Saving a Creator project and exporting an animation are separate steps. The former retains editing data in the service; the latter produces an asset for use elsewhere. Creator documents several output formats, including Lottie JSON, dotLottie, and conventional video formats. Decide the destination early. A classroom video, a website illustration, and an interactive quiz control do not need the same deliverable. Creator export guide

Small vector animations are a natural fit when the visual meaning can be expressed with a few shapes, lines, and transitions. A book opening after lesson completion or a diagram revealing its next connection can be described economically. A screen full of photographic footage has different requirements. The right question is whether the representation matches the content, not whether an agent can be persuaded to produce something in the requested format.

Imported assets also need inspection. Creator’s import documentation describes editable SVG geometry, image layers, and imported Lottie compositions. It lists SVG limitations including unsupported filters and some blend modes, and recommends outlining text for that import route. A source illustration can therefore change during conversion even when the file loads successfully. Compare its settled appearance with the original before animating it. Creator import documentation

Keep the original artwork and the editable Creator project as well as the export. If a future player changes behavior or a new app theme requires revision, you will need more than the screenshot used to approve the first version. An asset handoff should identify its intended size, background assumptions, playback behavior, and source project. Those details prevent a small animation from becoming an unexplained dependency.

Give the agent a motion brief

The companion motion-design repository organizes guidance around timing, easing, choreography, and the intended character of movement. It is instruction material for agents, separate from the MCP operations themselves. The repository’s existence supports a useful distinction: tools provide editing capabilities, while a skill can guide the decisions made with them. Neither substitutes for reviewing the actual result. LottieFiles motion-design repository

Write a brief around a user event and a visible consequence. “When the learner submits a correct answer, briefly confirm the result and then settle” is more useful than “make an exciting success animation.” Specify whether the learner can immediately continue, whether a sound is appropriate, and what information remains visible after movement stops. The animation should support the task’s rhythm, not demand attention merely because it can move.

Provide a few concrete constraints: use the supplied icon, preserve its proportions, keep the background transparent, animate once, and finish in a recognizable still state. Name the editable values that matter, such as accent color or label text. Ask the assistant to explain its beat sequence before it builds a complicated scene. This makes the plan reviewable while changes are still cheap.

A useful revision names the problem and the desired effect. If a celebratory burst delays the next question, ask for a shorter confirmation that settles sooner. If a diagram feels confusing, specify which relationship must become visible first. Repeatedly asking for more polish can encourage extra effects without resolving the actual communication problem. Direction becomes easier when both you and the agent can refer to named layers and meaningful animation segments.

Review at the size the learner will see. A graceful shape on a large editor canvas can turn into a distracting flicker inside a small button. Conversely, a subtle cue that works close up may disappear on a classroom projector. Choose the destination size before judging line weight, text size, or movement distance. Keep a static fallback as part of the design brief rather than an afterthought.

Build feedback for a language exercise

A useful first project is a feedback asset for an English vocabulary exercise. Define three visual states: waiting for an answer, accepted answer, and invitation to retry. Give each state a distinct shape or label so that color is supplementary. Keep the actual question, answer controls, and explanatory feedback in the application’s normal interface. The animation should reinforce the result rather than become the sole carrier of it.

Start by designing the settled frame for each state. For example, the accepted state might show a check beside a closed book, while retry displays a small return arrow beside the same book. Only after these frames are clear should you animate the transitions. This prevents attractive motion from hiding weak state design. Ask the agent to use shared geometry where possible so that the states feel like one component.

Creator documents state machines as named playback configurations connected by transitions, inputs, and interactions. That is an appropriate foundation for branching feedback, although the application still needs to supply correct events and data. A visual state machine does not know whether a translation is correct unless your app tells it. Creator state-machine guide

Write down the event mapping before integration. Submitting an answer begins evaluation; a confirmed result chooses accepted or retry; advancing to the next question resets the component. Test repeated submissions and rapid navigation. If an old animation finishes after the learner has moved on, it must not display stale feedback for the new question. These are application behavior requirements, not promises supplied by the asset format.

Keep celebration proportional. A brief positive response can mark completion, while a long sequence after every answer can interrupt practice. Retry should feel informative rather than punitive: emphasize the opportunity to inspect a hint or reconsider a choice. You can ask the agent for two timing variants and compare them in the real exercise. Choose based on the learning flow, not on which isolated preview looks more impressive.

Turn a diagram into a controlled explanation

A second project is a three-step explanation of a web request. Prepare a simple approved diagram containing a browser, a server, and a returned result. Define what each connecting line means. A line representing a request should not accidentally suggest a permanent connection or simultaneous bidirectional traffic. The teacher supplies the conceptual model; the agent supplies controlled visual sequencing.

Import the diagram or build it from a few named shapes. Reveal the outgoing request, activate the server, then reveal the response. Hold the completed state for discussion. Provide a replay control and a next-step mode in the surrounding lesson interface. Learners should be able to inspect the relationship at their own pace instead of trying to catch a continuously looping explanation.

The same pattern works for a grammatical relationship. Highlight a noun, reveal the adjective that agrees with it, then show a short explanation beside the pair. Preserve the original sentence while adding emphasis. If the animation rearranges the words, make the purpose explicit; otherwise learners may confuse a visual grouping with a rule about required word order. Motion should clarify the analysis already approved by the teacher.

Use separate semantic segments for important beats. This allows the surrounding app to replay the difficult step or pause before revealing an answer. Even if the first version is a linear clip, a clearly segmented source scene makes later interactivity easier to reason about. Avoid placing essential explanations only in transient animated text; include a persistent written explanation nearby.

For evaluation, show the final diagram to someone who has not seen the prompt. Ask what the arrows mean and what happened first. If the answer differs from your intention, revise the diagram or sequence rather than merely slowing everything down. A useful animation earns its place by improving the explanation’s accuracy or readability.

Reuse one design without multiplying maintenance

Motion Tokens connect selected properties with runtime values through dotLottie’s slots system. The current documentation includes text, color, and transform properties, and describes themes as collections of token values. It distinguishes changing source defaults in Creator from temporary adjustments during playback. This provides a documented basis for reusable visual assets whose appearance can adapt to an app. Motion Tokens documentation

For a course family, define a restrained set of controls: accent color, lesson label, and perhaps progress. Keep timing fixed until you have a reason to vary it. If every parameter is exposed, the asset becomes difficult to test. A small, well-documented control surface lets an average coder understand what can change without reopening the entire scene.

Test the extremes of each allowed value. A short lesson label may fit while a longer translation clips. A pale theme may erase an outline that was clear on a dark background. A progress value of zero or one may reveal an awkward endpoint. The agent can help enumerate these cases, but inspect the rendered variants yourself. Parameterization increases reuse and expands the set of situations that require review.

A helpful handoff includes a tiny table in the project notes: control name, purpose, allowed range, and an example value. Explain which text is instructional content and which is decorative. Keep the app’s canonical data outside the animation so that an accidental visual edit cannot change the learner’s score or answer key. The animation should consume approved state, not become a hidden database.

Once a small asset works, reuse its visual vocabulary across a family of interactions. A consistent response to completion can help learners understand the interface. Consistency does not require every event to play the same flourish; it means related events share recognizable behavior and unrelated events are distinguishable. This is a design decision that an agent can implement after you establish the rule.

Finish in the application where it will run

LottieFiles supplies runtime packages for several web and mobile environments. Its React quickstart demonstrates a component accepting an animation source and playback options. That establishes a documented integration route, but the tutorial’s looping autoplay example is not automatically appropriate for educational feedback. Choose playback behavior to match your event model. Official player documentation Official React player quickstart

Test the exported artifact separately from the editor preview. Check the first frame, the key explanatory moment, the settled frame, and any loop boundary. Then test interaction: start, stop, replay, repeated activation, and navigation away from the component. An animation that looks correct when played once may behave poorly when a learner clicks twice or an asynchronous result arrives late.

Accessibility belongs to the application as well as the asset. W3C’s guidance on interaction-triggered animation explains why users need control over nonessential motion and discusses respecting reduced-motion preferences. A static result state can often preserve the feedback without the movement. This report does not claim that an agent’s visual inspection constitutes accessibility certification. W3C animation guidance

Keep keyboard operation and meaningful status text in ordinary interface elements. An animated checkmark should accompany an understandable result message; a diagram should have a textual explanation. If reduced motion is enabled, the lesson should remain complete. For an educational project, removing the movement is an excellent test of whether the underlying information has been represented clearly.

Measure performance in context. Several simultaneous assets, large embedded images, complex paths, and repeated state transitions can behave differently from one isolated preview. Test on a representative device with the rest of the lesson loaded. Record the exported file, player version, and any known limitations. This creates a more useful production record than a screenshot and a claim that the asset is ready.

For the first evaluation, include a content revision after the animation has been approved. Replace the label with a longer phrase and switch the theme. Ask the assistant to preserve timing and interaction behavior while making the new content fit. This tests whether the scene is organized for maintenance. If the change requires reconstructing unrelated layers, simplify the source before building a larger library. Keep the approved old export alongside the revised one and compare their behavior in the same app screen. A repeatable revision process is a stronger sign of usefulness than the quality of the first generated frame, particularly for lessons whose wording changes after classroom feedback.

A practical authoring route, with design still to do

The two saved mentions support a final score of nine: an eight-point underlying opportunity plus the catalogue’s repeat-mention increment. Current primary documentation makes this more actionable than a vague animation demo. There is a documented authoring connection, an editable scene model, reusable controls, and a route into application runtimes.

The best starting point is one small asset with one meaningful job: acknowledge an answer, reveal a relationship, or explain a short process. Approve its static states, direct the motion, test the export, and integrate it into a real lesson. Broader agent compatibility and attractive first drafts matter less than whether the resulting asset is understandable, revisable, accessible, and dependable when learners actually use it.

entries.title: Working with AI in plain language: recover the source, then study the feedback loop
entries.summary: A Karpathy repost reduces AI work to conversational delegation. A verified candidate recording and the creator’s own project accounts support a more useful method: provide context, inspect artifacts, make specific corrections, and define what an autonomous run must preserve.
entries.reason: Observing a practitioner’s actual process can clarify delegation, review and iteration better than slogans about prompting, but the video’s identity and fuller workflow must be established; its quoted note-taking article is not an extra bookmark.
entries.html:
The useful idea is a working loop, but the attribution needs care

Ricker’s June 10 bookmark shares a long video attributed to Andrej Karpathy and presents plain-language delegation as the essential skill: describe a task, inspect what comes back, and give a short correction. The expanded post then extends that idea to work that continues on a schedule with tools. This is the poster’s interpretation. It should not be treated as a verified quotation or a complete account of Karpathy’s development method.

The captured post does not name or link the original recording. A reply disputes its apparent recency, but that commenter’s suggested age is also not proof. A strong candidate is How I use LLMs, which Karpathy links from his own website. The original YouTube metadata verifies publication on February 27, 2025 and a duration of 2:11:12. The bookmark’s raw player capture shows 2:10:02. The inspected poster resembles a practical chat screencast, but the exact correspondence or editing between the two recordings was not established.

That distinction still leaves a productive route for the reader: use the verified original as a reference, treat the saved post as an invitation to study a process, and avoid calling it a newly released June 2026 interview. The quoted Kimi-and-Obsidian article belongs to the post’s surrounding material; it is not another independently saved bookmark here and does not establish the video’s provenance.

The verified reference is broader than a prompting slogan

The original video’s creator-supplied chapter list covers search, document uploads, code execution and plotting, interactive artifacts, a coding editor, and several forms of media interaction. Its structure therefore supports a broader reading than “say a sentence and stop thinking”: different tasks use different capabilities. The chapter description establishes those topics; it does not establish that every example is reliable today or that a short excerpt captures all the qualifications in the recording.

For an educator, the distinction between capabilities matters more than remembering where a button appeared in an older interface. A language model can draft an explanation; a search tool can retrieve a source; a program can calculate values; an editor can modify an exercise; a renderer can show whether the result fits. A useful brief chooses which of these outcomes is needed and supplies evidence that lets the result be judged. The following workflows are original applications of that idea, not reconstructed demonstrations from the video.

Plain language works best when it contains a real specification

There is no need to wrap an ordinary task in an elaborate fictional role. There is still a need to say what success means. “Make a Latin exercise” leaves the agent to guess the passage, learner level, allowed vocabulary, answer format, and feedback policy. Those are educational decisions, not stylistic decorations. A short brief can carry them clearly without becoming a magic formula or a lengthy instruction hierarchy.

An initial task might ask for a browser exercise using a supplied six-sentence passage, with one selectable verb per sentence and a teacher-approved answer key. It should explain whether macrons matter, whether learners may revise an answer, and what feedback appears after an attempt. Require the first version to work from the supplied content, with no account system and no generated replacement passage. That keeps the experiment small enough for the teacher to inspect completely.

Also describe the handoff: provide the working files, a concise explanation of how to open the exercise, and a list of any behavior that remains unfinished. A screenshot alone cannot satisfy an interactive brief. If the agent is unsure whether two grammatical analyses should be accepted, it should surface that uncertainty rather than quietly choose one. The teacher’s subject knowledge turns an open-ended request into a reviewable piece of work.

A conversational request and an agent run are different systems

Anthropic’s engineering account of effective agents distinguishes fixed workflows from systems where a model chooses its next actions and tools. It also emphasizes feedback from the environment and explicit stopping conditions. This is a useful technical correction to the bookmark’s scheduling claim: putting a request on a timer does not by itself supply tools, reliable state, error handling, or evidence that the task finished.

In the proposed exercise project, the model needs the passage and rubric as context, access to the project files, and a way to inspect the running result. A failed build or missing file should change its next action. If it can only produce prose in chat, it can still help plan and explain, but it has not executed the application. Conversely, a tool-enabled agent may create files while misunderstanding the pedagogical requirement. Execution and suitability require separate evidence.

Keep stable requirements in a small project document once repeated conversation starts obscuring them. Store the passage and answer key as explicit inputs, not as remembered details scattered through a long discussion. When the teacher changes a rule, update that document and identify the affected examples. This makes the next iteration easier to review and helps a different agent or colleague continue the work without guessing which earlier instruction still applies.

Turn corrections into observable changes

Suppose the first version marks an answer wrong immediately after a tap, even though the learner is supposed to select all verbs before submitting. “Make it less frustrating” communicates a concern but leaves the behavior open. A better correction names the event and outcome: selecting a word should only change its selected state; correctness feedback should appear after Submit; selecting again should undo the choice. The agent can implement that behavior, and the teacher can check it directly.

Then supply two contrasting cases. In one, a learner selects the correct verb and submits. In the other, they select a noun, change their mind, choose the verb, and submit. The final feedback should reflect the final selection. These examples reveal a state-management problem that a flattering description of the interface would miss. They also give the agent concrete failure evidence if the second path still behaves incorrectly.

Keep the next change narrow. Once selection works, ask for the explanation panel. Once the explanation is correct, inspect the smaller-screen layout and keyboard interaction. This is not a universal rule that every task must be divided into tiny steps. It is a practical response when the teacher needs to learn what the system is building while preserving a working version. Larger changes become sensible as the acceptance criteria and the project’s behavior become clearer.

A useful conversation ends each iteration with an artifact and a decision. Accept the change, request a specific correction, or discard it and return to the previous version. Do not keep generating alternatives merely because generation is easy. The retained version should have a reason for existing: it solves a known problem or enables a defined learning activity.

Inspect the outcome, including the answer key

Anthropic’s agent evaluation guide separates a run’s transcript from its final outcome and discusses code-based, model-based, and human assessment. For this classroom prototype, the practical lesson is simple: an agent’s statement that it tested the exercise is not the exercise. Open the output, reproduce the important learner paths, and inspect the content against the supplied key.

Some checks can be mechanical. Every sentence should have an identifier, every expected answer should refer to a word in that sentence, and submitting the same final selection should produce the same result in this fixed-content version. Other checks need a teacher: whether a hint gives away too much, whether the explanation is grammatically sound, and whether a reasonable alternate analysis deserves credit. A model-generated rubric does not remove that responsibility.

Include a deliberately difficult case in the source fixture rather than testing only the easiest sentence. If the exercise supports multiple correct answers, demonstrate that with a real example and an explicit rule. Keep a small set of accepted cases when revising the application. This is more informative than asking an agent to write many tests that merely repeat its implementation assumptions. The purpose is to preserve the intended learner experience through change.

Karpathy’s own project account includes the work beyond the prompt

His April 2025 MenuGen write-up is a valuable firsthand companion. He describes quickly obtaining a local interface for turning photographed menus into illustrative food images, then encountering outdated API knowledge, access configuration, rate limits, and deployment work. He also distinguishes the generated dish pictures from what a particular restaurant will actually serve. This is the creator’s retrospective account, not an independent reproduction, but it directly complicates the idea that conversational fluency is the whole skill.

The educational parallel is clear. A worksheet preview can arrive quickly while printing, accessibility, saved progress, and reliable content still need work. Keep the first prototype’s purpose explicit: it is a way to discover whether the exercise is useful. Before sharing it widely, examine the real delivery conditions. Does it open on the intended school device? Can a colleague update the text? Does it still make sense when the network is unavailable or a supporting service changes?

A hosted model is not needed for every finished artifact. If the teacher approves all sentences, hints, and answers in advance, the final exercise may run as an ordinary static application. The agent can help create it without becoming part of every learner interaction. This alternative reduces moving parts and makes the lesson easier to preserve. Add live AI only where it provides a specific benefit that fixed content cannot supply.

What changes when work continues without supervision

Karpathy’s April 2026 event summary adds more recent context about delegation and uneven model capabilities. Its provenance deserves notice: he explicitly labels the summary and cleaned transcript as AI-generated material that he read for obvious mistakes. It is useful author-published context, not a verbatim transcript. Its emphasis on maintaining correctness and human judgment fits a more demanding workflow than the bookmark’s casual account of adding tools and a schedule.

Imagine a weekly job that drafts a new exercise from an approved passage folder. It needs to know which passage has already been processed, where drafts belong, and what should happen when an input is missing. Repeating a successful run must not create duplicate lessons or overwrite a teacher’s corrections. The job should stop with a useful report when it cannot satisfy the content requirements. A recurring trigger solves timing; these rules solve the recurring task.

Begin with draft production and human review. Keep the approved source material separate from the generated output, and retain a record of the input version used. If an exercise is later corrected, preserve that correction as an explicit content rule or revised source file. This gives the teacher a manageable review queue and a way to trace a mistake. Sending material directly to learners is a separate product decision, not an automatic consequence of making the agent run repeatedly.

Use the reference as a working session

A productive viewing exercise is to bring one small task and classify what each relevant capability would contribute. Could the task be completed with supplied documents alone? Does it need current sources, calculation, an interactive output, or a code change? Write down the evidence that would distinguish a successful result from a persuasive one. Then attempt a single bounded artifact and keep the initial brief, the first result, and the correction that mattered most.

For an English lesson, that artifact might be a comparison activity using two teacher-provided paragraphs. Ask the agent to identify claims, propose questions, and produce a printable draft. Independently check each answer against the paragraphs. If it invents supporting facts, refine the instruction to distinguish text evidence from outside context and rerun the same example. The improvement is observable in the revised questions and answers, not in how sophisticated the new prompt sounds.

The score of seven reflects the value of observing and practicing a feedback loop, alongside the bookmark’s weak attribution and oversimplified framing. The verified reference and Karpathy’s project writing offer a stronger starting point than the repost alone. Plain language lowers the barrier to beginning; subject knowledge, explicit outcomes, tool feedback, and careful revision make the result usable. None of the proposed exercises or autonomous workflows was built or tested for this report.

entries.title: Tripo H3.1: high detail is the start of an asset pipeline
entries.summary: H3.1 documents dense geometry, PBR materials and several output controls. Its usefulness for teaching assets depends on validating the specific destination: a web model, an animation and a printable object require different evidence.
entries.reason: Reusable generated geometry could accelerate educational scenes and prototypes, but each output category has different requirements for manifold meshes, topology, materials and optimization.
entries.html:
Sharper assets still need an acceptance test

The saved June 10 post by Oliver Prompts argues that the familiar criticism of melted-looking AI models is becoming outdated. It presents Tripo HD Model 3.1 as producing detailed models with clean topology for printing, games and film, without manual modeling. That is a promotional claim about a demonstrated result. It does not establish that every generated object is anatomically correct, suitable for deformation or ready for a particular printer.

The useful development is more specific: a creator can obtain a detailed candidate asset from text or images and spend more time deciding whether it serves the project. For a teacher, that could mean a rotatable historical prop, an illustrative specimen or a character used in a narrated scene. The assessment must follow the intended use. A convincing object in a short turntable video faces different requirements from a mobile lesson, an articulated mechanism or a physical teaching aid.

What H3.1 documentation actually establishes

Tripo’s developer model page identifies the stable snapshot as v3.1-20260211. It documents text, single-image and multiview inputs, mesh and PBR output, and up to two million faces. Texture detail and geometry detail are separate settings; quad output forces FBX. The page also lists low-poly and part-generation options. Its generation times and quality rankings are vendor descriptions, not measurements reproduced here.

The official introduction positions H3.1 around close-up objects, dense geometry and material quality. Read “production-ready” as a proposed destination rather than a certification. Production requirements vary: a cinematic prop can tolerate far more geometry than a small browser interaction, while a printed object needs physical thickness rather than a convincing painted surface.

Before generating, write a short asset specification. Name the object’s purpose, necessary parts, viewing distance, size convention and delivery format. Decide which errors would invalidate the lesson. If a Roman lamp is merely atmospheric scenery, a stylized approximation may be acceptable. If students must identify its functional openings, those openings need to exist and be checked. That decision should precede the image request.

Geometry, texture and topology answer different questions

A mesh defines the object’s surface through vertices and faces. A texture supplies information distributed across that surface. A material determines how the surface responds to lighting. The Khronos material tutorial explains the metallic–roughness representation and distinguishes normal maps from denser geometry: normal maps can suggest fine surface detail without adding equivalent geometric complexity. A ridge that looks convincing under one light may therefore disappear in the silhouette or on a print.

Topology concerns how the faces connect. More faces do not automatically create good edge flow around a bending joint, and a quad option does not prove that shoulders, fingers or a mouth deform well. Similarly, a beautiful exterior does not establish meaningful internal parts. An exploded educational model requires separable components with correct relationships, not just arbitrary fragments obtained by dividing the mesh.

A useful inspection sequence is to rotate the object without its textures, view the wireframe, restore the material and change the light. Check the underside and the back as carefully as the front. For an image-derived object, compare visible features with the reference and mark unobserved surfaces as inferred. These are proposed checks; no H3.1 output was generated or inspected as part of this report.

Prepare a lightweight teaching asset

For a browser lesson, retain the detailed original and make a separate delivery copy. Blender’s Decimate documentation describes reducing face count while trying to preserve shape. Reduction is a tradeoff, so compare the result at the actual size and angle learners will use. A missing groove may be irrelevant in scenery but essential in a classification exercise.

Export a format the destination understands. Blender’s glTF documentation explains that a GLB can package geometry, textures and related information in one file. It also documents supported animation and material behavior, which is why a Blender scene should not be assumed to survive export unchanged. Open the exported file in the target viewer before building the surrounding lesson.

The official glTF Validator checks structural correctness and reports issues and asset statistics. It cannot tell whether a historical object is accurate or an interface is understandable. Use format validation for technical faults, visual review for appearance and domain review for the content. Keeping those responsibilities separate makes debugging easier: a valid file can still depict the wrong object.

A first deliverable could be one model with rotate, reset and three labeled viewpoints. Add explanatory text outside the canvas and a static-image alternative. This tests the value of the object without committing to a large application.

Printing requires an actual solid

A printed teaching aid exposes a different set of problems. Thin handles can break, floating details may need support, cavities can be inaccessible and an attractive surface may contain invalid geometry. Blender’s 3D Print Toolbox provides geometry analysis, volume and surface calculations, repair tools and export support. Such utilities help prepare a candidate; they do not establish that a specific material, printer and scale will succeed.

For a proposed relief-map activity, begin with a deliberately simplified form whose features are large enough to feel and discuss. State whether vertical dimensions are exaggerated. Inspect the geometry without color, since painted shading will not become physical relief automatically. Ask a knowledgeable reviewer to check the labels and relationships before spending time on final fabrication.

Tripo’s own bas-relief guide recommends geometry-focused output and mesh inspection, including checking non-manifold problems. That is a useful qualification to the saved post’s broad readiness claim. An automatic generation stage can be valuable even when validation and cleanup remain necessary. The relevant measure is time to a usable teaching object, including unsuccessful attempts and preparation, rather than time to the first attractive preview.

Proposed lesson: investigate an object through evidence

A strong classroom use would pair a generated reconstruction with its source image and a short evidence sheet. Choose an ordinary historical vessel, tool or architectural ornament whose main features can be verified. Learners rotate the reconstruction, identify its likely function and distinguish directly visible evidence from uncertain completion. This teaches both the subject and the limits of image-based inference.

The teacher prepares three viewpoints and five questions. Which opening connects to the interior? Which surface would contact the hand? What feature is hidden in the reference photograph? Which detail was added by the generator? What additional photograph would reduce uncertainty? Answers should be grounded in references, not judged solely by whether they match the generated mesh.

Keep the model illustrative unless its accuracy has been established. For a language lesson, use it to practice descriptions and spatial expressions without implying archaeological authority. For a narrated video, alternate the original image, the rotating object and a highlighted uncertainty. That sequence is more informative than presenting a seamless reconstruction as though a complete scan had been obtained.

If the lesson depends on exact dimensions, mechanisms or internal anatomy, use verified measurements, authored geometry or an authoritative scan. H3.1 can still help create surrounding props. Assigning it an appropriate role is more useful than requiring one generator to supply every kind of truth in the scene.

Keep educational meaning outside the mesh

For an annotated object, create a separate content file containing the part identifier, label, explanation, source and preferred camera view. Connect each entry to a named mesh component or a checked position. This makes it possible to correct a translation, improve an explanation or replace a model without rewriting the entire activity. It also prevents generated geometry names from becoming accidental educational terminology.

Consider a vessel with a handle, body, foot and opening. The viewer might highlight one region while a learner selects its function from three choices. The answer belongs to the reviewed content record. It should not be inferred afresh from the model’s appearance every time the learner clicks. If optimization changes the mesh, verify each label anchor again; a technically successful export can still move a hotspot onto the wrong surface.

For a video, the same content record can supply captions and a shot list. For a worksheet, it can supply a labeled still. This creates a reusable teaching asset whose explanatory value survives changes in renderer, platform or visual style.

Run a small comparison before scaling

Choose three representative assets: one rounded object, one object with thin structures and one object with multiple functional parts. Use consistent references and record the model snapshot, settings and output format. Judge the results against the same checklist: silhouette, missing parts, surface continuity, material behavior, editability and destination performance. This is a proposed pilot, not a benchmark conducted for the report.

Record repair time as well as generation time. If one output needs ten minutes of cleanup and another requires rebuilding a critical component, the previews alone conceal the difference. Keep failed candidates in the evaluation record rather than selecting only the most flattering result. A useful success rate describes how often the process produces an acceptable asset for your actual class of objects.

For close-up video, test the final camera distance and lighting. For a browser, test the full page on a representative device. For animation, test the most demanding pose rather than only an idle turntable. For printing, inspect the sliced layers and physical scale. These are different acceptance gates; passing one should not be used to claim success at the others.

Costs and alternatives depend on the destination

The developer page prices tasks through credits, with additions for choices such as geometry quality and topology. Avoid treating a headline subscription as the cost of a finished model. Your effective cost includes candidates you discard, optional processing and human review. Pin the model snapshot and record settings if you need to recreate the workflow later; a product name alone is insufficient provenance.

Tripo’s Smart Mesh introduction explicitly positions its low-poly approach as complementary to H3.1’s detailed assets. That is the relevant tradeoff for a simple web lesson: dense geometry may be unnecessary if the object appears small or must load quickly. The vendor’s speed claims should still be treated as claims, not guarantees for your own references.

A purchased or openly licensed model may be preferable when exact construction and predictable topology matter. Hand-built geometry can be quicker for a simple apparatus with a few known dimensions. For displaying one reviewed model, model-viewer offers a documented web component and examples, reducing the need to build a custom rendering interface. For a fully authored scene or animation, Blender remains a useful preparation and review environment. Choose the smallest workflow that satisfies the lesson.

Judgment: useful detail, conditional readiness

7/10. H3.1 is a relevant route to detailed candidate assets, especially for close-up explanations and visual prototypes. The saved post overcompresses the distance between a sharp preview and a model ready for every downstream use. Its practical value increases when generation is followed by geometry inspection, optimization and domain review. A small repeatable pilot should decide whether it saves time for your assets; no universal readiness claim can substitute for that evidence.

entries.title: The Fable iOS workflow: give the agent a running app to inspect
entries.summary: The three-prompt story contains a more useful lesson: build a functional journey, then inspect and refine it with runtime evidence. A teaching app also needs explicit learning, persistence and accessibility criteria.
entries.reason: A concrete native-app workflow can be useful for educational tools, but prompt count alone says little about correctness, accessibility, platform behavior or the amount of subsequent review.
entries.html:
The valuable part of the three-prompt story

Anshu’s saved June 10 article describes creating a native iOS calorie tracker with Claude Fable 5. The author reports a functional first version followed by focused visual refinement, using Claude Code and command-line access to Apple’s development tools. The account describes roughly four hours and several iterations, despite its three-prompt headline. Its strongest idea is to give the agent ways to inspect the running interface, including recorded transitions, rather than accepting its description of the code.

The article is a creator’s experience, not an independently reproduced evaluation. Its reported token use, plan consumption and brief human involvement describe that session. They should not become a budget forecast for another app. The author’s claimed Apple design background adds context to the critique, but the useful evidence is the concrete workflow: specify an experience, inspect the result and redirect attention toward visible defects.

For a teacher building a native learning app, the opportunity is substantial. A coding agent can shorten the path to something that runs on a phone, letting the teacher evaluate the actual interaction earlier. The responsibility that remains is to define what learners should accomplish and determine whether the product supports it across content, accessibility and failure states.

Separate the historical model from today’s choice

Anthropic’s original announcement dates Fable 5 to June 9, making the bookmarked article a launch-period account. The current Fable product page presents Fable 5.1 and describes its availability separately. A historical successful workflow can remain useful even when model versions, access terms and pricing have changed. The old article’s subscription arithmetic should therefore remain historical testimony.

Choosing a model is only one part of reproducing the method. The agent also needs access to project files, a compatible build environment, a way to observe the running app and a clear definition of completion. Better reasoning cannot compensate for a missing simulator or for an app that depends on a service the developer has not configured.

There is no need to reproduce every tool choice from the article. The linked idb project provides command-line automation for iOS simulators and devices. That establishes the role of the named tool, not that a particular installation will work unchanged on every current machine. This report inspected the account and documentation without installing tools, building an app or replaying its prompts.

What makes an agent’s visual loop useful

A productive loop contains an observable target, an action, a captured result and a decision. For example: open a vocabulary card, reveal its explanation, then return to the collection. The review asks whether the text remains readable, whether the card retains its identity during the transition and whether the learner knows where they have returned. A screenshot of the final screen answers only part of that question.

Recording the transition can reveal a momentary flash, a misplaced image or an animation that obscures the next action. However, recording alone is not a performance measurement. A smooth-looking clip does not establish responsiveness on an older phone, energy use during a long lesson or behavior when a network response arrives at an inconvenient moment. Those require their own observations.

The important improvement is to make criticism specific. Instead of asking for a more premium interface, identify that the explanation jumps after an image loads, that the answer button moves under the learner’s finger or that returning to the list loses the scroll position. Each observation has a corresponding behavior that can be checked after a change.

Also preserve an earlier working version. Visual refinement can accidentally alter navigation, persistence or focus. A series of attractive screenshots is not enough if the new version forgets the selected lesson. Treat the functional journey as a constraint throughout the design pass, rather than assuming it will survive automatically.

A proposed three-stage brief for a Latin reading app

A useful adaptation would be a small native app for reading a teacher-selected Latin passage with optional vocabulary help. This is a proposed workflow, not an application built during research. Start with one passage and a reviewed glossary. The learner should read, reveal a hint when needed, record a difficult word and return later without losing their place.

The first stage defines the product and its boundaries. Specify the passage, source attribution, supported devices and the difference between a hint and a translation. Decide whether progress stays on the device or must synchronize. A first version can avoid accounts if the teaching purpose does not require them. That decision removes an entire set of sign-in and recovery interactions from the initial experience.

An original brief might say: build one complete reading journey using the supplied text and glossary; preserve the current paragraph and saved words after reopening; show a hint without replacing the original sentence; provide clear empty and error states; describe what was actually checked. This is more actionable than asking for an award-winning app because it establishes the user’s work.

The second stage addresses the design after the reading journey exists. Ask for a quiet reading surface, a clear distinction between original text and assistance, and consistent vocabulary cards. Name the transitions that matter: entering a passage, opening a hint, saving a word and returning to the passage. Have the agent inspect those sequences, then report defects with the relevant screen and trigger.

The third stage broadens the review beyond the ideal demonstration. Use a longer passage, unusually long vocabulary entries and the largest intended text settings. Reopen the app after leaving it midway through a sentence. Check whether saved words remain associated with the right passage. If assistance uses a network model, simulate an unavailable response and keep the reading text usable.

These stages resemble the article’s separation of functional creation from aesthetic attention, but add explicit learning and persistence criteria. The number of prompts is incidental. A fourth prompt that resolves an important ambiguity is better than preserving a headline at the expense of the learner.

Native polish depends on a coherent data model

Apple’s SwiftUI model-data documentation describes views updating in response to their data dependencies. Its guidance on interface state distinguishes transient view state from persistent storage. This matters because a convincing visual prototype can still confuse what is currently selected with what must survive the app closing.

In the reading example, the currently expanded hint is temporary presentation state. A learner’s saved vocabulary and reading position have a different lifetime. The app should not infer that a word was learned merely because its hint was closed. Keeping those meanings distinct makes both the implementation and the teaching experience easier to reason about.

Ask the agent to explain the ownership of each important value in plain language. Where does the passage come from? What records the saved word? When is a change written? What happens if writing fails? A teacher with moderate coding experience does not need to inspect every framework detail to notice that the answers contradict the interface.

For an AI-assisted explanation feature, keep source text separate from generated commentary. A generated paraphrase should not silently overwrite the original lesson. Store or display enough provenance to distinguish teacher-approved content from an on-demand answer. This is an educational product decision as much as a software architecture decision.

A beautiful app must remain usable when its presentation changes

Apple’s accessibility guidance emphasizes adaptable text and usable controls. Its motion guidance calls for purposeful animation and alternatives when motion is unsuitable. These principles are particularly relevant when a prompt encourages custom transitions and visual effects: the strongest effect in a demo may be the least helpful part of a reading lesson.

For the proposed app, larger text should reorganize the layout without hiding the hint or save action. Meaning should not depend on a red or green tint alone. A screen reader should distinguish the original word, its grammatical information and the action that saves it. These are design criteria to investigate, not claims that the bookmarked app failed them.

Apple’s audit documentation explains automated accessibility checks and explicitly notes that passing them does not guarantee a fully accessible app. This is a useful parallel to agent self-review. Automated observations can identify specific defects, while representative user journeys reveal whether the interaction makes sense.

For a video companion app, include the transcript as a first-class reading experience. A learner may need to search a phrase, study without sound or revisit one explanation. The transcript should not be decorative text below an impressive player. Evaluate the transitions between watching and reading with the same care given to the main animation.

External services change the scope of completion

The original account includes generated imagery and an agent connected to outside data and tools. In an educational adaptation, each service introduces a separate question: what data is sent, what response is trusted, what it costs and what happens when it fails. A working interface is only the visible end of that chain.

Begin with reviewed sample content while the interaction is being designed. This makes it easier to distinguish a layout problem from a slow service or an incorrect generated explanation. Once the core journey is coherent, add the service behind a defined boundary and make its loading, cancellation and failure behavior visible.

Do not turn developer convenience into application credential design. A secret available to a terminal agent is not automatically appropriate to bundle into a mobile app. Ask where each credential lives in the finished system and what an ordinary app user can retrieve. Keep the review focused on the shipped artifact, not only the development environment.

Finally, make the completion report factual. It should name the build or revision, the flows inspected and the remaining gaps. A short video can document an observed journey; it should not imply that all devices, all content and every service failure were covered. This clarity helps a teacher decide whether the app is ready for a private trial or still needs development.

Before a classroom trial, let a colleague follow the intended journey without explaining the interface aloud. Give them the same passage and task a learner would receive. Note where they hesitate, whether they can recover from a wrong tap and whether the assistance reveals more than the exercise intends. This small usability review answers a different question from a successful build: can someone who did not write the prompt understand the product? Keep the observations tied to concrete moments so the next agent pass can address them without redesigning everything. A confusing label may need a few words changed, while a recurring navigation problem may justify a structural revision.

Keep the feedback loop, discard the prompt-count contest

This bookmark earns a score of seven because it offers a concrete and transferable method: separate functional construction from focused design refinement, and give the agent access to evidence from the running interface. The detailed saved article is more useful than its headline because it reveals iterations, tools and human steering.

For teaching applications, the method becomes stronger when the brief includes learning behavior, data ownership and accessibility alongside visual ambition. The next persuasive evidence would be a reproducible project with documented checks across devices and a longer period of real use. Until then, treat the account as a promising workflow demonstration whose value lies in earlier, better feedback rather than an assurance of effortless production software.

entries.title: Text-to-Lottie: inspectable animation files with an agent-friendly rendering harness
entries.summary: Diffusion Studio pairs routed animation instructions with a local Skottie player, editable controls, and source export. Its strongest value is a reviewable file-to-preview workflow, with renderer compatibility and asset packaging still requiring attention.
entries.reason: A reusable generation and verification harness could make small interface animations easier to produce and revise; its representation, validation rules and supported effects need repository-level review.
entries.html:
An animation workspace that an agent can inspect

Konstantin Paulus’s June 8 announcement introduces an open-source skill and harness for generating Lottie animations with coding agents such as Codex or Claude Code. The saved post presents the result as production-ready and points readers toward the Diffusion Studio repository. That label is a creator claim, but the repository makes the underlying approach inspectable: the agent authors animation data, a local player renders it, and the work can be revised through files and preview controls. Saved launch post

This is especially relevant if you already build educational websites in a code editor. Instead of moving the whole workflow into a hosted animation service, you can keep the source animation beside other project files. A small animated diagram, lesson introduction, or feedback icon becomes a versioned asset that a coding agent can revise. The value is the surrounding feedback loop, not merely the ability to emit syntactically valid JSON.

The repository README describes projects containing scenes, each backed by a Lottie file, with a player that loads and updates those scenes. It recommends grounding prompts in supplied SVGs, screenshots, or real data and explicitly requesting useful controls. Those are sensible authoring practices, although the repository’s examples are not independent evidence of reliability for every prompt. Project repository and README

Research here examined the current skill, reference documents, package manifest, scene-discovery plugin, loading and export code, and a text-slot test file. Nothing was installed or executed. This distinction matters: a readable implementation can establish how a feature is intended to work and expose likely edge cases, while only execution and visual inspection can establish that a particular generated animation works.

The skill and the player do different jobs

The main skill file is a routing layer. It directs an agent toward references for tasks such as typography, SVG animation, diagrams, charts, and interface feedback. It also specifies a workflow of choosing a target scene, writing animation data, and inspecting rendered frames. These instructions are project content being researched here, not instructions invoked to create an animation in this session. Main authoring skill

The application itself is a TypeScript and SolidJS project built with Vite. Its manifest includes CanvasKit WebAssembly and a script that copies the runtime asset during installation. This is a concrete local software dependency, not simply a collection of prose prompts. Someone evaluating the project should account for the workspace and browser preview as well as the agent skill. Package manifest

Skottie is Skia’s player for Lottie-style JSON animation. The project uses CanvasKit to bring that rendering foundation into the browser. Its small initialization module shares one CanvasKit instance between the main view and thumbnails, avoiding duplicate initialization in that path. This source detail supports the description of a real rendering harness, without proving any particular performance level on your device. Official Skottie documentation CanvasKit initialization

For an average coder, the pipeline is approachable: a brief becomes structured animation data; the player turns that data into visible frames; inspection reveals what needs changing; the agent edits the source again. The important discipline is to keep those stages separate. A good prompt does not guarantee good geometry, valid geometry does not guarantee good motion, and good motion in the development player does not guarantee identical behavior after deployment.

The player contract gives each scene a predictable folder containing its animation and optional controls, images, and fonts. It also supports an exact-frame URL parameter for paused inspection. That makes a review request precise: inspect the frame where the label appears, rather than hoping a screenshot catches the right instant during playback. Player contract

What the implementation adds beyond prompting

The scene plugin discovers project folders, recognizes animation and asset files, and reports project and playback context. It also writes edited animation data back to the scene file and distinguishes those writes from external source changes when refreshing the browser. This means the UI and the coding agent can both affect the same source of truth. Scene-discovery and editing plugin

That shared source creates a practical editing rule: reread the current file before changing it. If you adjust a color in the player and the agent then overwrites the scene from an older mental model, the manual improvement can disappear. Name the scene explicitly and keep meaningful revisions in version control. “Change the open animation” is less reliable than a request that identifies the project, scene, and desired property.

Images and fonts are loaded as assets alongside the scene. The loader’s comments and code distinguish image filenames from font resolution: fonts are associated with embedded family names used by the animation, not simply by the filename you chose. This is a useful explanation for a scene that loads but displays missing text. Renaming a font file alone is not necessarily a repair. Scene asset loader

The export function packages source animations, image assets, and fonts into a ZIP. It reads saved source files rather than the player’s transient in-memory state. It is therefore a source bundle, not evidence that a video has been rendered or that every destination player will work. Save edits before exporting and inspect the contents of the delivered archive. Source ZIP export implementation

One code-level edge case deserves attention. The export function places assets into shared image and font folders using their basenames. From that implementation, different scene assets with the same basename could overwrite one another in the archive map. This is an inference from source inspection, not a reproduced bug. Unique asset names and a quick archive review are sensible precautions when exporting a project with several scenes.

These details explain why the harness is more useful than a long prompt alone. It provides a stable place to put the work, a renderer to inspect it, controls for revision, and an export path. They also identify the maintenance responsibilities you inherit when adopting it: dependency versions, file organization, assets, and destination-player testing.

Learn enough JSON to diagnose ordinary failures

The project’s specification map describes the top-level dimensions, frame rate, layer list, and frame interval. It treats the out point as exclusive: an animation starting at zero and ending at ninety exposes frames zero through eighty-nine. Static and animated properties use different structures, and keyframes must be ordered. You do not need to memorize the whole format, but these concepts help distinguish a timing mistake from a missing object. Project Lottie specification map

Think in both frames and seconds. If you ask for a three-second explanation at thirty frames per second, the planned span is ninety frames. A two-second final hold consumes a substantial share of that span. Writing those requirements explicitly prevents the agent from spending almost all the duration on entrances and leaving no time to read the explanation. For an instructional animation, the hold is part of the content.

Layers should represent meaningful components: the diagram’s source, destination, connecting path, and explanation. Avoid splitting everything into anonymous fragments unless the effect requires it. A later request to change the destination label should be a local edit. Naming and grouping are therefore practical usability features for both the human and the agent.

SVG conversion deserves its own review. The repository’s compatibility reference discusses styling, transforms, compound paths, masks, and differing renderer behavior. It recommends comparing the settled result with the source. A logo whose internal hole fills incorrectly or a diagram whose arrowhead disappears is not a harmless stylistic variation; it may change the meaning of the asset. SVG compatibility reference

Text needs similar care. The project includes tests aimed at preserving Unicode text while changing slot values and keeping text in both its editable slot and fallback representation. That is useful evidence that multilingual editing has received explicit attention. It does not prove correct rendering for every script, font, shaping requirement, or line-breaking case. Test the actual words and fonts your lesson uses. Unicode text-slot tests

A practical first project: explain a request

For a first educational asset, use a simple diagram showing a browser sending a request to a server and receiving a response. Supply an approved SVG or a precise layout sketch. Define the concept being taught and the meaning of each arrow. Ask for a transparent animation that fits beside lesson text, with a short initial pause, one outgoing trace, one response trace, and a stable final frame.

The repository’s technical-diagram recipe emphasizes reading order, useful nodes, and a clear meaning for connecting lines. That aligns with the task, but you should still provide the actual conceptual model. A generic network diagram can look plausible while implying the wrong dependency or sequence. The agent should animate the teacher’s approved explanation. Technical-diagram recipe

Build the final still first. Place the browser and server labels, establish the arrow directions, and verify that the diagram reads at its intended website size. Then add the temporal sequence. If the diagram is unclear while paused, motion is unlikely to rescue it. Conversely, a strong final still gives the learner something useful to inspect after playback finishes.

Ask for named controls only where they help reuse: an accent color and perhaps the two endpoint labels. Keep the source terminology fixed for the first lesson. A broad “make everything editable” request can create a panel full of controls whose interactions are difficult to test. The best control surface is small enough that another teacher can understand it without opening the animation data.

Review frames at the start, each arrow’s arrival, and the final hold. Then watch the whole motion. A still inspection can reveal clipped text but miss an abrupt acceleration or an awkward pause. Check whether the server appears to act before the request arrives; that timing error would undermine the explanation even if every individual frame were attractive.

Finally, place the exported animation beside the actual lesson copy. Add a replay control and a written description of the sequence. Ask a learner to explain what happened. If the response is inaccurate, revise the labels or causal order before adding polish. This proposed workflow uses the harness as an instructional authoring tool, not as a substitute for subject review.

A reusable language-learning illustration

A second project can teach how a word changes through a suffix. Prepare a short approved set of examples and choose one transformation for the animation. Keep the stem stationary, reveal the suffix, and show the resulting word with a concise explanation. A fixed stem makes the relationship visible; arbitrary movement of every letter would make the learner reconstruct it.

Decide whether editable text or outlined shapes matter more for this asset. Editable text is useful when the teacher will swap examples. Outlines can support deliberate path effects but make ordinary wording changes less convenient. Do not choose a handwriting effect merely because the tool can produce it. The animation should direct attention toward the linguistic transformation.

For a multilingual version, include the longest likely label, accented characters, and punctuation in the review set. Keep a record of which font asset is required. The player contract explains that paragraph-style text can wrap, but its box height does not act as a clipping boundary in the described implementation. A longer replacement can therefore extend downward even when the nominal box dimensions look reasonable. Player contract

Use a small content table outside the animation as the reviewed source: stem, suffix, result, explanation, and language. Let the agent create one scene per approved example, then compare them as a set. This makes inconsistencies easier to spot. If one scene needs a smaller font or a longer hold, record that exception rather than silently changing the style everywhere.

The exercise can have two exports: a demonstration showing the completed word and a question version that stops before revealing it. This is an original application idea, not a built-in exercise generator. The surrounding learning app remains responsible for answer handling and feedback. The animation’s role is to present the relationship clearly and consistently.

Use real numbers without inventing a story

The repository includes a recipe for data and statistics graphics. Its presence makes charts a supported authoring intention, but a chart’s educational correctness depends on the supplied data and visual mapping. Provide the actual values, units, labels, and source notes. Ask the agent to describe how each value determines a visible property before rendering a complicated animation. Data and statistics recipe

A good exercise compares two distributions of quiz responses. Use synthetic data for the first prototype and label it as such. Keep axes and scales stable while the two sets appear. Do not animate one set on a different scale merely to make it fill the canvas. The final frame should support a fair comparison, and the learner should be able to pause and inspect exact values.

Separate data changes from presentation changes. If a count increases, update the number and the geometry from the same reviewed record. If the color changes, the count should remain untouched. Ask the agent to explain which fields it changed. This is a small but important habit when a code-oriented workflow makes it easy to regenerate an entire file.

Review extremes before producing a batch: zero values, equal values, long category names, and a value larger than expected. These cases reveal whether the template is robust or merely flattering to the first dataset. A useful chart animation should preserve the relationship under ordinary variation, not just produce an appealing screenshot for one carefully chosen example.

Production readiness is a sequence of checks

The repository’s verification instructions require JSON validation and inspection in its designated Skottie player. They also call for checking motion rather than stopping after a clean render. This is a strong workflow expectation, but it remains an instruction to the agent. Reading it does not establish that an agent followed it or that the reviewed revision passed. Main authoring skill

Use four separate review questions. Does the file parse? Do all intended elements render? Does the motion communicate the intended sequence? Does the exported asset work in the destination application? Keep the answers distinct in the handoff. “Valid JSON” answers only the first question; “preview looks correct” still leaves deployment behavior unresolved.

Destination testing matters because Lottie has multiple players and renderers. The lottie-web project, for example, documents its own web playback interface and renderer options. If your app uses that player while the authoring harness uses Skottie, test the same artifact there. Do not assume that support in one renderer implies identical masks, text, gradients, or effects in another. lottie-web repository

For educational sites, also provide a useful nonmoving state and respect motion preferences. W3C guidance explains the need to let users avoid nonessential interaction-triggered movement. The app should remain understandable when the animation is reduced or skipped. A diagram can retain its final labels, and a result icon can appear immediately with accompanying text. W3C motion accessibility guidance

Keep the development workspace distinct from the public deployment. The inspected harness includes local authoring endpoints that create, edit, and delete scene files. It is an editing environment with filesystem responsibilities, not automatically a public multiuser animation service. A teacher generally needs to deploy the finished asset and player integration, not expose the authoring workspace to learners.

A concise delivery note should identify the scene folder, the reviewed animation file, required image and font assets, intended dimensions, playback mode, and destination player. Include the frame numbers used to approve important visual states. If the agent only inspected a local preview, say so. If another person later changes a label, they can then repeat the relevant review without reconstructing the whole conversation.

For a small course library, keep one approved example of each pattern and a deliberately difficult input beside it. A diagram with long labels or a word exercise containing unfamiliar characters is useful maintenance evidence. After updating dependencies or the authoring skill, revisit those examples before regenerating every lesson. This converts an attractive experiment into a manageable collection of assets with known expectations and a modest review burden.

The score of eight reflects the practical combination of open source, a concrete rendering harness, editable values, and agent-oriented review instructions. The best initial use is a small, sourced educational diagram or reusable language illustration. Judge it by how well you can inspect, revise, and deploy the result. The repository offers a credible process to evaluate; production quality remains something the individual artifact must earn.
