entries.title: GPT-5.5 creative builds: turning a launch gallery into bounded projects
entries.summary: A launch roundup connects 3D games, miniature worlds, robot descriptions and generated game media. Its useful lessons are about project structure and asset integration, while its model comparisons remain anecdotes.
entries.reason: Source-linked demonstrations can offer useful project ideas, while curation alone does not establish reproducibility or the cost of building comparable work.
entries.html:
A launch gallery with several different lessons

Min Choi’s April 24 collection is a curated showcase of projects attributed to GPT-5.5 near its launch. The opening example is a Seinfeld-apartment beat ’em up, credited to BijanBowen and described as made through Codex including its 3D assets. The expanded accessible conversation contains numbered entries one through six of the advertised ten. This report examines those visible examples; it does not invent the missing four or treat the collection as a complete survey.

The gallery is useful because its examples cross several boundaries: a familiar room becomes a playable space, a mechanical concept becomes structured robot data, a railway becomes an animated miniature world, and generated media becomes a game asset pipeline. For a teacher or builder, those are more transferable ideas than the accompanying declarations of a model being extraordinary.

The evidence is still a set of creator-selected demonstrations. Complete source projects, prompts, model settings, costs and comparable repeated trials were not available in the captured thread. A successful recording establishes less than a project that another person can download, run and modify. The report therefore separates reported accomplishments from documented technology and from proposed educational adaptations.

What the accessible examples actually say

The captured robot example quotes Jake Fitzgerald describing a seven-degree-of-freedom arm with functional kinematics, a custom interface and STEP parts/assembly produced in Codex, except for the gripper. That exception matters: the claim is not that every component was generated. His estimate that comparable work would previously have taken weeks is personal experience, not a controlled productivity measurement. No manufactured or experimentally validated robot is established by this post.

The toy railway example quotes Peter Gostev’s London miniature railway with landmarks and seasonal variation. He reports obtaining an excellent result from one complex prompt and refers to a comparison with GPT-5.4. The captured quotation ends before that comparison is complete, so it cannot support a precise judgment about either result. It does suggest a useful project form: a compact spatial scene that can express several states without becoming a full open-world game.

The fourth entry is an AGI reaction, a short opinion from Kitze. It offers no operational definition or evaluation of general intelligence. The battle-app example similarly contains strong comparative language: Max Blade reports a Pokémon-style battle app from one prompt and claims frequent failures from a competing model. Without matched prompts, settings, retries and test conditions, those statements should remain attributed reactions.

The most instructive breakdown is the multi-tool game example. Chong-U assigns code to GPT-5.5, sprites and backgrounds to an image model, walk cycles to Seedance, music and effects to ElevenLabs, and the playable runtime to Phaser 4. The curator writes “Phase 4,” while the quoted creator names Phaser. This is a coordinated media-and-code workflow, not evidence that one text model directly generated every finished medium.

The model and the surrounding tools have different roles

The official GPT-5.5 model reference identifies the April 23, 2026 snapshot and distinguishes text/image inputs from text output, alongside supported tools. That makes the gallery’s combination of code generation and external media production technically understandable. A coding model can write scene descriptions, asset-processing scripts and application logic; a tool-enabled environment can then execute those operations. The finished visual result depends on the whole system, including libraries, assets and human choices.

There is also a current-status change. The official retirement notice says GPT-5.5 retired from Codex for ChatGPT-signed-in users on October 14, 2026; OpenAI API use and Codex sessions authenticated with an API key were not affected. Thus this April collection is a historical demonstration set, not an instruction to expect the same model in every current Codex account. Its project patterns remain useful without assuming identical access or output.

When adapting a gallery example, describe the desired artifact and acceptance conditions first. A model name alone says little about whether the result includes editable source, working controls, an exportable scene or only an attractive recording. Preserve the build configuration and asset provenance so the project can be revised after the original model or service changes.

Turn a miniature environment into a lesson

A practical adaptation of the apartment and railway ideas is a compact language-learning town: a station, bridge, library and market arranged around one route. The learner follows directions, chooses a destination and explains the route in sequence. Begin with a simple plan and four approved location names. The instructional challenge is spatial language, so the buildings should be distinguishable and their placement stable.

Three.js’ scene-graph tutorial explains how objects occupy local coordinate spaces in a hierarchy. That helps organize a scene: a train’s wheels and windows can move with the train, while station signs remain attached to the station. Hierarchical transforms organize motion; they do not simulate transport physics. A miniature train following a curve can be an excellent illustration while remaining an intentionally simplified animation.

Ask the assistant to build the route and interaction with plain shapes before adding distinctive architecture. Confirm that the train stops at the chosen station and that reset restores the initial state. Then replace shapes with reviewed assets. This order gives every artistic addition an existing function and prevents a visually elaborate scene from concealing a missing learning interaction.

Seasonal changes can support a second exercise: compare the same location in summer and winter, identify what changed, or narrate a journey in different weather. Keep the route and labels fixed while changing selected scenery. Otherwise students may confuse a change in the scene’s layout with the concept being taught. An optional split view is useful only if the comparison remains readable on the target screen.

For video, turn the same scene into a short narrated route demonstration. Use three planned shots rather than unrestricted camera movement: an overview, a close view at the decision point and the arrival. Match each shot to a sentence. A reusable scene lets the teacher change the language difficulty without regenerating the geography each time.

From generated media to a functioning exercise

Phaser’s official version comparison confirms that Phaser 4 launched in April 2026 and describes its changed renderer alongside continuity in ordinary game concepts. The important point for this bookmark is its role as an interactive framework. It supplies the runtime in which sprites, input, scenes and rules become a playable application. Generating attractive images and audio does not by itself produce that behavior.

Phaser’s scene documentation distinguishes loading assets, constructing scene objects and updating the scene over time. Those boundaries give a coding assistant a manageable structure. In a vocabulary game, a loading stage prepares images and sounds; a question scene presents the task; a result state explains the answer. The learner should be able to retry without reloading every asset or losing the sound preference.

Phaser’s animation guide explains sprite animation as a sequence of frames with timing and repetition. A generated walk-cycle video still needs a usable set of frames, consistent scale and a clean loop for this form of game. Inspect whether the character’s outline changes unexpectedly or drifts within its frame. A technically playable loop can remain visually distracting enough to weaken the lesson.

For a first build, propose one room, one character, one exercise and one success condition. Use original characters and setting rather than depending on recognizable entertainment franchises. Keep answer checking separate from animation: the same correct response should count whether a frame is late or sound is muted. Add a replay button and text feedback so audio and motion reinforce the explanation without becoming the only way to receive it.

A robot model can teach geometry before it becomes hardware

ROS’ movable-robot example shows the underlying structure of a movable robot description: links are connected by joints, with local origins, axes and limits. This gives a precise meaning to an editable robot model beyond its rendered appearance. It also explains why a GUI with joint sliders can be useful: each control changes a parameter in a structured kinematic chain.

An appropriate educational adaptation is a virtual two-link arm. Let learners change two angles and predict where the endpoint will move. Show the local axes and trace the endpoint path. Only after this is understandable should the scene add more joints. A seven-joint example is impressive, but a smaller model makes the relationship between angle, position and coordinate frame much easier to inspect.

Keep the claim proportional to the evidence. A kinematic model describes permitted movement and geometry; a rendered arm reaching a target does not establish actuator sizing, structural strength, collision safety or manufacturing suitability. STEP output can be a useful CAD handoff without proving that the assembly works physically. The bookmark supports interest in generating structured artifacts, not a shortcut from a chat prompt to validated hardware.

A better way to judge your own attempt

Before starting, choose three observable requirements and one maintenance task. For the town scene, the requirements might be correct route selection, reliable reset and legible labels on a phone. The maintenance task could be adding a fifth destination without changing existing answers. This checks whether the generated project is useful to its owner, rather than merely capable of producing a convincing clip once.

An original brief for the railway adaptation could be: “Create a small teaching scene with a station, market, bridge and library. The learner chooses a destination from a spoken or written instruction. Make the train follow the selected route, stop clearly and show an explanation of the answer. Provide a reset action and keep all lesson text editable in one content file. Use simple placeholder buildings first, and deliver the source project with a short guide for adding another destination.” This communicates a concrete result without prescribing every rendering decision.

Set the visual budget around the learning goal. A readable miniature may need only simple shapes, a few textures and one moving train. Reflections, dense vegetation and cinematic weather should earn their place by improving orientation or comparison. If the scene struggles on the intended device, a fixed-camera version or a sequence of still images can preserve the same exercise. Evaluate that fallback as part of the design rather than assuming more dimensional detail always improves the lesson.

Record the first working version and subsequent interventions. Count the time spent choosing assets, correcting content, fixing build problems and checking the final result. If comparing models, use the same starting project and acceptance criteria, retain failed attempts and distinguish human repair from autonomous work. A single successful prompt can be a valid anecdote while remaining a poor estimate of expected success.

Test boring paths as well as the demonstration path: loading twice, restarting after a wrong answer, resizing the window, muting sound and selecting options quickly. Ask someone unfamiliar with the project to complete the exercise from its opening screen. Their confusion may expose missing instructions that a creator, already familiar with the intended interaction, does not notice.

Existing templates, a hand-built SVG exercise, a conventional Phaser starter or a small Three.js scene may be better starting points than recreating an entire viral example. The collection earns 7/10 for the breadth of concrete project ideas and the visible combination of coding with media tools. Its value is inspiration and transferable structure; independent reproducibility, cost and comparative model quality remain unresolved.

entries.title: Production readiness for AI-built apps: workload, durable work and recovery
entries.summary: A viral 25-point checklist highlights real operational risks but supplies no evidence for a universal 500-user breaking point. A classroom app provides a more useful way to evaluate state, slow jobs, releases, observation and recovery.
entries.reason: Production reliability is central to useful AI-centered development; concrete workloads and failure recovery matter more than an arbitrary user-count threshold.
entries.html:
What the 500-user warning gets right

Harshil Tomar’s April 25 bookmark presents 25 production failure modes for applications built with AI, spanning state, storage, databases, external services, deployment and recovery. Its headline predicts failure at 500 users. The expanded post is a practitioner’s checklist, followed by promotion of the author’s development business; it supplies no benchmark establishing that threshold.

The valuable observation is that a convincing demonstration leaves many operational questions unanswered. An exercise can work for its creator while losing an answer during a deployment. A video tool can generate one successful clip while accumulating jobs faster than it can finish them. These are failures of service design that attractive screens cannot reveal.

For a teacher building educational software, readiness means making a narrower, testable promise. A learner’s saved work survives an ordinary interruption. The teacher can tell whether submissions are complete. Optional AI assistance can slow down without preventing the lesson. Someone knows how to recover when those promises fail. This report develops those objectives through proposed workflows; no application was deployed or load-tested for the research.

The post merits attention without treating every recommended component as mandatory. Adding a replica, queue or distributed service creates another operational responsibility. The first architectural question is what the application must preserve and how its users actually behave.

Model a school day before counting accounts

Consider a proposed Latin practice app with 500 registered learners. On an ordinary afternoon, only a few might read exercises at once. At the start of a lesson, 30 learners could open the same assignment within seconds. Near a deadline, several classes might submit audio while a teacher exports results. These workloads differ in request rate, payload size, processing time and contention even though the account total is unchanged.

Write three short journeys: open and answer a quiz; upload a recording; review and export a class. For each, name the operations behind the screen. Opening a quiz might retrieve instructions and vocabulary. Submitting might write an attempt, update completion and request feedback. This inventory reveals whether a single click causes one cheap operation or many expensive ones.

Grafana’s k6 guidance distinguishes smoke, average-load, stress, soak, spike and breakpoint testing. These categories answer different questions: basic execution, expected demand, excess demand, sustained operation, abrupt bursts and eventual limits. Passing one does not establish the others.

For the proposed app, begin with a small rehearsal that checks correctness, then simulate the lesson-start burst and deadline uploads separately. A longer session could expose rising memory use or an accumulating queue. Use synthetic accounts and representative data volumes. Keep expensive generation mocked during initial infrastructure checks, then run a separately bounded end-to-end rehearsal if authorized. A mock can establish request handling but cannot establish provider latency or real generation cost.

Choose acceptance criteria before inspecting results. For example, every acknowledged submission should remain present after restart, and slow feedback should show a recoverable status. Numerical latency targets should reflect classroom tolerance and measured conditions. Record the environment, workload and exclusions alongside any result so that a successful rehearsal does not turn into an unsupported universal capacity claim.

Decide what must survive a process disappearing

The Twelve-Factor processes guidance separates disposable application processes from persistent state held in backing services. Memory and local files can support temporary work, but subsequent requests must not assume that the same process or its contents will still exist. This is relevant to restarts as well as multiple instances.

In the classroom example, distinguish a session identifier, an unfinished answer, a submitted answer and a generated hint. They have different lifetimes. A disposable hint cache may be acceptable; a submission existing only in server memory is not. The relevant design document can be a small table naming each item, its authoritative location, when it expires and what happens after interruption.

Server-side sessions are not inherently wrong. The problem is depending on one process’s private memory when requests can reach another process or the original process can restart. A shared session store or another appropriate session design can solve that problem. Conversely, adding a shared store without defining expiry, revocation and failure behavior leaves important decisions unresolved.

For live classroom interactions, treat a WebSocket connection as a delivery mechanism rather than the sole record of learning progress. A proposed reconnection flow would retrieve the current question and acknowledged answer state after reconnecting. Horizontal scaling does not automatically disconnect every user, but coordination, routing and recovery need deliberate design. A periodic refresh may be sufficient for a teacher’s progress dashboard and substantially easier to operate than a live collaboration system.

Protect meaning before chasing database scale

A single database can be entirely appropriate for a modest application. The bookmark’s universal read-replica prescription is unsupported by a measured workload. Before changing topology, inspect which operations are slow, how many connections they consume and whether the application requests unnecessary data. A replica will not repair an incorrect query or an inconsistent write workflow.

PostgreSQL’s indexing documentation explains the tradeoff: indexes can accelerate retrieval while adding overhead to the database. An absent foreign-key index does not mean every join necessarily becomes a full scan. The useful question is whether the important query has an appropriate plan at realistic data volumes.

Imagine a results page that loads every historical answer to display one class’s current completion count. Start by specifying the required result and inspecting the generated query. Filtering, aggregation and pagination may remove unnecessary work. Then evaluate indexes against the actual access pattern. Do not let an agent add indexes to every column simply because a checklist mentions performance.

The post also connects unparameterized search with slow responses. OWASP’s guidance on parameterized queries concerns separating SQL instructions from supplied values to prevent injection. That protection does not guarantee efficient search. A safe query can still scan excessive data; a fast query can still be unsafe. Review these properties separately.

PostgreSQL transactions provide an all-or-nothing boundary for related database operations. In the proposed quiz, recording an attempt and marking its completion should not leave a misleading half-finished result. Define the invariant in classroom terms: an assignment cannot appear completed unless the accepted answer exists. Ask the agent to identify the database operation that enforces it, then design a failure case between the relevant steps. External emails or model calls require additional coordination; a database transaction alone cannot undo an already delivered message.

Give slow work an explicit life cycle

A queue is useful when the user should not wait for a long task to finish, but it does not make the task disappear. Someone must define acceptance, ownership, retries, cancellation and completion. For a video-assignment tool, a proposed sequence is upload accepted, processing pending, transcription running, transcript ready and teacher reviewed. Each state should correspond to something observable.

The learner should receive a durable submission reference before seeing a reassuring success message. If processing later fails, the recording should remain available and the interface should explain that feedback is delayed. The teacher needs a distinction between missing student work and work awaiting processing. Without it, an infrastructure problem can become an unfair classroom judgment.

Separate urgent work from expensive optional work. Saving an answer belongs on the immediate path; generating a polished explanation can happen afterward. A receipt email can usually follow the saved event rather than determine whether the submission succeeds. A trivial application may need no separate queue initially, while a tool handling long media jobs likely needs a durable background-work mechanism. The decision follows the operation’s duration and consequences.

Plan for the same job being attempted again. Give the underlying submission a stable identity and make repeated processing preserve one authoritative result, or explicitly version alternatives. Specify what happens if a worker finishes the model call but crashes before recording completion. Blindly rerunning may incur cost twice. A queue dashboard showing an empty backlog also does not prove the results are correct; reconcile completed jobs with the submissions they were meant to serve.

Make dependency failure a product behavior

AWS’s Builders’ Library discussion explains why remote calls need considered timeouts and why retries can amplify failure. Backoff and jitter spread repeated attempts; operations with side effects need care because a timeout does not prove nothing happened. It also discusses the complexity introduced by circuit breakers, rather than treating them as universally required.

For AI feedback, define the fallback before selecting a mechanism. If the model is unavailable, the learner could still submit, see the teacher’s fixed rubric and return later for optional suggestions. Do not silently substitute a fabricated score. For a video generator, preserve the script and existing assets while marking the render as delayed. These choices maintain useful activity during an outage.

A retry budget should belong to the whole user operation. If the browser, application and worker all retry independently, one click may multiply into many provider calls. Google’s discussion of overload describes how retries and excess work can worsen an already stressed service. For the proposed app, reject or defer new optional jobs before sacrificing answer saving.

Specify what users can do while waiting. A disabled button with no explanation invites reloads and repeated submissions. A visible pending state with a stable reference provides a better recovery route. If a retry is safe, say so; if the system is checking whether work already completed, preserve that uncertainty. Reliability includes honest interface states, not just a server returning a response code.

Treat large files as a separate workload

Video and audio change the economics of a small app. A few simultaneous uploads can dominate bandwidth and storage while ordinary quiz requests remain cheap. A proposed media workflow should set explicit duration, size and format limits, show progress, and distinguish transfer completion from successful processing. An interrupted upload must not become a blank assignment marked complete.

Amazon S3’s presigned-upload documentation provides one concrete architecture: a client can upload using a URL authorized by the signer’s permissions without receiving that signer’s AWS credentials. Reusing an existing object key replaces that object, which makes naming and ownership decisions material. Other storage services offer different mechanisms; this is an example, not a required vendor choice.

For the classroom scenario, the application would authorize a specific submission, allocate an object reference, and confirm that processing is allowed only after the expected upload is present. The record connecting learner, assignment and object matters as much as the bytes. A successful storage upload with no matching submission record still produces an operational problem.

For public lesson images, caching and appropriate compression may reduce repeat transfers. The actual saving depends on the content, representation and cache behavior; the post’s fixed compression multiplier should not become a forecast. Private submissions require access controls compatible with any delivery cache. A simple static resource site and a student video portal should therefore receive different storage and delivery designs, despite sharing the same frontend framework.

Design deployment as a normal event

A release should not depend on every user being absent. The Twelve-Factor disposability guidance describes stopping new work, allowing requests to finish and handling worker termination so that jobs can recover. The general objective is a controlled transition, with resilience to unexpected termination as well.

For the proposed quiz app, rehearse a release while an answer is being saved and while feedback remains queued. Inspect the user-visible result and the stored record afterward. A disappearing spinner is insufficient evidence. The submission should either have a confirmed durable result or an explicit retry path that cannot duplicate the logical submission.

Database changes require their own release plan. Running a migration automatically at startup can be safe only if the actual migration system and deployment arrangement coordinate it correctly; merely placing the command in each instance is not a plan. Identify who runs it, how simultaneous execution is prevented, and which old and new application versions can use the resulting schema.

Kubernetes documentation distinguishes startup, liveness and readiness checks. Readiness concerns accepting traffic; liveness can trigger restart. It explicitly warns that poor liveness checks can cause cascading failures. This distinction is useful even when using a managed platform rather than Kubernetes. A temporarily unavailable AI provider should not automatically make every otherwise useful application instance restart.

Keep rollback practical. Restoring yesterday’s code may not undo a destructive data transformation. Prefer a release sequence that keeps existing records readable during transition, and document irreversible steps before execution. For a teacher’s tool, scheduling a risky migration outside lesson hours remains a sensible additional safeguard, even when the technical deployment process is robust.

Observe the promise users rely on

Google’s monitoring guidance identifies latency, traffic, errors and saturation as core service signals, while explaining why averages can conceal poor experiences. It also distinguishes useful alerts from noisy measurements. These ideas can guide a small application without recreating a large operations department.

For the classroom app, track successful submission acknowledgments, failed saves, pending feedback age and upload failures. Add a way to connect a user-visible reference to the relevant application events. Avoid recording full student responses merely to make logs convenient. A diagnostic trail can often use operation identifiers, timings and error categories instead.

Separate a fast failure from successful performance. A response that quickly displays an error is not an acceptable quiz submission. Similarly, a dashboard can remain responsive while every background job is stuck. Measure both the interactive request and the eventual outcome. A teacher waiting for transcripts needs the oldest pending job’s age more than an attractive average API response time.

Alerts should point to an action that the responsible person can take. Repeated submission failures during a teaching session deserve prompt attention. A brief delay in optional thumbnail generation may belong in a dashboard. Decide who receives notifications and when they are expected to respond. A solo teacher should design a service that degrades usefully outside those hours rather than imply continuous support that does not exist.

Prove that recovery restores a usable application

PostgreSQL’s backup documentation describes several backup approaches, including dumps, filesystem backups and continuous archiving. The relevant choice depends on the database arrangement and recovery needs. A backup indicator alone says little about whether the application can resume its intended work.

Write a proposed recovery exercise around a concrete event: an accidental deletion of one class’s assignment records. Restore into an isolated environment, inspect the assignment, attempt and feedback relationships, and check that associated media remains reachable. Record how much recent work is missing and how long the exercise takes. These observations establish the practical recovery gap without pretending it is zero.

Recovery also needs configuration, permissions and application compatibility. A database restored successfully may still reference unavailable objects or require an older application version. Keep the restore instructions accessible when the normal application is down, and identify which credentials and provider controls are required without copying secrets into the runbook.

A short incident guide should start with symptoms, immediate containment and evidence to preserve. For delayed AI feedback, it might instruct the operator to pause new generation, preserve submissions, inspect queue age and communicate the delay. For failed answer saving, the classroom fallback might be a printable exercise or an exported worksheet. That educational continuity plan is part of the product’s reliability, not an admission that engineering has failed.

Give the coding agent a bounded readiness assignment

A useful next task for an agent is an evidence review of one complete user journey. Ask it to trace an answer from the browser to persistent storage, identify external calls, describe retry behavior and locate the relevant deployment and recovery settings. Require file references and explicit unknowns. Documentation that merely states “production ready” is not evidence of those properties.

Then select the smallest change that addresses a demonstrated failure. A missing timeout may need a focused correction; a long video operation may justify a worker; a costly results query may need redesign. Request an explanation of the new failure modes introduced by the change. More services should correspond to a clearer operational benefit, not to a longer checklist.

Keep a compact release record containing the workload exercised, invariants checked, known limits, rollback route and recovery owner. Revisit it when adding a materially different feature, such as live collaboration or automatic video processing. There is no reason to rebuild an adequate static lesson site into a distributed system solely because the next bookmark mentions scalability.

The score of 8 reflects the importance of this subject to useful AI-built applications. The saved post is a good prompt to look beyond a successful demo, but its absolute prescriptions need qualification. The durable lesson is to make workload, saved-state guarantees, graceful failure and recovery concrete enough to inspect. Confidence should rise with that evidence, rather than with the number of infrastructure components or the number of registered users.

entries.title: Image Taste Mobile: use generated screens as a brief for a real application
entries.summary: The bookmarked image skill establishes visual direction, while implementation remains a separate task. A vocabulary-learning flow shows how to carry the reference into editable controls, complete states, accessible typography, and behavior that survives real devices.
entries.reason: A reference-to-code loop can improve visual direction, but an image does not establish interaction behavior, accessible structure or responsive layouts.
entries.html:
An image-first route to a mobile interface

In the April 25 announcement, bluedev introduces “image-taste-mobile,” praises ChatGPT Images 2.0 for generating interface screens, and proposes handing those images to a coding agent. The expanded capture includes a GitHub link and a reply confirming that the mobile image-generation folder was the intended resource. The post demonstrates a direction for working, not a measured comparison of implementation quality.

The inspected video poster shows a fitness-app concept inside a phone frame: a large heading, runner imagery, an activity card, and a bottom continuation control. It is useful evidence of the presentation style. It does not establish that the controls work, that the app exists as native code, or that the small text remains readable at different accessibility settings.

The current Taste Skill repository lists the mobile resource as imagegen-frontend-mobile. It distinguishes image-generation skills from implementation skills and explicitly describes a handoff to a coding agent. The historical announcement name and the current install name should therefore not be treated as interchangeable commands.

For a teacher-builder, the attraction is straightforward: a picture can communicate hierarchy, spacing, imagery, and mood more directly than a long aesthetic description. The limitation is equally important. A picture captures one state at one size. A working mobile application must behave correctly across many states, sizes, interruptions, and input methods.

What the skill does, and what it leaves open

The current skill file focuses on mobile screen concepts and flows for iOS, Android, and cross-platform products. It emphasizes hierarchy, readable text, consistency, platform awareness, controlled palettes, and coherent device framing. It explicitly excludes code generation. These are design instructions for producing images, not a compiler that turns an image into a correct application.

The skill’s numerical direction settings express preferences such as density or visual variation. They are not measured quality scores. Asking for greater consistency can steer generation, but a reader must still compare screens. A repeated logo, a coherent button shape, and stable navigation labels are observable outcomes; an instruction’s confidence is not evidence that those outcomes occurred.

OpenAI’s release page confirms ChatGPT Images 2.0 was introduced on April 21, 2026. The page now points readers toward a later image experience. That makes the bookmark historically specific: the workflow can remain useful while model selection changes. The creator’s praise should not be read as a current ranking across image models.

Use the image stage to resolve visual direction before committing to implementation details. Ask it to show the important information clearly, then inspect the result. Keep the original brief and approved wording outside the image so they remain recoverable when generated text is misspelled, cropped, or visually convincing but semantically wrong.

Start with a small vocabulary-learning flow

A useful first project is a proposed mobile companion for reviewing vocabulary from a teacher-selected reading. Limit the initial flow to three screens: choose a short practice set, answer one contextual question, and review the explanation. Avoid adding social feeds, rankings, complex statistics, and account management before the core activity is understandable.

Define the learning task in plain language. A learner sees a word inside its sentence, chooses a meaning, and receives an explanation tied to that context. The content record should include the source passage, approved answer, acceptable alternatives, and the reason a tempting distractor is wrong. The image generator should receive realistic sample content from that record, not invent the curriculum.

Write a short visual brief naming the intended device, reading distance, and tone. A calm reading companion might use generous line spacing, a strong sentence hierarchy, and restrained illustration. Request one primary action per screen and enough room for a multi-line explanation. Give a maximum amount of sample content so the model does not fill every gap with decorative statistics.

Generate the first question screen before the whole flow. Judge where your eye lands, whether the sentence can be read comfortably, and whether the learner can distinguish the question from feedback. If the primary task is unclear, another six polished screens will not solve it. Approve a direction before asking for related views.

Then generate the set-selection and review screens using the accepted question screen as a reference. Compare navigation placement, text styles, colors, and component shapes across all three. Differences may be appropriate when the task changes, but they should feel like deliberate variations within one application rather than three unrelated products.

Turn the approved picture into an implementation brief

Before coding, annotate the image with a small component map: top navigation, passage block, answer group, explanation region, and primary action. Describe which parts scroll and which remain visible. Identify actual assets separately from text and controls. A screenshot of a rounded button is not itself a button asset that should replace an accessible control.

Extract reusable values into a design record. Name text roles, spacing relationships, color roles, corner treatments, and image crops. You do not need to reverse-engineer every pixel perfectly. The goal is to preserve the intended hierarchy while allowing real content and device behavior to work. A slightly different spacing value may be the correct implementation if it prevents clipping.

Specify the interaction for every visible action. What happens when the learner presses Continue before selecting an answer? Can an answer be changed? Is an explanation revealed immediately or after a decision? What does Back preserve? The image cannot answer these questions reliably, and the coding agent should not have to guess.

Choose the implementation environment explicitly. A native SwiftUI app, a React Native application, and a responsive web prototype have different components and platform behavior. The same reference can guide all three, but it does not erase those differences. Start with the environment you can maintain and test rather than selecting a stack solely because a generated mockup resembles an iPhone.

Ask for one implemented screen with fixture data first. Provide the image, content record, behavior notes, and the existing project’s conventions. Require editable text and genuine controls. Review the result at the intended device size before introducing live generation, storage, or authentication. This isolates visual translation from unrelated infrastructure problems.

Design the states the hero image omits

A screen concept usually presents the best case: short labels, attractive imagery, populated content, and no keyboard. Build a state sheet for the less photogenic cases. Include an empty practice library, a long sentence, an unusually long answer, a loading passage, and a failed download. Each state needs a clear next action, even if it never appears in a promotional image.

For the vocabulary screen, distinguish incorrect from unanswered. A learner who has not chosen an option should receive a prompt to choose, not a failure animation. If the lesson content is unavailable, the message should explain that the exercise could not load. The application must not imply that the learner made a mistake because a request failed.

Test the keyboard when a free-text answer is supported. The submit control and relevant sentence should remain reachable. Avoid fixed heights copied from the reference that leave the answer field hidden behind the keyboard. Preserve the draft if the learner briefly leaves the application or switches to another screen.

Localization is another structural test. Replace the brief English labels with longer translations and use a sentence with unfamiliar diacritics. Does the layout wrap without concealing the primary action? Does truncation remove information needed to answer? Generated typography can suggest a style, but the implementation needs real font coverage and flexible layout.

Keep progress honest. A streak, accuracy ring, or completion percentage should appear only when backed by defined data. If the reference image contains attractive numbers, replace them with meaningful values or remove the widget. Decorative statistics are particularly misleading in education because they can suggest a measurement of learning that has never been made.

Platform behavior outranks screenshot fidelity

Apple’s typography guidance emphasizes legibility, hierarchy, and responding to text-size changes. Use it to evaluate a reference rather than treating every small caption as sacred. When a learner requests larger text, the application may need taller cards and additional scrolling. Preserving the screenshot’s exact composition is less important than preserving access to its information.

React Native’s accessibility documentation describes properties for labels, roles, state, and assistive-technology behavior. In that environment, the answer choices should expose what they are and whether they are selected. An image of a checkmark cannot provide that structure. Test with the screen reader used on the target platform, because semantics and focus order are part of the implementation.

Android’s adaptive-layout guidance likewise treats the available window as a design input. A phone-shaped reference should not become a fixed canvas stretched into every window. On a larger display, the passage and exercise may sit beside each other; on a narrow display, they may need a simple vertical sequence.

Inspect touch targets, contrast, reduced-motion behavior, and visible focus where relevant. Do not judge contrast from a compressed video poster alone. Measure the actual implemented colors and review text over the actual image crop. A background that looks calm in one generated state may become difficult to read when content shifts.

Use two review loops

Maintain a visual review and a behavioral review. In the visual review, compare the implemented screen with the approved direction: hierarchy, spacing, image placement, and consistency. In the behavioral review, complete the task with realistic content and interruptions. A screen can pass one and fail the other. Record the difference rather than asking the agent to “make it closer” without identifying the problem.

Use specific revision notes. “Keep the sentence above the answer group when text is enlarged” describes an observable requirement. “Make it more premium” invites another stylistic detour. When a change fixes one screen, inspect the shared component elsewhere so a larger button or new margin does not create a different problem.

For the proposed vocabulary app, a useful acceptance sequence is to choose a set, answer incorrectly, read the explanation, try another item, leave, and resume. Repeat with large text and a long passage. Ask a learner to explain why the accepted answer fits the context. Successful tapping alone does not establish that the exercise teaches the intended distinction.

Prepare assets separately from the screen mockup. If the chosen concept contains a useful illustration, obtain an appropriate standalone version instead of cutting a low-resolution fragment out of the entire phone image. Keep titles, buttons, and answer text as native interface content. Record the asset’s origin and any generation or editing history needed for your project. This also makes later changes easier: replacing a character illustration should not require rebuilding the screen’s controls, and correcting a vocabulary example should never require another image-generation request. The handoff is strongest when each visual element has a clear role and an editable counterpart.

Keep the image as a reference artifact alongside the implementation notes. If you later choose a different image model or redesign the review screen, you can identify what changed without losing the content and behavior contracts. This makes the image stage a useful design input rather than an opaque dependency.

A stronger brief, not a finished app

Image Taste Mobile earns a score of seven because it gives an average coder a practical way to establish visual direction before implementation. Its most useful contribution is the intermediate artifact: a coherent screen concept that can be discussed, revised, and handed to an agent. The current skill’s explicit image-only scope makes that boundary clear.

Budget for generation attempts, implementation, asset preparation, and testing. Keep sensitive student information out of mockups, and distinguish generated concept imagery from verified screenshots of a working product. Begin with one small flow and an approved content set. Expand when the implemented screens preserve both the visual intent and the learner’s ability to complete the task.

entries.title: Agent-S image workflows: from a visual proposal to an editable lesson
entries.summary: Shumer’s reply identifies a useful two-stage workflow: generate images as design references, then build real slides or applications. This report turns that idea into a teacher-operated production process with explicit content, editability, export and data checks.
entries.reason: A named agent workflow that combines visual synthesis with implementation deserves its own assessment; generated appearance must be evaluated alongside editability and correct behavior.
entries.html:
An image tool inside an agent changes the handoff

Matt Shumer’s April 22 bookmark describes adding GPT-Image-2 to Agent-S and praises the resulting slide decks and applications. Its strongest useful detail appears in the replies: when someone asks about decomposing slide images into components, Shumer says that he used the images as guides for building real slides. That suggests a two-stage production method: explore an appearance visually, then reconstruct it in an editable medium. The claim is more interesting than a polished screenshot, but the post does not independently establish the quality of the resulting slide objects or application behavior.

The linked product is agent-s.app, the commercial managed-agent service associated with this demonstration. A similarly named research project is not evidence for this service’s implementation. The inspected video poster shows an Agent-S workspace with a request for a Spotify board presentation and an image-delivery instruction. It records the working brief, not a completed deck. The full captured conversation resolves the product link and the creator’s intended image-to-slide handoff; it does not expose the generated files, chart data, or export settings.

For a teacher, this is a plausible way to accelerate visual exploration while retaining a document that can change next term. The important unit of success is therefore a usable teaching artifact: correct content, understandable visual hierarchy, editable text, and a delivery format that survives the classroom computer. A confident image is an intermediate proposal. It becomes useful teaching material only when those other requirements are deliberately carried through.

What the model, agent, and document each contribute

OpenAI’s GPT-Image-2 model documentation confirms an image-generation and editing model with text and image inputs. That supports the model identity in the post. It does not confirm the particular Agent-S configuration, how many attempts the creator made, or whether every displayed result came from an unchanged first output. Nor does an image model by itself create editable presentation semantics. A photographed-looking heading can still be pixels rather than a text box.

Think of the workflow as three connected representations. The content record holds claims, examples, sources, and numerical values. A generated visual proposes composition, illustration, color, and emphasis. The implementation translates that proposal into slide objects or application components. Errors arise when the middle representation silently becomes the source of truth: a plausible chart acquires invented numbers, a decorative control becomes an undocumented feature, or a beautiful paragraph replaces an approved quotation.

The current service’s terms describe agents running on managed computers with persistent state, and identify the product as experimental. This makes an ongoing project directory plausible, but persistence is not a backup guarantee. For this proposed workflow, maintain a downloadable project bundle containing the approved content, reference images, editable output, and any generation or assembly instructions. The ability to continue a conversation should not be the only way to recover a lesson.

A concrete five-slide teaching workflow

Consider a short English lesson about how an advertisement makes a claim. The learning objective is narrow: pupils should distinguish an assertion, the evidence offered for it, and an emotional appeal. Prepare five slide roles before generating anything: an opening example, a labeled analysis, a contrasting example, a paired task, and an exit question. Use a teacher-written fictional advertisement so that the exercise does not depend on reproducing a company’s campaign or accepting its claims.

Create a simple content record for each slide with its purpose, exact learner-facing text, teacher notes, and any source link. Mark illustrative statements as fictional. Specify which sentences must remain unchanged and which labels may be shortened. This record prevents a visual revision from also becoming an unnoticed editorial rewrite. A learner’s answer key belongs here too, including explanations for reasonable alternative answers; it should not be inferred later from whatever image looks convincing.

Ask the image tool for two visual directions for the opening slide only. Describe the audience, viewing distance, available space, and desired emphasis. For example, the advertisement could occupy one side while three annotation zones sit beside it. Compare whether the design makes the claim easy to locate before considering texture or decorative detail. Select one direction and explain the reasons: the example is readable, the annotation sequence follows the lesson, and the design leaves room for an unexpected pupil observation.

Then request an editable implementation using that image as a reference, with the approved text supplied separately. Require normal text objects for headings and instructions, separate shapes for annotation boxes, and a distinct illustration asset where artwork is useful. Ask for a manifest that maps each slide to its content record. This is an original proposed workflow, not a claim that Agent-S automatically performs these steps or exports a particular format without additional configuration.

After reviewing the first implemented slide, extend the same visual rules to the remaining four. Give the paired task more working space than the explanation slide. On the exit slide, reduce the visual support so that the learner must identify the distinction independently. Consistency means that repeated elements behave predictably; it does not require every slide to use the same layout. That distinction is especially valuable when an image model tends to produce an attractive but repetitive series.

Keep revisions specific enough to preserve the lesson

Once the five-slide draft exists, request changes against named objects and purposes. A useful revision might say that the example must remain unchanged, the evidence annotation needs more space, and the decorative background should become quieter. A vague request to make everything more impressive can alter the instructional sequence while improving the thumbnail. Save the accepted version before requesting another direction, and compare the two using the content record rather than memory.

Prepare a second version for a different class by changing one controlled variable: the reading difficulty of the advertisement. Keep the lesson objective, category labels, and exit question stable. This makes it possible to judge whether the adapted material still teaches the same distinction. If the agent changes the answer key or introduces additional concepts, treat those as editorial changes requiring review. The resulting pair of lessons is also a useful maintenance test: a reusable production process should support purposeful variation without forcing the teacher to reconstruct every slide.

Make editability observable

A useful acceptance test takes place in the intended presentation application. Change one instruction, replace one illustration, and move an annotation box. If these operations require regenerating an entire slide image, the delivery does not meet this brief. Reopen the exported file on the classroom machine and inspect line wrapping, missing fonts, cropping, and speaker notes. Rendering a PDF is a separate check: it confirms a distributable appearance, while the source presentation demonstrates future editability.

There are established ways to assemble such outputs programmatically. PptxGenJS documents text objects and charts built from named series, labels, and values. These are examples of an alternative implementation route, not identified dependencies of Shumer’s demonstration. A coding agent could use a presentation library, or the teacher could rebuild the chosen design in a familiar editor. The crucial requirement is a maintained connection between content and editable objects.

For a chart-based lesson, make that connection numerical. Supply a small table of deliberately fictional survey results, label it as classroom example data, and build the chart from that table. Change one value and check that the corresponding bar changes while the other categories remain stable. Compare axis labels and totals against the table. Do not ask an image generator to redraw a chart and then trust the apparent heights as a numerical representation.

Accessibility also belongs in the assembly stage. W3C’s guidance on complex images explains why charts and diagrams need text that communicates their information, sometimes including a fuller description or data table. For this lesson, supply a readable version of the fictional advertisement and an explanation of each annotation outside the image. A learner should be able to complete the reasoning task without decoding tiny baked-in labels.

The same handoff can inform an application

The bookmark also mentions apps. An appropriate small experiment would turn the advertisement lesson into an annotation exercise with three selectable categories. Use a generated screen to agree on the visual arrangement, then define the actual interactions separately: selecting a sentence, assigning a category, undoing a choice, requesting a hint, and submitting an explanation. A reference image cannot specify keyboard behavior, saved progress, or what happens when the same sentence supports more than one interpretation.

Ask for a first implementation using a fixed local content fixture. Review the complete exercise before adding model-generated hints. The answer checker should not quietly become an authoritative grader simply because an AI agent created the interface. For this open-ended topic, a teacher-approved rubric and examples of acceptable reasoning are more useful than an unexplained binary result. If a model later offers feedback, label it as suggested feedback and preserve the learner’s original answer.

A revealing revision test is to replace the short advertisement with a longer one. The screen must accommodate the additional text, retain a clear reading order, and keep the submit control reachable. Then remove the illustration entirely and check whether the lesson still makes sense. These tests expose whether the developer translated the design into a flexible application or merely recreated the composition for one favorable screenshot.

Operate it as a production workspace

The service requires users to be at least eighteen, so the educational proposal here is teacher-operated material production, not pupil accounts. Its terms describe prepaid credits covering agent runs and machine time; active work stops when the balance is exhausted. The public billing endpoint was not accessible during research, so current unit rates and a typical deck cost remain unverified. Budget a small first-slide experiment and inspect its actual usage before approving a whole course.

The privacy policy says messages and uploads are processed to operate the service. It states that these are not used to train the company’s own models, while third-party model providers apply their own terms and data practices. That is narrower than a blanket promise that uploaded material never reaches another provider. Use a teacher-authored source pack with fictional learner examples rather than a class roster, assessment records, or identifiable student work.

The credential guide separates website login through the secure desktop from API credentials stored in Secrets, and says ordinary chat is not the place for raw passwords or tokens. This is relevant when an agent needs a document service or image API, but it does not make every connected action harmless. Give the experiment only the access needed to produce the draft, and review the completed artifact before making it available to a class.

At each accepted milestone, export the working files and a brief revision note. Record which visuals are generated, which factual sources underpin the content, and what was changed manually. A colleague inheriting the lesson needs those decisions more than a long chat transcript. If the service or model changes, this small production record preserves enough structure to rebuild the material elsewhere.

A promising production pattern, with unfinished evidence

The score of seven reflects a useful integration idea: an agent can use visual synthesis to explore a design and then carry it into another medium. The creator’s reply gives the bookmark more substance than an isolated image gallery. However, no generated deck or application was executed or inspected here, and the captured poster does not establish factual accuracy, native editability, accessibility, cost, or repeatability. A downloadable source artifact with a documented revision would strengthen the case considerably. For now, the most transferable lesson is the handoff: preserve content separately, use images to settle visual direction, and judge the delivered teaching artifact by what a teacher and learner can actually do with it.

entries.title: LLM Council: useful disagreement without mistaking consensus for evidence
entries.summary: The bookmarked Claude skill adapts Karpathy’s multi-model council into five reasoning roles. Its value lies in exposing assumptions and comparing options; anonymous review and a confident synthesis do not by themselves make advice reliable.
entries.reason: Independent perspectives can expose weak reasoning, but agreement among models is not external evidence and correlated errors remain possible.
entries.html:
A structured disagreement exercise, not a trust guarantee

Ole Lehmann’s March 30 bookmark introduces a skill that asks five AI advisors to examine a decision, review one another’s responses anonymously, and produce a final recommendation. Its headline promises a way to trust Claude’s advice, following Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Council method. The full captured article also makes a sweeping claim that Claude invariably tells people what they want to hear. That is rhetorical framing, not a measured description of every response.

The underlying problem is real enough to investigate: a fluent answer can leave its assumptions unchallenged. A teacher deciding whether to build an interactive Latin environment, a video series, or a simpler exercise site may benefit from several deliberately different analyses. The useful outcome is a clearer decision and a testable next step. Agreement among generated advisors does not establish that their shared claims are true.

The full article describes five thinking roles, a randomized anonymous review round, and a final HTML report with a longer transcript. Its linked Google document could not be retrieved. A public repository attributes its skill to Lehmann, allowing a distributed implementation to be inspected without claiming it is identical to the inaccessible linked file. No council was executed or installed.

Two designs share the name

Karpathy’s original project is a local web application that sends a question to several models through OpenRouter, collects independent responses, requests anonymous comparative reviews, and asks a chairman model to synthesize the result. Its README describes an exploratory personal project supplied without an ongoing support commitment. Its checked-in model examples are historical configuration examples, not a current recommendation to use those particular versions.

The Claude skill distribution instead uses several subagents inside Claude, with different reasoning roles. It therefore creates variation in prompts and context, not automatically variation across model providers. Calling five advisors does not mean five independently trained systems have examined the question. That distinction matters when the suspected problem is a weakness shared by the underlying model.

Both approaches can expose alternatives that one short response misses. The original requires an application, routing service, and model access; the adaptation packages a procedure as instructions for an existing agent environment. Neither package supplies the user’s facts, establishes the competence of its reviewers, or guarantees that a final synthesis preserves the strongest objection.

What the published skill actually asks for

The inspected skill source uses five lenses: a critic looking for failure, a thinker questioning basic assumptions, an optimist looking for overlooked opportunity, an outsider checking intelligibility, and an executor seeking a practical next action. It first enriches and reframes the question, then runs independent responses, anonymized peer review, and synthesis. The final report includes agreement, unresolved disagreement, missed considerations, a recommendation, and a next step.

The source requests five new reviewers after the initial five advisors. This is a substantial workflow rather than a single clever prompt. It also contains tensions worth noticing: it encourages forceful, unbalanced perspectives and treats agreement as a confidence signal. Those choices may produce useful contrast, but they can reward theatrical certainty. The file’s final note about HTML output conflicts with its earlier instruction to present the result in chat, illustrating why even a small skill benefits from review.

For this reader, the sensible adaptation is to retain contrasting responsibilities while requiring each factual assertion to identify its evidence. An advisor can argue strongly for a position while distinguishing observed facts, assumptions, and proposed experiments. That is more useful than forcing every uncertainty into a confident verdict.

The author's example is a useful story, with missing controls

Lehmann describes choosing a live workshop with a recording instead of a self-paced course. The advisors highlight speed of preparation, course completion, accessibility to outsiders, and the combined format's value. He reports 180 signups and a 4.8/5 rating. These are an author's case study, not a comparison showing that the council caused the outcome. The article supplies no independent support for its broad completion-rate or production-time estimates.

The educational lesson is to check the premises before accepting the synthesis. Attendance does not establish learning or completion, and a live format can exclude people unable to attend. A teacher could use the council to identify these tradeoffs, then compare actual learner needs and available preparation time. The persuasive narrative should prompt an experiment rather than settle the choice of format.

Anonymity removes one cue, not every bias

Karpathy’s orchestration code labels answers with letters for review, then supplies model identities again to the chairman. The inspected implementation builds labels from response order and includes the collected response set in each review request. It does not implement the same randomized mapping explicitly requested by the Claude skill. The details of an implementation therefore matter more than the general phrase anonymous debate.

A label can hide which vendor wrote an answer, but style, terminology, length, and formatting remain visible. Reviewers can still prefer the most polished response or the one nearest the beginning. They may also mistake an unsupported but precise claim for expertise. A strong review asks which specific premise or inference is justified, rather than merely which answer sounds strongest.

The MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena judge study documented position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases in the evaluated model judges. That research does not measure this skill’s current performance, but it supplies sensible test categories. Reverse the answer order, shorten an overlong response, and remove author labels. If the recommendation changes without new evidence, the procedure is sensitive to presentation.

For an important decision, keep the original independent answers visible. A synthesis can accidentally turn a conditional objection into a minor footnote. The user should be able to see whether the chairman actually resolved a disagreement or merely compressed it.

The missing ingredient is often evidence

Research on language-model sycophancy studies the tendency of assistants to align with a user’s stated beliefs or preferences at the expense of correctness in evaluated settings. It supports concern about flattering agreement. It does not establish that every response from a named current model is sycophantic, or that a five-role prompt reliably removes the tendency.

A leading question can contaminate the whole council before any advisor begins. “Explain why my immersive Latin app will engage students” already supplies the desired conclusion. A neutral brief would ask which of several teaching formats best addresses a particular learning difficulty under a stated preparation budget, then provide what is known about the class and existing materials.

All advisors may reasonably converge if they share the same false premise. Suppose the brief says students cannot learn vocabulary without immersive graphics. Five analyses of production cost, interface design, and launch plans can leave that unsupported educational assumption untouched. Include an explicit reviewer responsibility to identify claims requiring outside evidence and questions that only a classroom trial can answer.

The strongest council output may therefore be a narrower question. Rather than recommending an entire product, it might propose comparing one interactive scene with an illustrated exercise using the same vocabulary. The recommendation becomes useful because it identifies what would change the decision.

A proposed decision session for an educational project

Consider a teacher with six hours per week for a month and an existing reading-comprehension website. Three possible improvements are a narrated video introduction, adaptive hints, and a three-dimensional scene. The actual goal is to help students connect textual evidence to interpretations, rather than simply to make the site look more advanced.

Prepare a one-page brief containing the learner group, current exercise, recurring difficulties, available assets, technical constraints, and the teacher’s review capacity. Provide examples of student mistakes using synthetic or anonymized responses. State which decisions are reversible and what success would look like. Do not ask the advisors to invent a budget or infer the class’s needs from a vague description.

Assign different investigative responsibilities. One advisor checks whether the proposed features address the observed learning problem. Another examines implementation and maintenance. A third considers accessibility and alternative presentations. A fourth searches for the smallest useful experiment. A fifth challenges the evidence and identifies likely failure cases. These responsibilities are an original adaptation, not the roles shipped in Lehmann’s file.

Require a common return format: recommendation, supporting facts, assumptions, most serious objection, and evidence that would change the recommendation. Keep responses short enough to compare. The peer-review stage should identify a specific weak premise and a specific overlooked constraint in each proposal, rather than awarding points for eloquence.

The synthesis might recommend one adaptive-hint prototype while preserving a disagreement about whether the bottleneck is vocabulary or reasoning. The next action would then be to review a small set of actual responses before implementing hint logic. This is a hypothetical example of useful council behavior; no such conclusion was generated or validated for this report.

Make the workflow inspectable

A simple decision record can contain the original brief, its version, each independent answer, anonymization mapping, reviews, synthesis, and the human decision. Record failed or missing advisor calls explicitly. A council that received only three successful answers should not present itself as a completed five-member process.

Keep research and judgment separate. Gather current facts once into a shared evidence packet, or explicitly assign different evidence-gathering tasks and reconcile them before the decision round. Otherwise each advisor may consult different versions of a product page or silently rely on memory. Diversity of evidence can be valuable, but accidental disagreement about basic facts wastes the review stage.

For a coding implementation, enforce a response schema outside the model. Validate required fields and preserve source locations. Do not give a council permission to publish, purchase, or modify accounts merely because it is called a decision system. Its output can remain a recommendation for the person or application responsible for the action.

Use separate contexts when testing independent reasoning. Repeatedly asking one continuing conversation to adopt five roles exposes later roles to earlier answers and can encourage convergence. Genuine separation is an architectural property, not something established by placing five names in a single response.

Evaluate the council against a simpler alternative

The baseline should be a well-framed single-model response with the same evidence and an explicit request to identify objections. Compare that with independent answers alone, then with the full peer-review process. This helps determine whether improvement comes from additional perspectives, better prompting, or the expensive review stage.

For factual questions, evaluate against verified answers. For product decisions, assess whether the process identifies relevant constraints, distinguishes assumptions, preserves uncertainty, and proposes a feasible experiment. A teacher can also score whether the final recommendation reflects the stated learning objective. Avoid using the same council to judge its own superiority.

Measure human review time as well as model usage. Five long answers and five reviews can create more work than they remove. A workflow that surfaces one previously missed critical issue may justify that overhead; one that generates eleven variations of obvious advice probably does not. Track whether recommendations change after real-world evidence arrives.

Use counterexamples deliberately. Give the council a tempting but unsupported claim, incomplete cost information, two genuinely equivalent options, and a decision that should be deferred. A reliable process should sometimes request evidence or recommend no change. A system pressured to deliver a decisive verdict every time can become less trustworthy precisely when the evidence is weakest.

Judgment: valuable for framing, conditional for decisions

The catalogue’s 7/10 score reflects a reusable method for exploring tradeoffs and exposing neglected assumptions. The inspectable skill is more concrete than a generic instruction to think harder, and the original project makes intermediate responses visible. Neither establishes that agreement is truth or that anonymous review guarantees good judgment.

Use a council when a decision has several defensible paths and enough evidence to support comparison. Keep its dissent, verify its factual premises, and turn its recommendation into a test when possible. For a simple lookup or routine transformation, a direct answer with a source is usually a clearer starting point.
