entries.title: Claude skills: turn repeated work into procedures you can test
entries.summary: Four bookmarks lead from design prompts and project folders to a more rigorous practice: package a focused task, supply the right references, and measure whether it helps. The report corrects unsupported memory paths, settings examples, and tenfold-productivity claims.
entries.reason: Well-scoped skills can make workflows repeatable and shareable, but they need clear triggers, maintained references and outcome-based evaluation.
entries.html:
Four bookmarks about making repeated work more dependable

The four saved posts converge on a useful idea: an AI assistant becomes easier to work with when it can find the procedures, examples, and project conventions that matter to a task. They differ considerably in evidence quality. One recommends seven skill resources, one makes exaggerated claims about a hidden folder, one points to an engineer's account of internal practice, and one links a verifiable Anthropic guide.

For a teacher or average coder, start with one recurring task: reviewing exercises, preparing an evidence-backed explainer, or verifying an application’s central interaction. Package the procedure, then check whether it improves the result. A large skill catalogue cannot substitute for that evaluation.

Seven recommendations, with different responsibilities

Om Patel’s complete March 28 post names seven resources. These are his recommendations; the capture does not pin repository versions or provide installation links for the list.

  • frontend-design: choose a visual direction before coding. Anthropic’s public source confirms the skill; aesthetic improvement still needs review against the brief.
  • simplify: clean up working code. Judge proposed simplifications by preserved behavior, not merely fewer lines.
  • browser-use: interact with pages through clicks, forms, screenshots, and parallel sessions, according to the post. Actual support depends on the installed browser runtime.
  • shannon: test an owned staging environment and report demonstrated vulnerabilities. The post’s “no false positives” claim is unsupported here; a claimed proof of concept still needs reproduction and review.
  • test-driven-development: establish tests before implementation. Prompt instructions alone cannot guarantee that the sequence was followed or that tests cover the intended behavior.
  • composio: connect external services with managed authentication. That description does not establish particular account access, supported actions, or permission to send or change data.
  • antigravity awesome-skills: a community collection advertised as exceeding 1,200 entries, with role-based bundles. The historical count is not a verified current inventory or a quality measure.

The list spans design guidance, testing methods, executable integrations, and a directory. Evaluate each proposed dependency separately. Om’s closing advice—to turn repeatedly explained work into a custom skill—fits the practical examples below.

The hidden-folder article needs technical corrections

CyrilXBT's March 26 article is available in an expanded capture. It recommends project instructions, reusable review and deployment prompts, and notes about decisions and failures. Those are sensible categories. Its tenfold-improvement headline, guarantees about future behavior, suggested memory paths, and purported production settings are not established by evidence. The useful workflow advice must be separated from the claim that a particular folder layout automatically creates a permanently informed assistant.

An engineer's account of skills in practice

Thariq's complete March 17 article describes lessons from using hundreds of skills at Anthropic. He groups them into nine areas: library guidance, product verification, data analysis, team processes, scaffolding, code review, deployment, investigation runbooks, and infrastructure maintenance. His recommendation is to give each skill a recognizable job and preserve the practical details that a generic assistant would lack. This is a practitioner's account of internal use, not an independently audited productivity study.

The article goes beyond instructions: it discusses scripts, reusable assets, setup configuration, persistent records, hooks, distribution, and usage measurement. A later official Anthropic publication, dated June 3, develops the same themes. The saved article provides the direct evidence for the practical lessons discussed below.

The thirty-three-page guide is verifiable

RoundtableSpace's March 8 post points to Anthropic's Complete Guide to Building Skills for Claude. The linked PDF is accessible and contains thirty-three pages. Its structure covers fundamentals, planning, testing, sharing, and troubleshooting. This is a stronger starting point than an unexplained installation list because it connects the file format to the work of deciding whether a skill triggers correctly and produces useful results.

A skill is a reusable procedure with supporting material

The Agent Skills specification defines a directory containing SKILL.md, with metadata describing the skill and a body of instructions. Supporting scripts, references, and assets can live alongside it. This is a portable organizational format, but particular hosts may add their own behavior. Sharing the basic format does not establish that every permission feature or execution option works identically in every assistant.

The central design distinction is between information needed to recognize a task and information needed to perform it. A brief description helps the assistant decide when the skill applies. Detailed references can be consulted after that decision. If the description is vague, excellent instructions may never be loaded. If it is too broad, the skill may interfere with unrelated requests.

Claude Code's current documentation says skills can be invoked directly or selected when relevant, and their bodies load when used. Older custom commands remain supported: a file in .claude/commands and a corresponding skill can both provide a slash command. Therefore, the older command examples in the hidden-folder article are not inherently obsolete. The newer folder form is useful when the task also needs templates, examples, or scripts.

Om also estimates about 100 startup tokens per skill. The specification uses roughly that figure for metadata, with instructions and resources loaded later; it is not a fixed runtime charge. Claude Code documents a listing budget that can omit descriptions when crowded. Many installed skills therefore do not guarantee negligible context use or reliable discovery.

A skill does not train the underlying model's weights or confer a new verified expertise. It supplies instructions and resources during work. If its grammar rubric is wrong, it can reproduce the wrong rubric consistently. If its verification script only checks that a file exists, it cannot establish that the file contains a correct lesson. Reliability depends on the whole procedure and the evidence it produces.

What to correct before copying the hidden-folder setup

The expanded article combines several mechanisms that should be kept distinct. A project instruction file tells Claude how to approach work. A reusable command or skill supplies a task-specific procedure. Auto memory stores selected learnings. Session transcripts preserve conversation records. Settings configure supported behavior. Giving these things similar names does not make them interchangeable.

The official memory documentation describes project instructions at CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md and default auto memory under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/. The article's proposed .claude/memory/project.md can be a manually maintained note, but that path alone does not give it automatic memory semantics. It needs an explicit loading or reference strategy. Instructions and memory are context, not an enforcement mechanism, so promises that Claude will always follow them are too strong.

The directory reference places local conversation transcripts under the user configuration directory's project area, using JSONL session files. That differs from the article's project-local .claude/conversations example. Do not build a backup, sharing, or memory workflow around a guessed transcript location. A human-maintained decision log is often easier to curate than treating every historical message as permanent project knowledge.

The article also supplies a settings object containing nested context, commands, memory, and output blocks. Those examples should not be treated as a verified current configuration. The settings documentation describes supported settings files, scope, precedence, and validation; a plausible JSON shape is insufficient. In particular, the documented memory controls differ from the article's illustrative nested memory block. Check each proposed key against the current reference before relying on it.

The practical correction is small: begin with the documented instruction and skill locations, keep custom notes explicitly referenced, and add settings only to solve a known problem. Do not copy a model identifier from a social article merely because it is labeled production-ready. A minimal working configuration that you can explain is easier to troubleshoot than a large configuration containing unverified controls.

The article's strongest reusable idea survives these corrections: preserve decisions and recurring mistakes in a form that can be reviewed. Its weakest idea is that hidden configuration automatically compounds intelligence. A note saying why a previous approach failed can improve the next attempt; it can also become stale. Date it, identify the conditions under which it applied, and remove it when the underlying system changes.

What frontend-design can and cannot contribute

The current frontend-design source asks for deliberate choices grounded in subject matter, an explicit visual plan, and critique against the brief. It also addresses interface language and review of the implemented result. This supports the general direction of Om Patel's recommendation. It does not establish a guaranteed aesthetic improvement, and the current file should not be assumed identical to the version available when the post was saved.

Give the design process teaching constraints: separate prompt, answer, and grammatical feedback in a Latin exercise; support a historical explainer with a timeline and source annotations; keep reading text quiet and progress visible. These tasks need different structures even within one visual identity.

Compare two versions of one screen with identical content and requirements. Can learners find the next action, understand the grammatical distinction, and recognize answer states without color alone? Retain changes that improve those outcomes. The skill provides a design process; the brief and review determine whether its choices serve the learner.

What Thariq's field report adds to a small project

Thariq recommends building skills from observed mistakes rather than filling them with generic coding advice. He also separates reusable procedures from setup details and changing records. The full article warns that an upgrade can remove data stored inside a skill directory and identifies ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} as a stable location for plugin data. This concerns explicitly managed workflow records, not a promise that every skill automatically remembers previous sessions.

For a lesson-production skill, that distinction suggests keeping the review rubric with the procedure, the current output destination in configuration, and the record of approved lessons in a stable project location. A copied skill should not inherit another teacher's destination or overwrite its history during an update. Check those assumptions before sharing the package.

The article also says that referring to another skill by name is not a native dependency-management system. Its usage logging helps reveal popular or rarely selected skills, but a logged invocation does not establish a correct result. For a proposed worksheet workflow that relies on a separate exporter, explicitly check that the exporter is available and inspect the resulting pages. Measure successful, reviewed exports as well as skill selection. This turns the author's operational advice into a testable local practice without treating internal popularity as evidence of educational quality.

Build one exercise-review skill around known failures

A useful first skill for a teacher is an exercise-bank reviewer. Define its job narrowly: inspect an existing collection and produce findings. It should not silently rewrite all questions, change the learning objective, or publish the result. The initial output is a report that a subject expert can review. This keeps the evidence of the original problem available.

Choose a small sample you know well. Include a valid exercise, an item with two acceptable answers, an answer-key mismatch, a repeated identifier, and an explanation that assumes untaught vocabulary. Write the expected finding for each case before asking Claude to inspect it. Otherwise, you may accept whatever issues it happens to mention as evidence of success.

Create a project skill folder such as .claude/skills/review-exercises/. The instruction file should explain the accepted inputs, the checks to perform, and the required report format. A reference file can contain the subject rubric, while an examples folder contains short accepted and rejected cases. This proposed arrangement applies the documented folder model; it is not an installed or tested package supplied by this report.

A concise draft instruction could say: “Review supplied exercises for the stated learner level. Preserve the original items. Report each finding with the item identifier, the evidence, the likely learner impact, and a proposed correction. Mark uncertain subject judgments for teacher review. If the level or answer policy is missing, identify that gap before evaluating suitability.” The important feature is an observable report contract, not the exact wording.

Use deterministic checks where the rule is mechanical. A script can identify missing identifiers, duplicate IDs, or absent required fields. The model can then focus on questions such as ambiguity and explanatory clarity. Keep the script's findings separate from the model's judgments so that the reader knows which conclusions came from a fixed rule and which involve interpretation.

For example, a duplicate-ID checker can establish that two records share the same identifier. It cannot establish which record should survive. A model may suggest merging them because their wording is similar, but the teacher should decide whether they intentionally test different skills. Combining computation with judgment is useful precisely because their responsibilities remain visible.

Test selection, output, and improvement separately

The Anthropic PDF recommends evaluating triggering, functional behavior, and comparison with a baseline. Apply that structure with a small table of cases. Some prompts should request exercise review directly, others should paraphrase the same task, and some should ask for unrelated work. Record whether the skill was used, whether its findings were correct, and how much intervention was needed. The PDF's illustrative efficiency numbers are examples, not a benchmark for your project.

Start with manual evaluation. Read every finding and label it useful, incorrect, unsupported, or too vague to act on. A reviewer that flags everything can appear thorough while creating work. Track false alarms as well as missed defects. For a teaching workflow, a plausible but wrong grammatical correction may be more damaging than a missed formatting inconsistency.

Next, compare the same task with and without the skill. Keep the input material and intended output constant. The comparison should answer a narrow question: did this resource package reduce repeated briefing or improve detection of the problems you care about? It does not need to establish a universal productivity multiplier. Record the model and tool versions because behavior can change after updates.

Preserve a few cases that you do not use while revising the instructions. Once the skill handles the development examples, try those held-out cases. Add a new subject, a different wording style, or a deliberately incomplete input. This checks whether the procedure generalizes beyond memorized examples. If it fails, improve the rule or the examples rather than simply inserting the expected answer.

Maintain a short record of recurring mistakes. A useful entry describes the failure, the condition that triggered it, and the correction. For instance, a vocabulary checker may wrongly reject an accepted spelling variant when the answer policy is unspecified. That suggests improving the input contract, not adding a blanket rule that every spelling variation is acceptable.

Repeat evaluation after a material change to the rubric, supporting scripts, or host behavior. There is no need to rerun a large test suite after correcting a harmless typo, but a changed trigger description deserves selection tests, and a changed checker deserves relevant functional cases. Match the effort to the part of the procedure that changed.

A concrete failure that should change the procedure

Suppose the review skill flags a Latin exercise because its English translation differs from the answer key. The learner's translation may still express the same meaning. A mechanical string comparison would identify a difference, while a useful educational review would ask whether the difference changes the grammatical point being tested. The skill should report the distinction and preserve both versions for the teacher.

Now suppose the exercise is specifically testing tense. Two translations that convey roughly the same event may still differ in the target feature. A blanket instruction to accept equivalent meaning would be too permissive. The input contract needs the learning objective and the answer policy, not merely the source sentence and a model answer.

This example suggests a precise improvement: require the reviewer to identify the assessed feature before judging alternative answers. Test that change on both a meaning-focused task and a tense-focused task. If it improves one while damaging the other, revise the decision rule or ask for missing context. Do not hide the tradeoff behind a higher overall score.

That is what useful skill engineering looks like in practice: an observed failure leads to a better input, a clearer decision, and a test that could reveal regression. The resulting procedure contains knowledge about your actual teaching task. It earns its place because it changes a specific outcome you care about.

A second useful skill: verify the app's learning loop

For an app builder, a verification skill can record how to run the project and check the central learner journey. Define a concrete path: open a lesson, answer incorrectly, read feedback, answer correctly, and proceed. Specify what should be visible and which state should change. This is more useful than a generic instruction to test the app thoroughly.

Include a fixture with known content and expected answers. If the application chooses random items, provide a repeatable test mode or seed where feasible. Otherwise, a failure may be difficult to reproduce. Ask the report to distinguish the steps actually executed from checks that were skipped because a dependency, browser, or account was unavailable.

Combine layers of evidence. A unit check can confirm answer normalization; an interaction check can confirm that the button and feedback work together; a screenshot can expose clipped text or unreadable contrast. None substitutes for all the others. Choose the checks that correspond to actual risks in your app rather than collecting impressive-looking artifacts.

Do not give the verification skill publication authority by accident. Its ordinary job can be to produce findings and a reviewable patch. Deployment, messages to learners, or changes to real records are separate actions with separate permissions. This is a design choice for the proposed workflow, not a claim that the skill format automatically creates an approval system.

Instructions, tools, and enforcement have different jobs

Claude Code's hook reference describes execution at defined lifecycle events, including checks before tool use. A deterministic hook can enforce a specific machine-checkable rule when configured correctly. A prose reminder asks the model to behave a certain way. Use that distinction when a requirement must hold even if the model misunderstands the task.

For example, a publishing workflow might validate that required metadata exists before allowing a release step. That check can establish presence and format. It cannot by itself certify that a historical explanation is accurate or a lesson is age-appropriate. Keep human editorial decisions visible rather than disguising them as an automatic green check.

Review imported skill contents before using them, especially scripts and instructions that invoke external services. The official skills repository supplies concrete examples to inspect, but a familiar folder name is not evidence that an arbitrary copy is identical. Record the source and revision of a skill you depend on, and understand what its supporting code does before giving it access to valuable material.

Share a skill once another person can understand its inputs and verify its outputs without the author's private context. Include setup requirements, an example, known limitations, and a maintainer. A procedure that depends on a particular local path or undocumented account is not ready for broad reuse simply because it can be copied into another repository.

Keep the procedures that earn their place

The four bookmarks are most valuable together when they redirect attention from clever one-off prompts to repeatable, inspectable work. The verified guide and current documentation provide the foundations; the design example shows a concrete use; the expanded hidden-folder article supplies ideas that require technical correction. No accessible evidence establishes a tenfold improvement or permanent obedience.

The score of ten reflects broad relevance to AI-assisted development and repeated interest. Begin with one recurring task, a small reference set, and known examples of failure. Keep the skill if it improves your own results or reduces repeated explanation without making review harder. A compact library of tested procedures is a stronger asset than a large collection of impressive names.

entries.title: The Claude arbitrage-bot claim: inspect the arithmetic before the mechanism
entries.summary: AdiiX’s full guide describes a prediction-market bot but mixes directional forecasting with arbitrage and contains unresolved accounting inconsistencies. Its strongest use is as material for an offline execution simulator and a lesson in evaluating financial claims.
entries.reason: The claimed implementation and return need independent provenance; its main value is learning how market mechanics and evidence can be misrepresented.
entries.html:
A spectacular claim with an inspectable narrative

AdiiX's March 27 article attributes an increase from roughly $300 to $2.38 million over four months to a Claude-assisted prediction-market bot. The saved item carries a paid-partnership label. Its complete captured guide describes a mechanism, several related strategies, operational steps, and risk controls. That is more informative than a balance screenshot, but it does not supply a reproducible repository, complete account ledger, or verified connection between Claude and the claimed wallet activity.

The useful reading task is to separate three questions: whether the accounting is correct, whether the proposed strategy has an advantage, and whether AI caused any observed success. Public transactions could help answer the first. They cannot establish the other two without additional evidence.

Its central example is a directional forecast

The guide describes watching Bitcoin on a centralized exchange and buying a prediction-market outcome before its quoted probability catches up. Its example assumes a move makes the eventual downside outcome 78% likely. That still leaves a 22% losing outcome. Calling the purchase effectively certain does not follow from its own assumption, and resale at a better price is not guaranteed.

Contractual arbitrage is different. In a simplified binary market, a matched Yes-and-No pair covers both outcomes. If executable acquisition costs total 97 cents against a combined one-dollar payout, the gross difference is three cents. Fees, depth, incomplete fills, and settlement conditions still matter. Polymarket's order-book documentation distinguishes displayed prices from executable quotes; a pleasing screen calculation is not a completed transaction.

The article also discusses oracle discrepancies, news interpretation, and market making. Those mechanisms carry different risks and should not share one supposed win rate. Its specific pricing-lag estimate, strategy win-rate ranges, monthly return estimates, and claimed Claude-versus-OpenClaw comparison lack enough supplied methods to establish their generality.

The numbers require reconciliation before explanation

The profile summary gives 100% wins and more than 33,950 predictions, while the narrative uses 98% and 26,738 trades. Different dates or counting conventions could explain those figures, but the article does not reconcile them. It also calls growth from $313 to about $438,000 a 140-fold increase; that calculation is approximately 1,400-fold.

The captured article presents an April 2026 final result although the bookmarked item is dated March 27. A later edit could explain this, but the capture does not establish the necessary revision history. These discrepancies do not prove that every underlying transaction is fictitious. They mean the published account cannot be accepted as a coherent performance record without further work.

Likewise, a high win rate says little without win and loss sizes. Ninety-nine small gains can be overwhelmed by one large loss. Deposits, withdrawals, open positions, fees, and external exposure belong in the accounting before a final balance becomes a return.

A reviewable evidence packet would identify the complete wallet addresses, observation dates, transaction records, position valuation method, and source of any outside funding. It would define whether a trade means an order, fill, position, or settled prediction. For AI attribution, it would also need dated software and decision logs. A wallet can demonstrate activity without revealing who wrote the software or which model influenced a particular order.

Execution and resolution can change the result

The official order lifecycle separates order acceptance, matching, settlement, and confirmation. A simulator must represent partial success and unresolved requests. For a two-leg idea, one filled leg creates exposure until the other completes or the position is unwound. Retrying an uncertain request without reconciliation can duplicate that exposure.

Current fee documentation describes market-dependent taker charges. Historical analysis needs the rules applicable to the relevant market and date. Spread crossing, available depth, and time spent waiting must also enter the result. A tiny gross discrepancy may disappear before it becomes a net gain.

Resolution rules determine the payout source and edge cases. A price on one exchange is not automatically the settlement reference for another contract. Similar market titles do not establish equivalent obligations.

Build a small evidence laboratory

For an average coder, a useful project is an offline replay with fictional money. Begin with two synthetic order books, known event outcomes, and an append-only ledger. Show the intended order, available quantity, simulated fill, costs, and resulting exposure. Add controls for quote age and execution delay so the user can see which assumption changes the outcome.

Keep the directional experiment separate. Define what information was available when the decision occurred, how a probability was estimated, and when success is measured. Reserve a later period before tuning anything. Preserve unsuccessful variants: the backtest-overfitting research explains why choosing the best result after many attempts changes the evidential burden.

The article recommends paper testing and risk limits, but its proposed one-week sample and win-rate cutoff cannot establish a durable advantage. Evaluate calibration, net outcomes, losses, and failed execution together. Compare the same replay against a simple baseline, including doing nothing, rather than assuming model involvement improves it.

A teacher can turn the laboratory into a numerical-literacy lesson. Give learners a large ending balance caused mostly by deposits, a high win rate with negative profit, and a low win rate with positive profit. Ask them to write accurate headlines and identify the missing evidence. The exercise teaches why attractive percentages need denominators and definitions.

Save each scenario with its assumptions and expected ledger totals. Learners can then change one condition at a time and explain the difference. This makes the project reproducible without connecting a wallet or chasing a current market opportunity.

Useful for scrutiny, unproven as a system

Score four reflects a detailed but unreliable promotional case study. The full article provides enough substance to examine market mechanics and identify contradictions; it does not establish its extraordinary return, a dependable pricing advantage, or a model-specific benefit.

A coding assistant could help implement the replay, test accounting identities, and explain settlement rules. Those outputs can be checked independently. Producing working code would still be evidence of implementation, not evidence that the strategy makes money.

entries.title: Build a first agent around one inspectable job
entries.summary: A beginner course and Google technical guide become a practical plan for an exercise repair assistant, with explicit tools, evidence, memory, evaluation, and stopping rules. The report also corrects unsafe calculator code and overbroad claims about automatic memory.
entries.reason: Foundational architecture is more durable than any individual model launch and gives an intermediate coder a basis for building bounded educational or content workflows.
entries.html:
Two routes from curiosity to a working system

The two bookmarks approach the same useful question: what must a beginner understand to build an agent that does a specific job? hoeem's March 26 course supplies an eight-part introduction covering the tool loop, workflow patterns, construction, tools, memory, testing, multiple agents, and a concluding build strategy. Its strongest advice is to define the job before choosing the machinery. The headline's claim that no equivalent full course existed is promotional positioning, not a verified historical finding.

Ihtesham Ali's March 11 bookmark points to Google's technical guide for startups, describing it as a 64-page resource. Google's official landing page confirms a guide spanning construction, deployment, retrieval, multimodal systems, quality, safety, and operations. Its announcement is dated October 8, 2025, so the March post should not be interpreted as the original publication date. The large linked PDF could not be retrieved in full for this report; its advertised page count and every chapter were not independently checked.

The first resource was available as a full captured article. It is an accessible orientation, with simplifications that need attention before using its examples in an application. Google's material connects the topic to a broader deployment platform. Neither reading a course nor selecting a framework establishes that a product is reliable. The practical bridge is a small task, explicit inputs and outputs, carefully limited tools, and examples that reveal failure.

Understand what chooses the next step

A useful distinction is whether code fixes the sequence or the model chooses it while working. A fixed application might retrieve a document, ask for a summary, validate the result, and display it. An agent might decide that the first document is insufficient, formulate a second search, inspect another passage, and then stop with a supported answer. Both can use language models; only the latter needs discretion over its path.

Anthropic's engineering account distinguishes predefined workflows from systems in which the model directs tool use. It describes chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestration, and evaluation loops as reusable patterns, while recommending simple approaches when they suffice. The course adopts this framework. However, predefined control flow does not imply that every model output is deterministic, and a routing workflow can still take different branches for different inputs. Predictable structure and identical results are different properties.

The runtime makes the model's proposed action real. It presents available functions, checks a requested call, executes permitted code, returns the observation, and decides whether another step is allowed. A model that writes “I searched the library” has not searched anything unless a tool actually ran. Similarly, a polished final answer cannot establish that a draft was saved. Separate generated statements from recorded events from the beginning.

For learning, draw this loop on paper before choosing a framework. Mark which decisions require language understanding and which can be implemented with ordinary code. This often reveals that the supposedly autonomous task only needs one classification or a single transformation.

What to retain and correct in the beginner course

The course recommends a narrow role, clear goal, minimal tools, rules, output format, and realistic examples. It then introduces memory and multiple agents as additions justified by need. That progression is useful. Its claims that a first version can usually be built in a day, or that no memory covers a stated percentage of cases, are informal estimates without a demonstrated evaluation population. A runnable prototype and a dependable classroom service require different amounts of work.

One concrete example needs replacement: the calculator tool evaluates a supplied expression using Python's eval, with built-ins restricted. Python's documentation warns that this function executes arbitrary code and that changing the built-ins mapping is not a security boundary. A beginner should expose specific numeric operations with validated arguments, or use a deliberately constrained expression parser. A model-selected string should not become arbitrary Python execution merely because the function is named calculator.

The course also treats short-term memory as something usually available automatically. Actual continuity depends on how the application passes history and configures storage. Its SDK version numbers describe a March snapshot; they should not be copied as current setup guidance in October. Likewise, provider comparisons are broad editorial preferences, not evidence that one vendor exclusively supports a particular architecture.

The transferable lesson is to inspect an example at every boundary: what is accepted, what code executes, what persists, and how failure is returned. Asking an assistant to generate the implementation can help, but the generated code needs the same examination as code copied from an article.

A first project: an exercise repair assistant

Consider an original project for a teacher who maintains reading-comprehension exercises. The assistant receives one exercise, its answer key, and access to an approved collection of source passages. It checks whether the answer is supported, identifies an ambiguity, and proposes a revised exercise when necessary. It saves a reviewable draft. The teacher remains responsible for accepting the change.

This is a manageable task because success is visible. The original question, cited passage, proposed correction, and reason can appear together. It also exercises genuine agent decisions: the system may need to locate a passage, compare two interpretations, or explain that the approved collection does not resolve the issue. It does not require access to student accounts, messaging, payments, or a school administration system.

Start with five exercises you already understand. Include one correct item, one answer-key mistake, one ambiguous question, one passage missing from the collection, and one item that depends on knowledge outside the passage. Write your expected handling before generating answers. These examples define the product more clearly than a long instruction to behave like an expert teacher.

Use a compact input record: exercise identifier, question, answer choices if applicable, current answer, source collection identifier, and learning objective. The proposed output should contain a status, evidence references, diagnosis, suggested revision, and unresolved questions. Distinguish “supported,” “needs revision,” and “insufficient evidence.” Do not force every input into a correction; unnecessary changes are failures too.

Build three small capabilities

The proposed assistant needs a search function over the approved collection, a function to read an identified passage, and a function to save a draft. These are application functions, not verified SDK syntax:

search_library(query, collection_id) → matching passage identifiers
read_excerpt(document_id, section_id) → text and source metadata
save_draft(exercise_id, proposal, run_id) → saved artifact identifier

The application should supply the allowed collection, rather than letting the model choose arbitrary storage. A passage identifier should resolve only inside that collection. The draft function should choose the storage location in code, validate the proposal, and return what was actually saved. An unrestricted file path adds capability the task does not need.

Google ADK's custom-tool documentation explains how function names, descriptions, parameters, and returned results expose capabilities to an agent. The practical design question is whether the model can distinguish when a tool is useful and what its result means. Give the search function a description that distinguishes finding candidate passages from verifying an answer. A search hit is evidence to inspect, not a verdict.

Return explicit outcomes such as success, no matches, invalid identifier, and temporary failure. A timeout must not look like an empty collection. Include document version, section location, and a stable reference with every excerpt. Preserve these fields when the agent writes its proposal so the teacher can open the exact evidence later.

The draft operation should tolerate a repeated request without silently creating many copies. A run identifier and exercise identifier can identify the intended draft. If the save result is uncertain, inspect whether the draft exists before retrying. This is ordinary application reliability, made more important by a model that may repeat a call when confused.

Choose a framework after the boundaries are clear

ADK's agent overview describes units built from a model, instructions, and optional tools, with composition available when complexity warrants it. That makes the Google guide relevant to this project: the same three capabilities can be exposed through an agent framework, while deterministic validation remains ordinary application code. The framework coordinates the loop; it does not supply the educational standard against which an answer should be judged.

A practical comparison is to implement the smallest fixed workflow first: search once, read the best candidate, generate a structured assessment, and save after validation. Then identify cases it cannot handle. If the missing capability is reformulating a search after an irrelevant result, allow that decision within a bounded loop. If the missing capability is checking required fields, write a validator. These problems do not require the same solution.

Choose one SDK whose current documentation and deployment environment you can maintain. Record its version alongside the example project. Avoid combining several orchestration frameworks merely because each appears in a tutorial. Additional layers can make it harder to discover which component owns history, retries, tool approvals, and termination.

For the first interface, a form with a clear result panel is sufficient. Show the original item, diagnosis, evidence, and proposed replacement. A chat box is optional. The user needs to understand the assistant's work and accept or reject a draft; conversational presentation alone does not make that process better.

Keep history, state, knowledge, and files distinct

ADK separates sessions, state, and memory: a session records an interaction, state holds working information, and a memory service can provide information across interactions. Its in-memory development services do not imply persistence after a process restarts. These are implementation choices with different lifetimes, rather than a single feature called remembering.

For the exercise assistant, working state might contain the current exercise and passages already inspected. The approved source collection is external knowledge. The accepted draft is an artifact. The conversation is a record of requests and observations. Keeping these distinct makes it possible to replace a faulty answer without corrupting the underlying source or treating a rejected suggestion as established knowledge.

OpenAI's session-memory cookbook demonstrates explicit session use and discusses trimming versus summarizing history. Trimming can discard an older constraint; summarization can distort it. Neither is an automatic guarantee of durable, accurate memory. For this small project, store the learning objective and approved collection identifier as application state instead of relying on the model to remember them from an earlier message.

ADK artifacts provide named, versioned file-like data managed separately from session state. Whether using that service or a simpler application store, retain the original exercise, proposed version, evidence references, and acceptance decision. The point is recoverability: a teacher should be able to understand and undo an accepted revision without reconstructing a long conversation.

Grounding requires more than finding a passage

Retrieval can supply relevant material, but relevance does not establish that the answer follows from it. A passage might contain the same character names while describing a different event. A grammar explanation may address a different construction. An apparently authoritative excerpt may be an outdated version of the teacher's own notes.

Require the assessment to identify which claim the cited passage supports. For a reading question, distinguish explicit textual evidence from a plausible inference. For a Latin exercise, distinguish the printed form from the grammatical interpretation. When two interpretations remain defensible, the useful result may be a rewritten question that removes the ambiguity, accompanied by an explanation of the original problem.

Keep source text clearly separate from instructions. A document may contain an example command, a quotation addressing an assistant, or an accidental instruction to ignore earlier rules. The application's policy should continue to come from trusted configuration. The retrieved passage is material to analyze. This matters even in an approved library, because approval of a document's educational relevance does not make every sentence an instruction to the software.

Begin with synthetic exercises and materials you are entitled to process. This makes debugging easier because test cases can be shared and repeated without carrying personal classroom information. If later versions use student responses, decide explicitly which fields are necessary and which records should persist. A useful pedagogical diagnosis rarely requires every identifying detail available in the original system.

Test the result and the route taken

ADK's evaluation guidance considers both final responses and the trajectory of tool use. That distinction is useful here. A correct-looking answer could come from an invented citation, while a valid alternative search sequence might produce excellent work. Test important invariants rather than requiring every successful run to imitate one exact transcript.

Expand the initial examples into a small evaluation set. Include a correct item that should remain unchanged, a wrong answer, a genuinely ambiguous passage, an absent source, a stale document version, an irrelevant search hit, a malformed exercise record, a temporary search failure, a repeated save, and source text containing misleading instructions. Also include a case where the assistant must stop because its available evidence cannot answer the question.

Use deterministic checks for structural facts: required fields exist, referenced passages were actually returned, drafts stay inside the permitted store, and the call budget is respected. Use a teacher's rubric for semantic quality: does the explanation follow from the passage, preserve the learning objective, and help the learner? An additional model can assist review, but agreement between two generated judgments is not a substitute for a trusted answer or human assessment.

Keep some cases aside while improving the prompt. Otherwise, it is easy to make ten familiar examples look excellent without improving general behavior. When a regression appears, preserve the failing input and trace, diagnose one likely cause, and compare the revised version against the earlier one. Measure unnecessary edits and unresolved cases alongside successful corrections.

A useful development sequence has four visible deliverables. First, produce the input and output records by hand for the five starter exercises. Second, implement the tools against a tiny local collection and test them without a model. Third, connect the model to those functions and inspect the complete event record for each example. Fourth, add the review interface only after the draft content and failure statuses are understandable.

Each stage should leave something that can be examined independently. If search retrieves the wrong passage, improve search before rewriting the diagnosis prompt. If the model cites the right passage but draws an unsupported conclusion, revise the reasoning criteria and add a counterexample. If the saved draft differs from the validated output, investigate the storage boundary. This sequence turns an apparently mysterious agent failure into a specific question about one component, while keeping the project small enough for an intermediate coder to maintain.

Make stopping and failure understandable

The application should enforce maximum tool calls, elapsed time, and a bounded retry policy. Repeating the same search with the same result is a reason to stop and report insufficient evidence. A model instruction to avoid excessive work is useful guidance; a runtime limit is what makes the bound dependable.

ADK's safety guidance distinguishes tool identities, authorization, and controls inside tools. Applied to this project, the search credential needs access to the approved library, while the draft writer needs only its draft area. A descriptive role such as careful reviewer does not enforce either boundary. The tool implementation and underlying permissions do.

In a website, keep service credentials in the server environment and expose a narrow application endpoint to the browser. Display concrete states: searching, inspecting evidence, draft saved, or stopped with an explanation. Show a saved artifact identifier only after the save succeeds. These details prevent the interface from confusing an intended action with a completed one.

Record usage across the entire run, including retries and evaluation calls. Compare the agent with the fixed workflow on completion rate, teacher review time, latency, and cost per accepted correction. A more elaborate system earns its complexity only when it solves meaningful additional cases. Separate testing of the software from any claim that it improves student learning; that requires its own classroom evidence.

A useful foundation when the first job stays small

The group's 8/10 score reflects durable engineering value and two complementary saved resources. The beginner course makes the components approachable; Google's guide and current documentation extend the path toward operational systems. The most useful reading habit is to preserve their architectural ideas while checking code, dates, and capability claims against current primary documentation.

A strong first milestone is one exercise reviewed with traceable evidence and a recoverable draft, including an honest failure path. Once that works across varied examples, extend the scope deliberately. The proposed exercise assistant has not been implemented or tested for this report; it is a concrete plan for turning the bookmarks into an inspectable project.

entries.title: Candle onboarding: demonstrate the shared activity before asking for commitment
entries.summary: A saved Candle walkthrough offers useful ideas for a visible first action and contextual questions. Its early review request and aggressive historical discount sequence deserve a separate judgment from its clear product demonstration.
entries.reason: A concrete onboarding study can improve educational-app introductions; the observed design should be distinguished from measured conversion or learning effects.
entries.html:
A demonstration before a commitment

César Álvarez’s March 21 bookmark praises an app he calls “Clandle” for opening with a demonstration video, asking contextual questions, and requesting a review during onboarding. The spelling is misleading: its inspected video poster explicitly identifies Candle: Couples & Relationship, published by Encore AI Labs. This is a relationship app with shared questions, games, photos, and other activities. The identification comes from the original poster and official listing, not from guessing at a similarly named tool.

The walkthrough is a useful design reference because it makes the app’s promise visible before asking someone to understand its navigation. Its value does not depend on accepting the author’s praise wholesale. The poster includes download and revenue assertions that were not independently verified. Neither popularity nor an attractive walkthrough establishes that a particular onboarding step causes conversion, retention, or learning. The captured text provides a creator’s analysis, not an instrumented study.

Understand the shared activity before the interface

Candle’s official site presents small shared activities as a recurring relationship experience. Its onboarding challenge is therefore partly social: a prospective user needs to understand an activity and why another person would participate. That is different from merely choosing a theme or creating an account. For a collaborative classroom tool, the transferable question is whether a learner can understand the shared task before a partner is available. A sample interaction can answer that without requiring invitations immediately.

Version context matters. Candle’s current App Store history lists an October 8 update with a new onboarding experience. The March bookmark is consequently a historical design example, not a reliable map of every screen a new user sees today. This report examines the reported patterns and verified product identities; it does not present a first-hand walkthrough of the current installed applications or reproduce historical prices as current offers.

Demonstrate a useful action early

The strongest idea is to show an action and its result before explaining the entire product. For a Latin reading app, a brief example could begin with one sentence, show the learner selecting a word, reveal a contextual hint, and return to the sentence. That communicates the interaction more directly than a succession of claims about personalized learning. The demonstration should use the same controls and terminology that the learner encounters immediately afterward.

Apple’s onboarding guidance recommends a quick, optional experience and teaching through interaction where possible. An original adaptation would therefore offer a small working example alongside the video. A learner can try selecting the word, undo the selection, and continue without creating an account. A teacher who already understands the interface can skip directly to lesson setup. Optionality should be visible at the point where it is needed, not hidden behind a lengthy sequence.

A demonstration has its own production requirements. Keep important instructions readable without audio, let people replay it, and provide a stable explanation if the video fails to load. On a slow classroom connection, the initial task should not wait for a large promotional asset. W3C’s pause, stop, and hide guidance is relevant when moving content runs automatically alongside other information. An endlessly animated introduction can consume the attention the lesson needs.

Ask questions whose answers change something

The bookmark treats early data collection as a positive pattern. Its usefulness depends on what happens next. Asking where someone discovered the app may help marketing attribution, but it does not necessarily improve their first task. A reading exercise can initially need only a language, a passage, and perhaps a preferred hint level. A detailed profile, school name, learning history, and motivation survey may add effort before the learner has experienced any benefit.

For each proposed onboarding question, write down the decision it controls. “Which passage are you studying?” can choose the exercise. “Would you like word hints?” can set a reversible preference. If the answer changes nothing yet, postpone or remove the question. When an AI feature uses the answer, show the effect concretely: selecting beginner support reveals a simpler explanation, rather than displaying a generic claim that the app has understood the learner deeply.

Do not invent a diagnosis from a short quiz. For a vocabulary tool, a few sample items can suggest a starting exercise, but they cannot establish a comprehensive proficiency level. Let the learner change that starting point. Likewise, a progress animation should represent work that actually happens. If the application is selecting a predefined lesson, describe that selection honestly instead of implying that a complex personalized curriculum is being computed behind decorative progress bars.

An early review request deserves criticism

The bookmark’s praise for requesting a review during onboarding conflicts directly with Apple’s ratings and reviews guidance. Apple advises waiting until people have engaged with the app and avoiding requests on first launch or during onboarding. A person who has only watched a sales demonstration can judge its presentation, but has little basis for rating the product’s lasting usefulness. The post identifies a conversion tactic; it does not establish a good default for a learning tool.

Separate three feedback needs. A comprehension question asks whether the learner understands the next action. A usability question asks whether something was confusing. A public app review asks for a broader judgment about the experience. These should not share one generic star prompt. After the first exercise, a neutral optional question about confusing instructions can improve the lesson. A later review request belongs at a natural break after meaningful use, with dismissal leaving the activity unaffected.

The same distinction applies to praise and emotional animation. Celebrate finishing a practice attempt without implying mastery that has not been assessed. A mascot can acknowledge effort, but it should not shame a pupil for taking longer or skipping a reminder. Candle’s flame mascot can make the introduction recognizable, but a school activity needs its own tone and feedback appropriate to the learning task.

Connect permissions and payment to an understood benefit

Permissions should follow the feature that needs them. Apple’s documentation on protected resources explains that an app must provide a meaningful purpose and handle the person’s authorization choice. In an English pronunciation exercise, microphone access makes sense when the learner chooses to record speech. Explain what is recorded and provide a text-based exercise if recording is declined. Opening the app is not, by itself, a reason to ask for every permission the product might eventually use.

An educational app should tie each request to its own dependencies. A reading demonstration does not need a camera. A reminder is optional unless the user chooses a reminder-based workflow. Check denied, later-enabled, and revoked permissions as carefully as successful setup. A graceful fallback should let someone understand the lesson before deciding whether to enable additional capabilities.

The expanded post makes its commercial emphasis explicit. Álvarez reports a €9.99 monthly price, a seven-day trial, a 71% annual-plan discount, and an 81% offer after closing the paywall. These are his March observations, not verified current prices or evidence of causal conversion gains. In replies he also asserts that early review requests improve ratings, without supplying a study. A teacher-builder should distinguish an effective product explanation from repeated attempts to turn a refusal into a purchase. If an introduction has demonstrated value, its next action can still offer a clear choice without making dismissal trigger another negotiation.

If a teaching product has paid features, show what is available before asking someone to invest in a long setup. Make the plan, renewal period, trial terms, and route back to the available experience understandable. This is an original design recommendation, not a finding about the current price or paywall behavior of the bookmarked app. A school pilot can avoid the issue entirely by using a clearly bounded free sample that requires no payment details.

Design for the person whose partner has not arrived

Candle’s shared-use premise raises a useful question for educational apps: what happens before the other participant joins? A pair-work language activity should let the first learner understand the task without exposing them to an empty room or forcing an invitation before the value is clear. A short sample dialogue can demonstrate the exchange with an explicitly labeled example partner.

After that sample, distinguish practice from live collaboration. The learner should know whether a response came from another person, a prepared example, or an AI role-play feature. Show the next step clearly: wait for a classmate, join a teacher’s group, or continue individual practice. Do not present simulated participation as evidence that a real partner is present.

Keep the initial account and invitation decisions proportional to the task. A teacher-led classroom might use a short session code, while a persistent homework exchange needs a different identity and progress model. Those are implementation choices for the proposed learning product, not claims about Candle’s internal architecture. Test the first-person-alone, second-person-joining, and disconnected-partner states before polishing the invitation animation.

This is where a demonstration earns its place. It can make the shared activity understandable before the social setup is complete. The first useful action should still lead to a real, recoverable experience once the introductory video ends.

Build a short educational flow from these observations

A useful first prototype could contain five moments: a concrete example, a safe attempt, one relevant preference, the first real task, and an optional next-step choice. For the Latin app, show a sentence and its hint interaction, let the learner try a different word, ask whether hints should be available automatically, open the selected passage, and offer to save progress after the exercise. These are proposed steps, not a measured optimum or a reconstruction of Candle.

Give an AI coding agent a small flow specification with the text, allowed actions, and destination for each moment. Include Back, Skip, and the behavior after closing and reopening the app. Keep the sample content fixed while testing the navigation; adding generated passages too early makes it harder to tell whether a failure comes from the flow or the content. A later model-generated hint should have a visibly recoverable loading and error state.

Review motion in terms of orientation. A selected preference can settle into its confirmed state; the next question can appear without making the learner chase it across the screen. Test larger text, keyboard focus, and the device’s reduced-motion setting. Preserve answers when someone returns to a prior step. A visually smooth forward sequence is incomplete if the first correction erases the learner’s work or leaves the interface in an impossible state.

Design the second visit at the same time

A first-run sequence also creates state that the rest of the product must understand. Store completion separately from optional preferences, so that changing the hint setting does not restart the introduction. Provide a way to replay the sample without deleting progress. If a teacher opens the app on a shared classroom device, make it clear whether the current preferences belong to that device or to a signed-in learner. Avoid presenting yesterday’s choices as a newly inferred personal profile.

Include an interrupted setup in the prototype review. Close the app after the practice action, reopen it, and check that the next screen offers a sensible continuation. Then try without connectivity. A bundled sample can still teach the interaction even if account creation or AI hints are unavailable, provided the interface explains which features need a connection. These details are easy to miss in a short promotional recording, yet they determine whether onboarding remains usable during an ordinary lesson.

Measure understanding as well as completion

Before comparing variants, define the first useful outcome. For this example, it is completing one passage interaction and understanding how to request a hint. Record where volunteers hesitate, what they believe will happen when they tap a control, and whether they can recover from a mistake. A short moderated session can reveal misunderstandings that a completion percentage conceals. This is a proposed evaluation, not a claim that a particular number of users would prove the design successful.

If a later experiment compares video-first and interactive-first versions, keep the lesson, audience, and available features comparable. Look beyond the number who reach the final onboarding screen. Check whether they start the actual exercise, use support appropriately, and return without needing the introduction again. A longer flow can produce more clicks while delaying learning; a shorter one can look efficient while leaving essential instructions unexplained. The decision should follow the task evidence.

This bookmark earns six as a concrete design reference that also contains a pattern worth rejecting. It shows how a demonstration, questions, motion, and motivation can form a coherent introduction. Its unverified commercial claims and historical walkthrough evidence limit stronger conclusions. For educational AI products, borrow the clarity of a visible first action, make personalization real and reversible, and let meaningful use precede demands for ratings, extensive data, or commitment.

entries.title: Steve Schoger’s Claude workflow: turn design judgment into precise edits
entries.summary: The useful shift is a designer directing a running page through focused changes, with code as the editable medium. This report connects the captured demonstration to practical reading activities, temporary review controls and current tool availability.
entries.reason: A practitioner-led workflow may reveal useful ways to iterate on hierarchy, layout and interaction, provided the actual examples and revisions are inspected.
entries.html:
Designing through a conversation with the running page

Steve Schoger’s March 20 bookmark introduces an hour-long account of using Claude Code as his main design tool. The attraction is a practitioner showing how decisions develop, rather than a claim that one prompt replaces design judgment. For an average coder, the useful question is whether conversational changes can make the browser itself a practical place to explore an interface.

The original video is Designing with Claude Code. Direct playback was unavailable here. A timestamped caption mirror, which identifies its text as YouTube’s automatic captions, describes a finance-app marketing page. It records a deliberately simple initial brief, replacement of invented UI with actual app screenshots, neutral-color adjustments, variable-font choices, revised hierarchy, and a temporary inline tool for positioning cropped images. Later passages discuss feature sections, demonstration testimonials, decorative divisions and comparison with an earlier version. Caption errors are possible, so these are a bounded account of the recorded workflow rather than a verified visual reconstruction.

A creator correction in the captured thread adds a concrete caution about the example identity. Schoger says the supposedly invented Axiom logo was actually a real logo; he had drawn the mark and asked ChatGPT for a name, then used its suggestion without checking. The account does not establish an independent assessment of similarity. It does show why a plausible generated name should remain provisional. For a classroom project, label invented identities as drafts and check existing uses before presenting them as an original public brand.

The important interpretation is that the person directs the design while the agent handles much of the implementation. Knowing what feels wrong, selecting a better relationship between elements, and deciding when to stop remain substantive work. This can be approachable without being effortless. A teacher already makes analogous judgments when deciding which sentence needs emphasis or how much explanation a learner can absorb at once.

The related tools have changed since March

The caption record says the demonstration starts without an added skill and later mentions ui.sh as work in progress with the Tailwind team. Do not retroactively attribute the demonstrated result to today’s skill collection. The current ui.sh Design page describes guidance for hierarchy, typography, spacing, components and responsive states. Its Ideas page describes generating alternative directions and comparing them through an option picker. These are documented later workflows, not a reproduction of the video.

Availability also matters. Tailwind’s September 9 announcement says the team is joining Shopify and closing new signups for commercial products including ui.sh, while retaining access for existing customers. The public instructions and example images should therefore be treated as readable references rather than a promise that a new reader can purchase access. The underlying conversational design method does not require buying that particular product.

The inspected ui.sh comparison shows two treatments of a team page. One uses a centered headline, gradient emphasis and separate cards; the other uses left alignment, a restrained accent and large portraits. This demonstrates different composition choices. It is a vendor-selected comparison, not a controlled experiment proving the skill’s general superiority. A portrait-based layout also depends on suitable imagery, which a school project may not have permission or reason to use.

Learn a small vocabulary that makes feedback precise

The most useful design vocabulary names relationships. Hierarchy describes what appears important first. Alignment establishes a shared edge. Spacing distinguishes related content from separate groups. Contrast makes differences visible. A prompt such as “make the instructions easier to find by placing them directly above the exercise, with less emphasis than the question” is more actionable than “make this look polished.” The first tells the agent what relationship to change.

Typography rewards similarly specific requests. The Inter project documents variable weights, optical sizes and features such as tabular numbers. These capabilities permit fine control, but the presence of a variable font does not guarantee good reading. For an educational page, inspect the actual passage, punctuation and language-specific characters. A type treatment that makes a short promotional headline elegant may be uncomfortable for a long explanation.

Line width is another practical parameter. The CSS length reference defines the ch unit relative to the advance width of the zero glyph, rather than as a literal count of arbitrary characters. It can help size a text block, but proportional letters vary. Ask the agent to propose a reading measure, then inspect actual lines at several sizes. Do not turn a convenient unit into a universal readability formula.

Tailwind’s text-wrapping documentation distinguishes balanced lines from the browser’s prettier wrapping behavior. These can improve headings, but they are presentation tools. A heading that is vague remains vague after its lines are balanced. Edit the wording before tuning the wrap, and check the result after a translation or content change.

A practical session: redesign an English reading activity

Start with a working activity containing one passage, one analytical question and one worked response. Save a copy before redesigning. The purpose is to make the relationship between evidence and interpretation easier to understand. Give the agent the actual text and explain which material is the source, which is the learner’s response, and which is the teacher’s commentary. Those roles should survive every visual experiment.

Request two structural alternatives before asking for detailed polish. One could place commentary beside the passage on wide screens; another could keep the passage above expandable commentary. Hold the wording constant. Compare where the learner’s attention must move to connect a claim with the sentence supporting it. The better structure depends on passage length, device size and the kind of task, so evaluate those conditions rather than choosing by first impression.

Once a direction is selected, refine one relationship at a time. Perhaps the question is too far from the relevant passage. Perhaps a source note looks like an instruction. Perhaps the worked response has so much emphasis that students read it before trying. State the observed problem and intended effect, then ask the agent to change only the relevant area. Keep the previous version available so an improvement can be distinguished from mere novelty.

Use realistic difficult content. Include a long quotation, a brief quotation, a student response that wraps over several lines, and a missing response. If the design relies on equal-height cards, these variations will reveal whether the arrangement still works. Do not shorten useful explanations simply to preserve symmetry. The interface should serve the material that will actually be taught.

Finish the session by having someone complete the activity without verbal guidance. Ask them to locate evidence, write an interpretation and revisit the explanation. Record hesitation and misunderstanding. This does not measure learning effectiveness, but it can reveal whether the design communicates the task. The proposed activity was not built or tested for this report.

Let the agent build temporary controls for judgment

Some visual decisions are easier to make by moving a control than by describing coordinates. A useful original application is a temporary comparison panel for a history explainer. It could adjust image crop, caption width and annotation position while preserving the source image. The teacher chooses the framing that keeps the relevant detail visible, then asks the agent to save those values and remove the editing interface.

The CSS object-position property is one mechanism for positioning replaced content inside its box. It provides a technical foundation for a crop control, but the author still decides what belongs in view. For a photograph of an inscription, cropping out the object’s surroundings may improve letter visibility while removing useful historical context. Keep a link to the complete image and explain why the crop was chosen.

Temporary controls are also useful for diagrams. A slider can adjust label spacing, a toggle can compare two annotation densities, and a selector can preview a short or long passage. These are tools for making a decision, not necessarily features to ship. Before removing them, record the chosen settings and inspect the finished page without the controls occupying space.

For video preparation, a small preview panel could switch between title-card, quotation and source-credit states. Review whether each remains readable at the intended output size. A layout that works in a full browser window may fail when embedded in a presentation or reduced to a phone screen. The agent can generate variations, while the teacher decides which serves the narration and checks the actual export later.

Use real content to make visual decisions honest

A school website can borrow the clarity of a marketing page without adopting its assumptions. A prominent product screenshot might become a real exercise preview. A feature section might show what learners will do and what support is available. A call to action might open a sample lesson. Each element should provide evidence of the actual experience rather than fill a familiar template slot.

Testimonials and impressive statistics require particular editorial care. If a prototype uses invented people or placeholder outcomes, keep that status explicit and replace them before publication. A polished card does not make an endorsement real. For an educational project with no evaluation data, explain the intended learning activity and show a worked example instead of inventing success rates. This is a concrete content decision, not a visual limitation.

Build a content inventory with each claim’s source, approval status and intended location. A coding assistant can help preserve that inventory during layout revisions. Ask it to report any wording changes separately from styling changes. A request to make a section shorter should not silently turn a qualified statement into a stronger promise. The teacher remains responsible for the accuracy of the final text.

For a Latin course site, the most persuasive visual may be a carefully annotated sentence rather than a generic image of classical architecture. The annotation can demonstrate the method while also supplying a distinctive graphic. That choice connects identity with content. It gives the page something specific to communicate and reduces the temptation to decorate an otherwise interchangeable layout.

Keep implementation quality visible

Designing in code shortens the distance between an idea and a rendered result, but it can also hide complexity from the person making visual decisions. Ask the agent to identify the components and styles changed after each substantial revision. If repeated sections have diverged into separate implementations, consolidate them once the design direction is stable. Premature abstraction can obstruct exploration; never consolidating can make later corrections expensive.

Check interaction states as well as the ideal screenshot. A reading control needs visible keyboard focus. A form needs an understandable error. A navigation item needs a clear current state. A long explanation should remain accessible when text is enlarged. These are part of design, even if a demonstration concentrates on composition. Current Claude Code guidance emphasizes supplying concrete verification evidence rather than relying on an assertion that work is finished.

Compare alternatives using a short decision record: what changed, why it changed, what improved, and what remains unresolved. Preserve at least one rejected version with its reason. This makes the process teachable. Students can see that a design decision is an argument about communication, not simply a personal preference or a model’s unexplained answer.

The score of 7 reflects the value of a practitioner-led approach and the accessibility of making focused changes in a working page. The strongest lesson is to translate visual judgment into specific, testable instructions. The limits are equally concrete: the original video was not directly viewed here, automatic captions may contain errors, vendor examples are selected, and no workflow speed or learning benefit was measured. For a first attempt, choose a page whose content you already understand. That leaves attention available for observing layout and interaction, instead of simultaneously judging unfamiliar subject matter. Use the method to improve a real communication task, with enough evidence to explain why the final version is better.
