entries.title: Nunchi autoresearch: evaluate the experiment before believing its score
entries.summary: Nunchi automates strategy edits and historical evaluation. Its strongest contribution is an inspectable research loop; current code and older instructions differ, and striking reported backtests require a reproducible evaluator, strict chronology, and untouched evidence.
entries.reason: The research-loop structure is technically interesting, but financial data requires strong controls against leakage, overfitting and unrealistic execution assumptions.
entries.html:
Automated experimentation is the interesting claim

Nunchi's 20 March announcement introduces an open-source trading-research loop inspired by Karpathy's autoresearch. Its phrasing suggests an agent teaching itself to trade. A more precise interpretation is an agent repeatedly proposing strategy-code changes, receiving a historical evaluation score, and retaining changes that improve that score. This distinction determines what the experiment can establish.

The project README reports 103 autonomous experiments and a large improvement in simulated Sharpe ratio, from approximately 2.7 to 21.4, with a very small reported drawdown. Those are project-reported backtest figures, not verified returns. The documented design restricts edits to a strategy file and keeps the evaluator separate. That separation is valuable, but it cannot make an inaccurate evaluator economically realistic.

For a teacher or average coder, the strongest reason to study this project is its experiment structure. It makes hypotheses executable, records decisions, and exposes the difference between optimizing a score and discovering something that survives unfamiliar data. The same lessons apply to quiz selection, search ranking, and educational simulations.

What the loop actually learns

Karpathy's original autoresearch repository organizes automated research around a mutable training program, a fixed evaluation setup, and a constrained experiment budget. Nunchi adapts the pattern to strategies rather than model-training code. The shared idea is disciplined iteration: change something, measure it under a stated contract, and decide whether to retain it.

This is not necessarily model-weight training. The coding agent can remain the same while the program it edits changes. Improvements may come from parameter adjustments, new features, removing an unhelpful rule, or exploiting an accidental property of the simulator. The output is a selected program and its research history.

A useful mental exercise is to replace “trading strategy” with “sorting algorithm.” If the evaluator checks only ten short lists, an agent may discover a program that excels on those lists and fails on larger ones. More autonomous experiments intensify the search, but do not widen the evaluator's coverage. In finance, the analogous failures are harder to see because historical markets supply only one realized sequence.

The research loop therefore needs two contracts: what the agent may modify, and what evidence counts as improvement. The first protects the test from direct rewriting. The second protects the research conclusion from becoming merely the highest number found.

Read the current evaluator, not just the launch results

The current evaluation source includes BTC, ETH, SOL, GOLD, and OIL, with train, validation, and test boundaries spanning January to May 2026. The older research instructions describe BTC, ETH, and SOL with a July 2024–March 2025 validation window. Meanwhile, the out-of-sample runner's comment still describes an April–December 2025 test period. These retrieved files do not describe one consistent historical experiment.

This does not establish that earlier results were fabricated. It establishes that a reader cannot reproduce a headline by combining today's code with yesterday's description and assuming they match. A serious reproduction needs a commit identifier, data snapshot, split definitions, selected strategy, and exact command or entry point.

The evaluator also provides the current completed bar to the strategy and then simulates execution from that bar's close, with fixed slippage and fees. That convention deserves scrutiny for any signal using the bar's closing information. The source catches strategy exceptions and substitutes no signals. These are code observations, not a complete audit or an executed test.

Before interpreting a score, require the run to disclose whether every intended timestamp was processed and whether exceptions occurred. A result generated under a partial or silently failing run is not comparable with a full successful run, even if both print the same metric names.

A winning validation score can be a selection artifact

Suppose a research process tries one hundred plausible variations and reports only the best. Even when each variation has no durable advantage, some can fit the historical period unusually well. Repeatedly inspecting validation results turns that period into part of the selection process. It is no longer an untouched examination.

The primary research paper The Probability of Backtest Overfitting examines this general selection problem. Its relevance here is methodological: the number and diversity of attempted strategies matter when judging a chosen result. A leaderboard's best row cannot stand in for the whole search history.

Keep discarded attempts, failed runs, and parameter changes in the research ledger. Record why each change was proposed before seeing its outcome. This helps distinguish a coherent hypothesis from a story invented to explain a favorable number afterward.

An untouched final period should remain inaccessible to the editing agent until a candidate is frozen. If the result is disappointing and the agent revises the strategy in response, that period has become development evidence. The next final evaluation requires genuinely new data or a separately reserved test. Naming a file “test” cannot enforce that boundary by itself.

Build the chronology explicitly

For each feature, define when its value became available. A daily total is not available at the day's opening. A revised economic series may contain information published months later. Even apparently simple rolling statistics can leak future values through an incorrect shift, a full-sample normalization, or a join that ignores publication time.

Freqtrade's lookahead-analysis documentation explains how backtesting over a fully populated dataframe can hide future access. Automated comparisons can reveal some such problems, but they do not validate every data source or execution assumption. Use targeted checks alongside a clear time model.

A proposed evaluation record should include observation time, publication time where relevant, decision time, and simulated execution time. Require observation and publication to precede the decision, and execution to follow it. If the simulator assumes instantaneous action at a boundary, disclose that approximation and test a delayed alternative.

TimeSeriesSplit provides ordered splits with a configurable gap. It is a useful building block, not a complete financial evaluation policy. The required gap depends on feature lookbacks, label horizons, and overlapping outcomes. Randomly mixing adjacent observations can create a deceptively easy task.

Execution assumptions deserve their own experiments

A strategy's theoretical signal is only one component of a simulated result. Fees, spreads, funding, latency, partial fills, and unavailable liquidity can dominate a small statistical edge. These quantities should be parameters with documented units and provenance, rather than hidden constants accepted because the backtest runs successfully.

Nunchi includes a stress-test script that varies slippage and taker fees and examines quarterly subsets. This is a constructive addition. It remains a sensitivity test inside the same simulator, so agreement across those runs cannot rule out an accounting or timing defect shared by all of them.

Funding is an example of a detail that requires venue-specific checking. Hyperliquid's documentation describes hourly funding payments and the relationship to an eight-hour rate calculation. A research implementation must establish whether a downloaded field represents the hourly payment rate or a differently scaled rate before applying it. A familiar-looking division factor is not sufficient evidence.

For a proposed replication, first create tiny synthetic scenarios with manually calculable results: one position opened and closed at the same price, one price change, one funding event, and one partial reduction. Compare the ledger with hand calculations. These tests address accounting correctness before market complexity makes discrepancies difficult to diagnose.

A bounded replication plan for an average coder

Begin with a written question such as whether a simple feature improves a fixed simulated baseline after stated costs. Freeze the dataset and evaluator. Keep the first experiment small enough that its complete trade ledger can be inspected. Do not attach a wallet or execution service; the object of study is the research procedure.

Create an experiment manifest containing code revision, data hash, split windows, objective, cost settings, model identifier, and budget. Limit how many candidates can be attempted. Require each proposed edit to name its expected effect and the observation that would count against it. A simpler unsuccessful hypothesis can be more informative than an unexplained winning composite.

Use a plain baseline with comparable market exposure and costs. Report performance across periods and instruments, not only the aggregate. Remove individual strategy components to test whether each contributes. If a small parameter change destroys the result, record that sensitivity rather than presenting the best setting as an established rule.

After selecting one candidate, freeze it and evaluate the reserved data once. Produce a short research note with the full attempt count, failures, assumptions, and negative findings. The desired outcome is a reproducible conclusion about this experiment. A result that fails under more realistic assumptions is still a successful research exercise.

Make the research ledger tell the whole story

A useful experiment table needs more than a score column. Record the parent candidate, hypothesis, changed parameters, elapsed time, completed observations, exception count, and retention decision. Store the exact cost assumptions beside the result. If a run reaches a time limit, classify it as incomplete rather than comparing its partial history with a full baseline.

Keep a separate selection log showing when researchers saw each dataset. This is particularly important in an autonomous loop, where an agent may read an earlier report containing supposedly hidden results. Access boundaries must cover logs and summaries as well as raw files. A test period is no longer hidden if its detailed performance has already appeared in the agent's context.

For review, choose a handful of representative decisions and reconstruct them from the information available at that moment. Show the input features, selected target, simulated fill, fee, and subsequent valuation. This small audit trail often teaches more than an attractive equity curve. It can reveal whether a surprising gain came from the intended hypothesis, an accounting convention, or a data alignment error that deserves correction.

Transfer the loop to educational software

A lower-stakes adaptation could optimize the ordering of a vocabulary review session. Let an agent modify one scheduling function while a fixed simulator generates fictional learners with different forgetting patterns. The evaluator measures retained items, repetition burden, and whether struggling learners are neglected. No student records are necessary for the initial experiment.

Reserve several learner profiles that the agent cannot inspect. A scheduler that performs well only for the most common profile should not win automatically. Include a simple spaced schedule as the baseline and require a readable explanation of each change. This makes fairness and generalization visible in a form students can understand.

The same exercise exposes the limits of simulation. A fictional learner model cannot establish real educational effectiveness. It can reveal implementation bugs and test behavior under specified assumptions. A later classroom study would need its own design and appropriate school processes; the simulator is preparation, not validation of learning outcomes.

For a lesson on scientific reasoning, ask students to compare the best development score with the reserved-profile result. They can explain why searching more candidates sometimes widens that gap. Nunchi's ambitious financial setting becomes a concrete doorway into hypothesis testing, measurement design, and honest reporting.

Useful research machinery, unresolved economic evidence

Score seven reflects the value of the automated experiment architecture and the availability of inspectable code. The project's headline results remain self-reported simulations. Current source inconsistencies make version pinning essential, while timing, accounting, data access, and repeated selection all require independent scrutiny.

The productive use is to study and improve the research process: fixed evaluators, explicit assumptions, complete logs, constrained edits, and reserved evidence. More experiments can discover better candidates, but they can also discover weaknesses in a benchmark. The distinction is settled by careful evaluation, not by the word autonomous.

entries.title: Karpathy’s autoresearch: a bounded laboratory for useful experiments
entries.summary: Karpathy’s compact training loop makes automated experimentation inspectable through a fixed evaluator and reversible changes. The deployment guide and personal-laboratory account become useful when their overnight promises are translated into hardware-specific baselines, replication, and bounded educational experiments.
entries.reason: An explicit proposal-test-keep-or-revert loop is broadly important for AI development, but its value depends on a meaningful evaluator and reproducible experiments.
entries.html:
A small laboratory with a clear score

Autoresearch is most interesting when understood as a controlled experiment loop rather than a promise of an autonomous research institution. Andrej Karpathy’s public project gives a coding agent a compact language-model training setup, a restricted place to make changes, and a numerical evaluation. The agent proposes a change, runs training, reads the result, retains or discards the change, and tries again. The human designs the experiment environment and the instructions that govern the search.

The two bookmarks approach the same framework from different positions: a deployment guide helps a newcomer understand the training loop, while a personal experiment report imagines a continuously operating research team. Both make the method approachable, but useful autonomy still depends on the experiment design. A running process needs a meaningful objective, trustworthy measurement, and evidence that improvements survive outside the examples used to discover them.

For a teacher with average coding knowledge, the most accessible application is probably not training a language model. It is improving a bounded workflow: extracting exercise content from documents, generating structured practice questions, producing accessible lesson pages, or selecting useful passages from a reference collection. Autoresearch contributes a discipline: change something specific, measure the consequences, retain evidence, and compare with a baseline. The GPU training repository is one concrete implementation of that discipline.

What the two saved accounts establish

Alex Finn’s expanded March 20 post describes agents experimenting with system prompts, local models, and low-rank adaptations, alongside agents discussing a new application. He proposes moving more work onto local hardware. These are descriptions of his setup and ambitions, not a published comparison of research outcomes. Neither continuous operation nor agent debate establishes that the resulting ideas are correct or useful.

Hoeem’s complete March 8 deployment article walks through hardware, setup, a manual training run, autonomous iteration, logs, and troubleshooting. It distinguishes the original project from a Mac adaptation. Its strongest advice is to establish a working baseline before delegating experiments. Its weaker shortcuts describe validation loss as general intelligence, estimate overnight throughput from the training window, and use popularity as reassurance about source code.

Those shortcuts need correction rather than dismissal. A practical guide can lower the entry barrier while simplifying away important experimental qualifications. This report checks the underlying repositories, explains what the score measures, and turns the workflow into a bounded pilot. It does not reproduce dated subscription prices or assume that every machine mentioned in an early tutorial supports the current code.

The original design is intentionally constrained

The original repository organizes the experiment around three files. The agent changes training code; fixed preparation utilities supply data handling and evaluation; a human-edited instruction file defines the research process. Training uses a five-minute budget excluding startup and compilation, with lower validation bits per byte as the objective. Current upstream requirements specify an NVIDIA GPU and point to community forks for other platforms. This report did not install or run either the original or a fork.

The research instructions require a baseline, a dedicated branch, and an experiment log. They restrict edits to the training file, prohibit changing the evaluation and adding dependencies, and describe retaining improvements while reverting unsuccessful changes. They also ask the agent to keep working until interrupted. That last instruction is a research-demo choice, not a sensible default for every classroom builder: an adaptation should have an explicit overall budget and a useful stopping report.

The separation between mutable candidate and fixed evaluator is the important architectural feature. If the worker can change both the solution and the definition of success, the resulting score becomes difficult to interpret. Even a well-intentioned edit to “fix” evaluation can make results incomparable. When the evaluator genuinely needs correction, treat that as a new experiment series and rerun the baseline under the revised rules.

This restriction is a research protocol, not automatically a security guarantee. Instructions saying a file must remain unchanged do not themselves make the filesystem read-only. A robust adaptation can check file hashes or enforce access boundaries, while preserving a clean baseline that can be restored. The appropriate controls depend on what the experiment is allowed to touch.

Choose a baseline for the machine actually available

The Mac adaptation linked by the deployment guide changes the execution environment. Its README describes Apple Metal support, removal of a hard dependency on the original attention implementation, and different handling of compilation and memory. It is a separate implementation whose results should be compared against its own recorded baseline. A numerical result from another machine is context, not a target every reader should expect to reproduce.

Apple’s PyTorch guidance explains the MPS backend used for accelerated operations on supported Macs. Hardware identity, operating system, framework version, and backend availability all matter. Check those against the chosen repository revision instead of inferring compatibility from the computer’s purchase year. A small trial that succeeds provides better evidence than a broad statement that all recent computers should work.

The guide’s reassurance about a small, popular fork should also be interpreted carefully. Inspectable source and a visible history make review possible; they are not a guarantee that every dependency or future change is appropriate. For this project, the practical review is focused: what files can the experimenter edit, what data is downloaded, which tools run, and where results are written? Keep the experiment separate from unrelated personal projects.

Local execution shifts costs rather than eliminating them. Memory and GPU capacity constrain which candidates fit, electricity and hardware time remain resources, and an agent may still call a hosted service. Do not purchase hardware just to imitate a personal-laboratory post. First identify a question worth testing and whether the resources already available can answer a smaller version of it.

What bits per byte measures—and what it does not

The inspected evaluation implementation computes predictive loss over validation text, normalizes it by byte length, and converts it to bits. This makes the objective less tied to a particular tokenization than a simple per-token score. In ordinary terms, a lower number means the trained model assigns better probabilities to the evaluation text under this measurement. It does not directly measure factual reliability, teaching skill, conversational usefulness, or the quality of a finished application.

The training source also distinguishes timed training from total runtime. Its budget accounting excludes initial warmup steps and reports both training and total seconds. Consequently, dividing an evening by five minutes is only a rough upper-level estimate of throughput: editing, startup, evaluation, failed experiments, and agent deliberation also take time. The number of completed experiments is an outcome to observe, not an entitlement supplied by the prompt.

A fixed time budget asks a specific question: which candidate performs better with this amount of training on this environment? It does not answer which architecture is best after a week of training or on another device. A larger model may look poor because it makes fewer updates within the budget; a smaller model may benefit from speed. That tradeoff is part of the experiment rather than a flaw, provided the conclusion stays within its scope.

The same distinction applies to educational tools. Optimizing worksheet generation under a thirty-second deadline may favor a different method from preparing a carefully reviewed examination. State the operational budget alongside the quality target so that the winner solves the actual problem.

Read the progress curve as a search history

The repository includes an original progress chart labeled with eighty-three experiments and fifteen retained improvements. Its gray points show rejected candidates, while the green line tracks the best retained score. This is a meaningful illustration of selective progress: most attempts need not be improvements for the search to move forward. It is an author-provided example, not a replicated result from this report.

One visible annotation identifies a random-seed change among the retained results. That is an especially useful reason to distinguish a better observed run from a better method. A favorable initialization can improve one measurement without establishing that an architectural change is robust. The chart alone does not provide uncertainty intervals or a full replication analysis.

For your own experiments, preserve unsuccessful trials rather than presenting only the descending best-score line. Record the hypothesis, the actual change, the score, resource use, and whether the run was valid. A crash is not a zero-quality solution measured on the same scale; it is a failed trial requiring separate interpretation. A polished chart should make that difference clear.

Keep the original output for each accepted candidate. If the score was computed incorrectly or the evaluator later changes, you need enough evidence to reassess the decision. A summary sentence such as “better explanations” is much weaker than the examples, rubric decisions, and revision that produced it.

Search can optimize noise as well as quality

Repeatedly choosing the best result from many trials creates a selection problem. Some candidates will look unusually good by chance. The more adaptively the next trial depends on the previous score, the more the evaluation becomes part of the search. Research on adaptive data analysis and holdout reuse explains why repeatedly consulting a nominally held-out dataset can itself cause overfitting. Merely naming a file “test” does not preserve its independence.

Use development examples for frequent feedback and reserve a separate final set for occasional confirmation. When an improvement is small, rerun the baseline and candidate under comparable conditions. For model training, test more than one seed where resources permit. For generated lesson content, repeat representative prompts and examine variation rather than accepting the best-looking sample. A genuine improvement should survive reasonable changes in the particular run.

PyTorch’s reproducibility guidance documents sources of randomness and limits to reproducibility across environments and releases. The practical lesson is to record versions, hardware, data, and random settings when they can affect a result. Reproducibility does not mean pretending all variability disappears; it means making the relevant conditions visible and testing whether conclusions survive it.

Decide in advance what size of improvement would justify extra complexity. An obscure implementation that gains a fraction of a point may be a poor choice for a solo teacher who must maintain it. Retaining a simpler candidate with indistinguishable performance can be a better engineering decision than chasing the smallest numerical gain.

A training pilot that teaches experimental reasoning

For a teacher or builder who specifically wants to understand language-model training, begin with a deliberately small question: does changing one optimizer setting improve the measured outcome within the same time budget? This is a proposed learning exercise, not a performance claim. Its output should be an experiment record a learner can explain, even if the candidate fails to beat the baseline.

First record the repository revision, environment, selected backend, data identity, and baseline result. Run the baseline again before asking an agent to optimize anything. The difference between those runs gives an initial indication of variability. If either run crashes or the evaluator fails, resolve that operational problem before treating a candidate score as comparable evidence.

Next write the hypothesis in plain language: the proposed setting may learn useful patterns faster, but may also make training unstable. Identify the one permitted change and leave the data and scoring rules alone. Ask the agent to state the expected tradeoff before it sees the result. This makes the later explanation less likely to become a story invented after the fact.

Compare the candidate with the baseline on quality, runtime, memory, and validity. A candidate that crashes has taught something about the available resource envelope, but it has not achieved a meaningful zero loss. A candidate that scores slightly better deserves replication before adoption. A candidate that scores similarly with simpler code may be preferable for learning and maintenance.

Finish with a short laboratory note: question, method, observation, uncertainty, and next useful experiment. Ask learners to distinguish the observation that this run scored lower from the broader claim that this setting is generally better. Then ask what additional runs or environments would support the broader claim. This turns an impressive automation demonstration into a lesson about inference.

Retain the failed candidate’s diff and its log even after returning the working tree to the accepted version. If the next experiment revisits that idea, the agent should explain what new evidence or changed condition makes another attempt worthwhile. A research process improves when it remembers why a proposal failed, not merely when it accumulates commits.

A second experiment: finding the right passage

A useful coding project is a search helper for a teacher-approved collection of Latin or history notes. The task is to retrieve the passage that supports an answer, not to improvise the answer from memory. Build a set of questions with known relevant passages, including a few questions the collection cannot answer. The explicit no-answer cases prevent the system from appearing helpful by always returning something.

Start with a simple baseline such as keyword search. Let the experimenter vary one bounded component: text chunk size, query normalization, ranking weights, or a prompt used to select among retrieved passages. Keep the source collection and evaluator fixed during a series. Record both missed relevant passages and irrelevant passages returned. A search method that retrieves everything can achieve high recall while being unusable for a busy teacher.

Inspect failure categories before choosing the next change. If questions fail because the source material is absent, changing retrieval cannot solve the problem. If Latin inflection prevents matching, normalization may help. If long chapters bury relevant sentences, chunking may matter. The loop should formulate a hypothesis tied to observed failures rather than randomly rewrite the entire application after every score.

Use a final set containing different wording and different documents. Then manually check a few high-confidence results and a few abstentions. This reveals whether the method learned a useful retrieval behavior or merely adapted to familiar question phrasing. The example requires no model training, yet preserves the original project’s central relationship between a bounded candidate, fixed observations, and selective retention.

Transfer the experiment structure, then rebuild the evaluator

Finn’s wider ambitions include prompt experiments and discussion about application ideas. These can borrow the proposal-test-retain pattern, but they need different evidence from model training. A discussion that produces ten ideas has generated candidates. It has not evaluated demand, implementation feasibility, or teaching value. An independent observation must connect the proposed idea to the outcome it claims to improve.

Consider a proposed interactive Latin vocabulary room. One version labels objects directly; another reveals a label only after the learner tries to recall it. A rendering agent can implement both versions, and automated checks can confirm that labels and controls work. Whether the interaction helps retention is a separate educational question. An automated aesthetic score or longer session time cannot settle it by itself.

The experimental adaptation should therefore separate software validity from learning evaluation. Keep both designs accessible and functional, document their intended difference, and arrange teacher review before planning any classroom comparison. For early development, a useful outcome may simply be that one design produces fewer ambiguous instructions. Do not rename that narrower result improved learning.

The same rule applies to application performance. If the objective is faster page load, retain functional checks while measuring speed. Removing the exercise entirely might make a page very fast while destroying its purpose. A good evaluator encodes the task’s essential constraints, and a human remains responsible for noticing which important properties the current score leaves out.

Negative results also deserve a useful description. Suppose adding more examples to a lesson-generation instruction improves formatting but makes explanations repetitive. Record both effects and retain the examples that exposed the tradeoff. A later experiment might keep the formatting guidance while removing the repeated explanation pattern. Without a clear record, an agent can rediscover the same failed idea several times and mistake repetition for exploration.

Keep search efficiency separate from final quality. One process may reach a good candidate quickly but plateau; another may take longer and discover a better approach. For a teacher preparing tomorrow’s lesson, the first may be preferable. For a reusable tool that will serve hundreds of future activities, the second may justify further investigation. Decide which situation applies before interpreting an experiment count as success. The purpose of automation is to make useful questions cheaper to investigate, while preserving enough evidence to decide whether their answers deserve to be trusted.

A practical operating plan for a small builder

Begin with a single candidate file or instruction package, one reliable evaluation command, a baseline, and a small experiment budget. Ask for a hypothesis before each edit and an evidence-based decision afterward. Preserve the current accepted version separately from the latest experiment. This makes it possible to stop at any time without losing a usable artifact.

Budget the whole process: the agent’s reasoning, external services, evaluation work, failed attempts, and human review. A short training window does not cap total spending. Likewise, a free repository does not make hardware or API use free. For a first trial, use already available resources and a narrow task rather than buying infrastructure to match an impressive demonstration.

Define several legitimate outcomes: improved candidate, no meaningful improvement, evaluator defect, insufficient evidence, or blocked environment. A run that discovers a broken evaluation can be valuable even if it produces no accepted change. What matters is that the report names that outcome honestly. Do not force every session to end with a success narrative.

Stop when the budget is reached, recent experiments repeat the same idea without useful evidence, or the next step requires a decision outside the agreed scope. Review the experiment log before expanding the search. Parallel agents may increase throughput, but they also create competing branches, duplicated experiments, and more review work. The simplest successful loop is the best baseline for deciding whether that complexity is justified.

Autoresearch earns its high collection score because it offers a compact, inspectable example of automated experimentation and inspires several practical adaptations. The two retained bookmarks bring its collection score to nine; they do not establish that every proposed application works. Adopt its experimental discipline before its overnight rhetoric. For a teacher-builder, a small workflow that demonstrably improves on unseen examples is more useful than a continuously running system whose definition of progress has never been tested.

entries.title: Obsidian and Claude Code: a traceable workspace for lessons and app ideas
entries.summary: A local note vault can supply reusable evidence and context for an AI assistant. The useful version starts with a small, reviewable course workspace rather than assuming the saved video establishes a complete personal assistant.
entries.reason: A local, inspectable knowledge base can support research and content creation, but indexing, permissions and factual provenance matter more than the assistant metaphor.
entries.html:
A personal knowledge workspace, with a narrower promise than JARVIS

The saved CyrilXBT post recommends combining Obsidian with Claude Code and presents the result as a personal JARVIS that takes an hour to establish. Its attached recording is displayed as 58 minutes and 57 seconds. The capture does not supply a transcript, a dependable chapter list, a repository, or the identity of an integration plugin. Consequently, the useful claim to investigate is the combination itself: can a readable collection of notes become working material for an assistant that can search, edit, and create files?

That is a credible starting point. It does not establish that the recording delivers a general personal assistant, nor that one hour is sufficient for a reader's particular archive. This report evaluates a practical workspace built from documented capabilities. The workflows below are original proposals, not a reconstruction of unseen video instructions or evidence that the setup has been tested here.

For a teacher, the attraction is continuity. Lesson ideas, source extracts, exercise drafts, and observations from previous lessons often occupy disconnected documents. A useful assistant would locate the relevant material, preserve its provenance, and help turn it into the next teachable object. For an app builder, the same arrangement could connect research notes to requirements and implementation decisions. The advantage comes from the quality of those connections, not from the number of notes imported.

Why the two tools can work together

Obsidian defines a vault as a local folder. This makes the basic integration unusually understandable: the notes are files that another authorized program can work with. Claude Code can operate on a working directory, while Obsidian supplies a writing and navigation interface. A specialized bridge may add conveniences, but a minimal file-based experiment does not require assuming an undocumented native partnership between the products.

Think of the vault as a small library with an editorial desk. The library holds source notes and established material; the desk holds proposed changes. Claude can help at the desk, but the presence of a file in the library does not make its contents true. A confident summary of an unreliable note remains unreliable. Separating original sources from your interpretation prevents the assistant from turning yesterday's tentative thought into today's apparent evidence.

Obsidian properties provide structured fields such as text, lists, dates, and checkboxes, stored in YAML at the beginning of a note. A modest shared vocabulary helps both human browsing and machine processing. For a source note, useful fields might include the source URL, access date, topic, and review status. For a lesson, use level, objective, estimated duration, and publication state. These are proposed conventions rather than a schema Obsidian requires.

Claude Code's memory documentation distinguishes instructions you maintain in CLAUDE.md from auto memory written by the assistant. Neither is equivalent to loading every note in a vault. Instructions guide how work should be done; the task still needs the relevant evidence. An enormous archive is not automatically present in the model's working context simply because it is available on disk.

Start with one course, not your entire archive

Create a separate experimental vault containing a small teaching unit. Copy ten or twenty documents that you already understand, rather than moving the only originals. Include one lesson plan, a vocabulary list, a few source notes, and a short record of common learner mistakes. The aim is to make errors visible: you should know enough about the material to notice when the assistant invents a relationship or overlooks a constraint.

Use a simple layout: Sources for attributed material, Concepts for your explanations, Lessons for approved sequences, Drafts for generated work, and Review for unresolved questions. Add an index note that explains those categories and links to a representative example of each. Avoid spending the first session designing a perfect universal taxonomy. A workable folder structure that you consistently use is more valuable than a comprehensive structure that makes filing burdensome.

Write a short project instruction file explaining the audience, language conventions, output location, and evidence requirements. For example: generated lessons belong in Drafts; references must point to existing source notes; uncertain grammatical analyses must be flagged; source files should remain intact unless a specific correction is requested. Treat this as a clear working brief. Ordinary instructions are not a technical barrier against unwanted writes, so use the tool's actual access and permission controls for boundaries that must be enforced.

Give the first task a limited target: inspect the index and selected notes, then produce an inventory of what they cover and what is missing. Do not ask for a semester curriculum immediately. Check the inventory against the files. If it confuses an example sentence with an authoritative rule, correct the structure before building more content on top of it. Early retrieval errors become expensive when they are repeated across many lessons.

A useful initial instruction could be: “Using only these twelve notes, propose a twenty-minute practice session on the accusative case. For every exercise, identify the source note and the skill being practised. Put unresolved questions in a separate review list.” This makes the output inspectable. You can judge source use, pedagogical sequence, and factual accuracy independently instead of accepting a polished worksheet as a single undifferentiated result.

From notes to exercises with an audit trail

Consider a Latin lesson on direct objects. Begin with an approved explanation and a small vocabulary set. Ask Claude to identify the concepts the learner must already know, then propose a progression from recognition to production. A recognition task might ask which noun receives the action; a production task might require completing an ending. The assistant should explain why each distractor would appeal to a learner with a particular misconception.

Keep answers and explanations in a teacher file separate from the student handout. This is an editorial choice that reduces accidental answer leakage when material is exported. Require stable exercise identifiers so that a later correction can be traced across worksheet, answer key, and app content. If exercise LAT-ACC-07 changes, you should not have to search by an almost identical sentence in three places.

Next, request a review pass aimed at ambiguity. Could two answers be accepted? Does an unfamiliar word accidentally test vocabulary rather than case recognition? Is the example natural enough to teach? These questions depend on subject expertise. Claude can help surface candidates, but a second model response is not independent linguistic authority. Where a point matters, check the approved grammar source rather than settling the disagreement through repeated prompting.

After the lesson, add a brief reflection note recording which exercise confused learners and why. Use aggregated observations rather than identifiable student records. Then ask for a revision that cites the reflection and preserves the successful parts. This creates a concrete learning loop: evidence from teaching changes the next version. It is more useful than asking the assistant to continually “improve” a lesson without a stated problem.

The same pattern works for English reading comprehension. Store the text, permission or provenance information, learning objective, and approved answer rationale together. Generate questions with explicit evidence spans, then reject items whose answers depend on outside knowledge. The vault becomes a record of why an exercise exists and how it was checked, rather than merely a larger repository of AI-generated worksheets.

Turn research into an app brief without losing the distinction

For an educational app, create a feature note that links to the teaching problem. A proposed spaced-practice screen, for example, should connect to observed learner difficulties and a precise interaction: present one item, accept an answer, explain the result, and select a next item. Ask Claude to separate known requirements, assumptions, and open decisions before generating implementation tasks.

Move the implementation into a suitable code project when it becomes software work. Keep the vault as the place for the rationale and curriculum content, and link to the code revision or release note. This avoids mixing disposable build output with carefully maintained notes. It also makes it easier to answer a later question: did the application behave incorrectly, or was the underlying teaching rule itself wrong?

A useful handoff document includes an input example, expected output, an edge case, and a failure state. For a quiz generator, the edge case might be an item with two valid answers; the failure state should explain how the interface asks for review rather than silently selecting one. These details are usually more valuable to an average coder than a lengthy aspirational description of an intelligent learning platform.

Once the same editorial process repeats, consider packaging it as a small Claude Code skill. For example, a lesson-review skill could load your rubric and produce a consistent report. Skills can contain instructions and supporting resources, and their bodies are loaded when used. This can reduce repeated briefing, but the proposed skill still needs examples and tests; moving a vague prompt into a named folder does not make it reliable.

Make retrieval and maintenance observable

Build a small retrieval check before expanding the vault. Write five questions whose answers are in known notes and two whose answers are absent. Ask the assistant to identify its source files and explicitly report missing evidence. A good result includes appropriate abstention. A system that invents an answer for every question can appear more capable while being less useful for teaching.

Test one misleading case as well: an outdated note that conflicts with a newer approved explanation. Mark the dates and statuses clearly, then see whether the assistant notices the conflict. Do not solve this by hiding every difficult document. Real archives contain drafts, contradictions, and abandoned ideas. The workflow should preserve those distinctions instead of flattening everything into a single voice of authority.

Review changes as changes. For small batches, inspect the before-and-after text and the list of modified files. For larger projects, version control can support that comparison if you are comfortable using it, but it should not become a prerequisite for the first experiment. At minimum, maintain dated copies outside the live working folder and practise restoring one.

Obsidian's backup guidance explicitly distinguishes synchronization from backup. Synchronization spreads current changes across devices; that can include an unwanted deletion or rewrite. A separate recoverable copy matters particularly when an assistant can modify many files quickly. The point is practical recoverability, not a complicated infrastructure project.

What the combination does not solve

A local vault does not imply local model inference. Obsidian's Sync security documentation concerns how its own synchronization protects remote data; it does not determine what another tool sends to its model service. Treat the Claude connection as a separate data flow. For school work, an experimental vault of public curriculum material and invented examples is easier to evaluate than a folder containing identifiable student information.

Plugins also add another trust relationship. The official community-plugin documentation explains that they run third-party code and require explicit enablement. Since the saved recording does not identify its integration, this report does not recommend an unknown plugin or imply that one is needed. Start with the smallest file workflow, then evaluate a bridge only when it solves a specific inconvenience.

There is also a maintenance cost. Generated cross-links can become clutter, summaries can duplicate originals, and inconsistent properties can make a seemingly organized vault difficult to search. Review a sample each week and remove conventions that do not improve retrieval. A simple folder of well-named documents may be the better choice if you rarely revisit or connect material.

The score of seven reflects a useful, accessible combination with strong relevance to sustained teaching and app development. Its best outcome is a traceable workspace that helps you reuse what you know and identify what you do not. The saved one-hour JARVIS framing remains a promotional promise. The combination earns its place when a small trial produces more dependable lessons or clearer implementation briefs with less repeated explanation.

entries.title: Paperclip: managing agent work through tasks, budgets, and reviewable handoffs
entries.summary: Paperclip coordinates existing agents through persistent tasks, wake-up events, adapters, and governance. A small educational production pipeline shows where this architecture can help—and what the “AI company” metaphor leaves for the human operator.
entries.reason: Shared goals, role boundaries and observable work can make multi-agent systems more useful; a quick setup does not establish autonomous business operation.
entries.html:
What an “AI company” actually contains

The saved Paperclip article advertises a company run entirely by agents, free software, and a five-minute setup. The technically useful idea is more concrete: put persistent tasks, agent roles, budgets, and review decisions in one system instead of coordinating a collection of unrelated chats. That can matter when several agents contribute to a project over days. It does not make an organization competent simply by giving its agents executive titles.

Nick Spisak’s March 16 article, now preserved in full, presents eight features: organizational roles, linked goals, scheduled wakes, budgets, task records, runtime integration, multiple companies, and governance. It follows these with setup instructions and a proposed onboarding sequence. Its practical audience is people already coordinating several agents. The walkthrough is promotional rather than a measured demonstration; current implementation details below are checked against Paperclip’s own documentation.

The current project README describes a server and web interface that coordinate existing agent runtimes. The central objects include tasks, goals, organizations, connections, and recorded activity. Paperclip supplies coordination around the workers; the workers still need models, tools, credentials, and appropriate environments. Open-source availability concerns the software license, while actual operation can incur inference, hosting, storage, and external-service costs.

For a teacher-builder, the promising use case is an ongoing educational production process: research a topic, prepare a lesson, build an activity, check it, and collect the final artifacts for review. The relevant question is whether Paperclip makes that process easier to supervise than a simple task board and one capable assistant.

Translate the organization chart into responsibilities

Paperclip’s core concepts connect agents, task assignments, goal ancestry, and status. A task has one assignee at a time, and checkout provides a coordination mechanism so competing runs do not both claim the same item. This is useful work management. It does not prove that two different tasks cannot accidentally request the same work or that two agents cannot modify a shared external file.

Think of a role as a contract for work, not a personality. A research worker collects sources and states uncertainty. A lesson writer transforms approved material into teaching content. A builder implements an interaction. A reviewer checks the result against the brief. Each role needs defined inputs, outputs, allowed tools, and a handoff condition. Naming an agent “chief education officer” supplies none of those by itself.

A goal should explain the educational outcome. “Produce a lesson on the Roman republic” is still broad. “Prepare a thirty-minute introduction in which learners distinguish three institutions and explain one limitation of the simplified model” gives downstream tasks a purpose. Link the worksheet, diagram, and interactive exercise to that goal so that their owners can decide what to omit as well as what to add.

A hierarchy can help escalate unresolved choices, but it also adds messages and opportunities for misunderstanding. For one teacher, a coordinator plus two specialists may already be enough. Create another role only when it owns a distinct decision or deliverable that the existing roles handle poorly. A large organization chart can become a visual substitute for a clear production process.

Agents wake for work rather than thinking continuously

The documented heartbeat protocol gives each wake a sequence: establish identity, inspect assignments, claim a task, read its context, act, and leave durable progress. It also distinguishes task status from run liveness. A run that ended normally is not automatically a completed task. This distinction helps prevent an orchestration system from turning an empty or planning-only response into a misleading success.

A heartbeat is best understood as an opportunity to advance work. If a source review is complete, it might hand a documented source pack to the writer. If the source is inaccessible, it should record that blocker and identify the decision needed. If a delegated task is still running, the parent should wait for the appropriate completion event rather than repeatedly asking whether anything has happened.

Current routine documentation distinguishes scheduled tasks from timer heartbeats and describes policies for overlapping or missed runs. It also notes that disabling timer heartbeats differs from pausing an agent: an active agent can still wake for assigned work. These details matter because needless polling can spend resources without producing anything. For a weekly lesson update, a specific routine is easier to understand than a manager waking every few minutes to look for purpose.

Before scheduling, decide what happens if the previous run is unfinished or the server was offline. A daily content task should not necessarily produce several duplicate drafts after a weekend outage. Coalescing, skipping, or catching up are product decisions about the work, not merely technical defaults to accept without thought.

The adapter is part of the reliability boundary

Paperclip’s adapter documentation describes the bridge to the runtime that performs the work. An adapter launches or calls that runtime, passes task context, captures results and usage, and handles environment checks and session state. The documentation also distinguishes richer structured transcripts from generic process output. Consequently, two agents shown in the same dashboard may provide different levels of observability and recovery.

For a first pilot, choose a runtime you already understand and verify a complete small task through its adapter. Can it read the intended repository? Can it produce a file in the right place? Does its result appear with enough detail to review? Does a failed command remain visible as a failure? These checks are more informative than selecting several supported logos and assuming they behave identically.

Session continuity and task continuity are different. A runtime may resume its prior conversation, while Paperclip separately retains the task record. If the conversation cannot be resumed, the durable task context should still explain what was done and what should happen next. Conversely, an old conversation should not override a revised task brief merely because the agent remembers an earlier plan.

Keep shared artifacts explicit. A task comment saying “the worksheet is finished” should point to the exact worksheet revision. A builder receiving a design should know whether it is approved or provisional. Where multiple agents share a repository, coordinate edits and integration deliberately; assigning different tickets does not prevent overlapping changes to the same component.

A practical pipeline: one historical explainer

Consider an original proposed project: a five-minute narrated explanation of Roman roads, accompanied by an interactive map and a short retrieval quiz. Start with a teacher-approved question: how did roads support movement and administration, and what should learners avoid assuming about travel speed or coverage? Specify the intended age group, the maximum length, and the sources the class can access.

The research task produces a claim table. Each claim includes a source, a concise supporting passage location, any uncertainty, and a suggestion for visual treatment. It should distinguish a directly supported statement from an inference. The teacher reviews the table before the writing task begins. This is a meaningful approval because it fixes the factual foundation for several downstream artifacts.

The script task then produces narration, on-screen labels, and a scene list tied to the approved claims. It should not introduce fresh historical assertions merely to make the video more dramatic. The map task receives the relevant geographic data and an explicit instruction about uncertainty: an illustrative route must not be presented as a surveyed historical boundary. These are content contracts that an organization chart alone cannot supply.

The builder implements a small interaction, such as selecting a route to reveal its teaching note. The reviewer checks keyboard access, readable labels, and whether the quiz answers are supported by the lesson. A separate media review checks that narration, captions, and visuals agree. The final teacher decision concerns the assembled experience, because individually correct artifacts can still contradict one another when combined.

In Paperclip, these can be related tasks with named owners and artifact links. The useful outcome is a traceable chain from approved claim to script line to visual scene to quiz question. That chain helps when a teacher later corrects a date or changes an explanation: the affected outputs can be identified instead of regenerated blindly.

Make every handoff reviewable

A good handoff contains the artifact, its version, the checks performed, unresolved questions, and the exact next action. It should not require the recipient to read a long conversation to infer what is ready. For the explainer, the writer might hand over a numbered script with source references and mark two sentences requiring teacher judgment. The builder can proceed with approved scenes while those questions remain visible.

Define acceptance before assigning work. A research task is complete when every retained claim has adequate evidence and uncertainties are marked, not when the agent has browsed a large number of pages. A coding task is complete when the specified interaction works under the agreed checks, not when files have been written. A review task is complete when findings identify reproducible defects or explain why the criteria passed.

Use explicit revision requests. “Make it better” invites another round of subjective optimization. “The map label obscures the route on a narrow screen; move it or provide an accessible list alternative” supplies an observable problem. When a reviewer raises a concern outside the task’s scope, create a separate decision rather than quietly expanding the current assignment indefinitely.

Inspect transitions as well as outputs. A common process failure is that each agent finishes its part but nobody owns the integrated result. Assign one owner to assemble the deliverables, check consistency, and prepare the final review package. This is coordination work with a measurable output, not an excuse for an agent to repeatedly summarize everyone else’s activity.

Approval stages need a concrete object

Paperclip’s approval documentation describes governance around agent hiring, strategy, and budget decisions. Current project material also discusses configured review stages. These are useful mechanisms, but the exact policy and enabled settings matter. Do not infer from the presence of an Approvals page that every consequential action in every connected runtime is automatically intercepted.

For the teaching project, approval should attach to something inspectable: a claim table, a script revision, a proposed new agent role, or a release package. Approving a vague intention such as “make the lesson accurate” gives no useful boundary. A later revision should make clear whether it changes something already approved and whether another review is needed.

Separate internal production from external publication. Agents can prepare a website build, a video file, and a release note while the teacher reviews the final package. The publishing task can remain a distinct step with its own authority. This keeps the process practical: the teacher reviews finished work rather than approving every harmless edit, while the system still has a clear point at which a draft becomes public.

Approval load is also a design variable. If every minor change requires intervention, the process may consume more attention than it saves. Reserve human decisions for educational judgment, scope changes, access changes, and release choices that matter. Use deterministic checks for routine structural requirements and clearly delegated authority for reversible production work.

Connected does not mean universally available

The connector access documentation distinguishes app tools, messaging channels, model credentials, and mixed-purpose services. For app tools, it separates the connection, whose credential is used, agent eligibility, and action permissions. Messaging channels have different controls. This is a valuable correction to the assumption that connecting an account automatically gives every agent the same permitted actions.

Map access to the work. A source researcher needs the approved reference collection; it does not need publication credentials. A reviewer needs the candidate artifact and evidence, while a builder needs a writable project workspace. A coordinator may need task-management access without needing the contents of every private teaching document. This reduces confusion as well as exposure: fewer irrelevant tools make the intended job easier to understand.

Keep student information out of a first pilot because it is unnecessary for proving the production process. Use synthetic examples or teacher-authored content. If a later workflow genuinely needs learner records, evaluate that as a separate project requirement with appropriate institutional decisions. The existence of organization boundaries in the interface should not be treated as proof that every external runtime, log, or connected service handles data identically.

A persistent record also needs editorial care. Tool outputs and source documents can contain instructions that are unrelated to the teacher’s task. Workers should treat those as source material, not as authority to change their role or access. Reviewers need enough provenance to distinguish a teacher-approved rule from a suggestion copied out of a fetched page.

A budget dashboard is only as complete as its accounting

Current cost documentation describes budget policies and automatic pauses, and notes that an agent created through the app flow may not yet have its own budget policy. The README additionally qualifies enforcement as based on recorded spending, with reporting and in-progress work able to delay stopping. A configured cap is therefore valuable, but should not be interpreted as a universal guarantee that every external charge stops at an exact instant.

This directly qualifies the saved article’s categorical promise that spending limits eliminate surprise bills. Enforcement based on reported usage can reduce exposure without creating an instantaneous ceiling across every connected service. Before trusting a budget for unattended work, inspect when the relevant adapter reports consumption and what happens to work already in progress. The marketing claim and the documented mechanism should not be treated as equivalent.

Separate visible inference spending from total project cost. Rendering a video, storing large media, calling an external service, and maintaining a server can all sit outside the number you first notice. Reconcile the dashboard with the services actually used during a pilot. If an adapter reports estimated or incomplete costs, preserve that uncertainty instead of presenting the total as invoice-authoritative.

Measure cost per accepted deliverable alongside human review time. A research worker producing twenty weak sources may be less useful than one producing five carefully checked sources. A manager that spends most of its budget asking workers for status may be creating overhead. Reducing needless wakeups and improving task briefs can matter more than changing the model assigned to every role.

Give the pilot a finite output and a review date. For example, prepare one explainer package, then inspect spending and failure modes before starting the next. This creates a natural decision point. Continually adding tasks to justify an already running “company” reverses the purpose of the system: the infrastructure should serve the educational work.

For a second project, reuse the process before reusing the content. A successful Roman-roads package does not prove that the same source rubric fits a contemporary science explanation. Keep the useful handoff format, then revise the evidence requirements and subject review. This is where an organizational tool can compound value: stable production habits become reusable while domain judgments remain explicit. Track which task templates were reused successfully and which needed intervention. If every project requires rebuilding the entire organization, the apparent automation may be hiding a large setup cost. If a few clear roles consistently deliver reviewable artifacts, the system has demonstrated something more valuable than a populated dashboard.

Test recovery, not just the happy path

A useful pilot should include a deliberately blocked task, a failed check, a revised brief, and a restart. Does the blocked task identify what it needs? Does a failed build remain visible? Does the worker notice that the teacher changed the intended learner level? After restarting, can the operator tell which artifact is current and which work remains unfinished?

Test duplicate prevention at the level that matters. Atomic task checkout addresses competing ownership of the same task, but two separate tasks can still request the same worksheet or publish the same update. Use stable deliverable identifiers and a clear owner for each output. Where external actions are involved, check the target system before repeating an uncertain operation.

Backups and portability solve different problems. Paperclip’s export/import guidance concerns reusable organization packages, while full recovery requires preserving the relevant instance data and artifacts. Review exported material before sharing it: a reusable team definition should not accidentally include local paths, private content, or credentials embedded as ordinary text. An attractive template is not a substitute for a tested recovery plan.

The article also describes ClipMart as a forthcoming library of reusable companies. That is a dated roadmap statement, not evidence of current marketplace availability. More generally, importing a team template cannot supply your curriculum goals, source standards, or release decisions. Likewise, a quick onboarding command can establish a running service without establishing that its workers have appropriate credentials, reliable tools, and useful acceptance criteria. Treat installation time and time to a dependable workflow as separate measurements.

After the pilot, compare with a simpler baseline: one assistant, a written task list, and a folder of versioned outputs. Paperclip earns its place when it reduces lost context, ambiguous ownership, or coordination work enough to cover its operating burden. If the project consists of one occasional worksheet, its organization machinery may add little value.

The score of eight reflects Paperclip’s potentially substantial impact on coordinating ongoing agent work. The inspected documentation supports a real management layer, while the saved article’s company and setup claims remain promotional framing. Adopt it when you have a repeatable production process that needs durable ownership and review. Begin with a small team whose work you can evaluate, and expand only when the next role solves an observed problem.
