entries.title: Astra and TradingView: what the seven-step workflow really requires
entries.summary: A seven-step integration pitch becomes a useful study in data permissions, event timing, correlated indicators, and reproducible evaluation. A classroom replay tool captures its educational value without adopting unverified access or profit claims.
entries.reason: The workflow makes multimodal analysis and tool integration concrete; claimed continual operation and profitability remain separate questions.
entries.html:
Seven steps hide several different engineering problems

Roan's September 13, 2026 bookmark proposes connecting GPT-6 Astra to TradingView-related tooling. Its seven steps cover a repository, a claimed 300-agent monitoring layer, callable indicators, generated Pine strategies and backtests, technical-rating checks, replay, and Telegram chart alerts. It promises tenfold signal coverage and free premium access, while quoting a broader trading-system article. Those are the creator's claims; the quoted article is context, not an additional bookmark.

The useful idea is an AI assistant working with structured observations and reproducible experiments. The unsupported leap is that connecting those components establishes a powerful or profitable trading system. This report examines the integration as an educational software design. No continuous operation, throughput improvement, premium entitlement, or financial performance was independently demonstrated by the saved post. The model name identifies the proposed stack, rather than serving as evidence of its results.

What the linked repository actually establishes

The author reply identifies Mathieu2301/TradingView-API. Its current documentation explicitly describes an independent community project, unaffiliated with TradingView. Version 4 is a breaking TypeScript rewrite without a compatibility layer. Documented functions cover candles, quotes, studies, strategy reports, screening, and technical ratings; lower-level sessions expose replay. This establishes an inspectable interface project, not an official financial-data service agreement.

The same documentation says unauthenticated access can involve shorter intraday history, delayed or substitute feeds, and no Pine studies. Authentication supplies the access available to the account. Consequently, the bookmark's September setup description should not be treated as a current guarantee that one installation unlocks every feature. Version, account permissions, and data availability are distinct dependencies.

For a builder, record those dependencies beside each proposed feature. A chart display might work while a custom study fails. An unavailable study should produce a specific status, not an invented value or a silently substituted indicator. The application remains understandable when partial success is represented explicitly.

Free code does not establish unrestricted data access

TradingView's published policies describe display-only licensing and restrictions on non-display uses, including automated trading and algorithmic decision-making. The existence of a community client does not supply authorization for the workflow promoted in the post. A production design would need permissions that actually cover its intended data use.

TradingView's Bar Replay documentation also ties historical depth to symbol, interval, available storage, and subscription. Even broad historical access means the history that exists for that instrument, not unlimited observations at every resolution. The post's unrestricted replay framing is therefore not established by official documentation.

A classroom prototype can avoid making access assumptions altogether. Supply an original synthetic price series with a declared random seed and show it through a local chart. The lesson then concerns event order, indicator interpretation, and explanation quality. If real observations are added later, record the actual provider and allowed use as part of the dataset's description. This is a practical design choice, not a claim that the prototype reproduces the advertised service.

A streaming chart has more than one clock

Pine's repainting documentation explains why values on an open real-time bar can differ from the values ultimately stored in history. A signal computed during a developing bar need not survive its close. Historical and live calculations can therefore appear inconsistent without the charting library having fabricated data.

A proposed data record should distinguish when an event occurred, when the application received it, and whether the bar was complete. Suppose a fictional five-minute bar crosses a threshold at 10:03 and ends below it at 10:05. An agent looking at the first observation and a replay using only the completed bar have received different evidence. Their disagreement is a timing question before it is a reasoning question.

Build the timeline so users can inspect that difference. Color an unfinished bar subtly, retain its revisions in the experiment log, and label the snapshot used for each explanation. A delayed message should keep its original event time. Otherwise, an impressive animated feed can obscure exactly which information was available when the assistant spoke.

Twenty-six indicators are not twenty-six independent witnesses

TradingView's Technical Ratings reference describes a composite of fifteen moving-average or filter ratings and eleven oscillator ratings. Constituent conditions become negative, neutral, or positive values, which are combined into category scores. This is a documented calculation with defined inputs, not an independent analyst judging the model's reasoning.

If an assistant already uses price-derived trend measures, consulting another price-derived composite may repeat much of the same information. Agreement should be displayed as agreement between methods, without multiplying it into a probability of correctness. Two thermometers beside one another do not become two different weather stations simply because their cases have different colors.

An educational interface could group indicators by the kind of question they ask and show their shared input series. Let students remove one group and observe whether the conclusion changes. The exercise encourages a useful engineering habit: inspect dependence among signals before rewarding a system for collecting more of them. Count distinct evidence, not just tool calls.

Compilation is the first test, not the last

TradingView's strategy documentation distinguishes simulated order execution from actual trading and discusses commissions, slippage, lookahead bias, selection bias, and out-of-sample evaluation. A Pine strategy that compiles can still rely on information unavailable at its supposed decision time. A favorable simulated result can still depend on optimistic execution assumptions.

For a learning app, require the assistant to write a plain-language hypothesis before producing strategy code. The hypothesis should specify the observable condition, decision timing, comparison, and a reason it might fail. Then review the generated implementation against those statements. A mismatch is informative even if the resulting curve looks attractive.

Separate the period used to revise the hypothesis from the period reserved for checking it. Bailey and colleagues' backtest-overfitting research addresses the risk of selecting appealing historical strategies from many trials. Faster testing increases the number of candidates one can inspect; it does not make selection effects disappear.

Keep unsuccessful experiments in the notebook. A gallery showing only the best output hides how much searching produced it. The number of attempted variants belongs beside the final result, together with the assumptions that were held constant.

Give every tool a narrow, inspectable job

A manageable prototype needs three responsibilities: retrieve an observation from the local dataset, calculate a specified transformation, and explain a completed experiment. These can be ordinary functions behind a small interface. An LLM can request them, but should not supply the numerical results that the functions are meant to calculate.

For example, a chart request can name a dataset version, an interval, and an end time. Its result can include the requested window, missing-data flags, and a stable snapshot identifier. An explanation request can reference that identifier rather than silently retrieve a newer chart. The user can then reproduce the exact evidence behind a sentence.

Use a small vocabulary of outcomes: completed, insufficient history, invalid request, and unavailable observation. Treat these as normal states. Asking an assistant to sound confident despite an incomplete tool response turns a routine data limitation into an interpretability problem. A well-designed empty state teaches more than a plausible but unsupported answer.

Build a classroom replay detective

The most useful original project here is a replay detective: a local web page where learners diagnose why two apparently identical analyses disagree. Prepare three synthetic datasets with conspicuous fictional labels. One contains a missing interval, one contains an open-bar revision, and one contains a sudden change in variability. None should be presented as a historical market or a forecast.

Begin with a single line chart, a play button, and a side panel showing the current evidence record. Advance one observation at a time. At selected points, ask learners to choose whether enough information exists to describe a completed pattern. Save their answers before revealing later observations. This makes hindsight visible through the interface rather than merely warning about it in text.

Next, introduce two fictional agents. One describes only completed observations; the other comments on the latest partial observation. Their outputs should be labeled by role, not ranked as universally better or worse. Ask learners to explain a disagreement using timestamps and completion status. The goal is identifying the question each agent answered.

Finally, let students repair a misleading summary. A sentence such as “the pattern persisted throughout the interval” should require evidence from the whole interval. If only a partial snapshot exists, the learner must narrow the wording. An average coder can implement this with arrays, a deterministic playback cursor, and a simple chart; no trading connection or large agent fleet is needed.

Assess the explanation, not the drama of the chart

Define a rubric before introducing optional generated commentary. Award credit for identifying the dataset, preserving timing, naming missing information, and keeping observation separate from interpretation. Penalize claims that introduce unseen evidence. A concise explanation with a correct limitation should outperform an elaborate story that cannot be traced to the record.

For an English lesson, give students three verbs: changed, suggested, and predicted. Have them rewrite the same observation using each verb and explain what extra evidence the stronger wording would need. In a Latin lesson, the exercise can focus on accurately expressing temporal relationships while preserving the underlying facts. The chart supplies a shared reference; linguistic precision becomes the assessed skill.

If an LLM grades the responses, retain examples that a teacher has already marked and compare the judgments. Include deliberately persuasive errors as well as awkward but accurate answers. This tests whether the grader rewards evidence use or merely polished prose. The proposed activity evaluates explanation quality, not financial judgment.

Make a notification an evidence receipt

The bookmark's chart-and-metrics alert suggests a useful interface pattern: a compact message linking back to the exact experiment. In the classroom version, show the dataset identifier, observation cutoff, hypothesis version, and unresolved limitations. A chart thumbnail can orient the reader, but the underlying numerical record should remain available.

William Sharpe's original exposition distinguishes historical reward-to-variability measurements from prospective quantities and explains their dependence on the measurement period. A Sharpe number in a notification therefore needs its return definition and observation window. It cannot stand alone as a label meaning that an agent is reliable.

Likewise, a displayed drawdown or proposed position-size number should not distract from missing evidence. For this educational adaptation, omit order sizing entirely and replace it with a clearly defined explanation score. The result is still a concrete agent workflow: a calculation produces evidence, an assistant interprets it, and the recipient can audit the interpretation without taking a market action.

Measure useful work before multiplying agents

A separate engineering experiment can test the monitoring claim without using markets. Generate a fixed stream of fictional events and compare one worker with several workers. Measure completed analyses, duplicate outputs, elapsed time, and missed events. Keep the input and task definition identical. More messages per second are not necessarily more useful coverage.

Add an intentional slow response and an interrupted connection. The interface should reveal which observations were processed and which remain pending. Require each worker to acknowledge a unique event identifier, so retries cannot masquerade as new discoveries. These modest checks expose whether parallelism improves the application or merely increases activity. Only after a smaller system has understandable behavior would a larger fleet become an informative experiment.

Editorial judgment: 6/10

This bookmark earns 6/10 because it makes data access, tool use, simulation, and reporting concrete enough to study. Its promotional access and scale claims are not established by current documentation, and no profitable system was verified. The strongest reusable outcome is an auditable replay-and-explanation tool. Reproducible integration measurements and properly authorized, clearly defined data access would make the broader architecture more convincing.

entries.title: Luna workers and completion callbacks: stop paying the parent to wait
entries.summary: Antonio Leiva replaces his earlier model router with bounded Luna jobs and completion delivery. The practical value lies in delegating preparation, execution and verification while keeping the parent responsible for scope and acceptance.
entries.reason: Event-driven delegation is a reusable way to separate expensive reasoning from routine execution; savings depend on the real task boundary and host behavior.
entries.html:
The saving comes from handing over the whole routine job

Antonio Leiva's September 21, 2026 bookmark describes a change of direction. After trying Jev for model selection, he concludes that the larger waste lies in supervision: an expensive parent keeps checking progress, or prepares the work so thoroughly that the cheaper worker has little left to do. His replacement design uses a Luna worker and a completion message that lets the parent resume when needed.

The full post uses academy releases as its example, with slow UI tests extending a run to ten, twenty or thirty minutes. Leiva reports a calculated ninety-nine-percent saving. A captured reply also points to his rejected router, where he observed cache reuse of 32% versus 99.35% with one model kept fixed. Those cache figures came from different feature implementations. They are not a matched benchmark, and neither observation establishes a general saving.

This is a delegation and waiting pattern. Its attraction for a teacher-builder is simple: reserve expensive judgment for defining and reviewing the work, while a bounded worker handles an established procedure. It does not claim that every difficult task should be dispatched to the cheapest model.

What the linked recipe actually specifies

The published gist combines project instructions with a custom worker. It delegates preparation, execution and verification together, chooses reasoning effort per assignment, and distinguishes ordinary return delivery from a callback. Callback jobs carry a unique job identifier and the actual parent destination. The worker reports completion, failure or a decision that blocks progress; the parent avoids a polling loop. The recipe also limits children from delegating further.

The worker file explicitly pins gpt-5.6-luna. It should not be silently rewritten as GPT-6 Luna: the official release chronology places GPT-6 Luna's release on September 22, after this bookmark. The GPT-5.6 Luna model page verifies the older identifier and multiple reasoning levels. Availability and suitability still depend on the account and task.

Current Codex documentation adds useful compatibility checks. Custom agents inherit the parent's permissions, provider and MCP servers. A model or effort pinned in the agent file takes precedence over the resolved defaults. Service tier follows the root session's preference, so the gist's service_tier entry should not be treated as a current independent worker override. Preserve the design while checking the host's actual configuration rules.

The gist describes an app-specific messaging mechanism, not a universal callback guarantee across every Codex environment. A native child result and a message that wakes an idle parent are different delivery paths. Establish which path the current host supports before allowing the parent to stop supervising.

A thin parent still owns judgment

A thin parent does a small amount of necessary coordination: identify the objective, establish scope, choose the worker and decide how the result will be accepted. It does not turn the assignment into a transcript of commands for the worker to repeat. Nor does it abdicate responsibility for a poorly specified or consequential decision.

For example, deciding whether a quiz's answer logic should change is teacher-facing judgment. Applying an already approved answer table, running its checks and reporting discrepancies can be a bounded worker job. The parent should hand over the latter as a complete unit. If it first reads every file, performs the transformation and interprets all failures, the apparent delegation has saved little.

The task must be large enough to justify a handoff but small enough to verify. Renaming one label rarely needs a separate agent. Preparing a set of lesson assets and checking all required outputs may. Long elapsed time alone is insufficient: an ordinary script can wait for a process without using a language model at every interval.

Keep the parent responsible for decisions that cross the original scope. A worker discovering an unexpected database change or a disputed answer should return the evidence and the specific decision needed. That is useful autonomy: routine work proceeds, while new judgment returns to the right place.

Write a handoff that can survive without the parent

A good handoff names the outcome, the relevant inputs, the allowed actions and the completion evidence. It supplies context the worker cannot safely infer, such as which lesson revision is approved. It leaves routine inspection to the worker rather than pasting an entire conversation whose important constraints may be buried.

Here is an original example for a classroom website. It illustrates the boundary; it has not been executed:

Job: vocabulary-import-lesson-07
Outcome: update lesson 07 from the approved vocabulary file.
Inputs: the named source file and current project revision.
Scope: edit this lesson's data and its existing import check only.
Preserve: item IDs, answer alternatives, and other lessons.
Checks: parse the data, compare all items, run the relevant check.
Return: changed paths, counts, check result, and unresolved questions.
Do not publish the site or change the approved vocabulary.

The teacher can inspect that assignment before execution and inspect its result afterward. Success does not require reading the worker's entire conversation. If the input contains a duplicate identifier, the worker should report it rather than inventing a new one and silently changing the lesson's meaning.

For concurrent editing, assign files clearly. Two workers can investigate separate problems while still colliding on a shared configuration file. Define ownership before starting, and require a worker to notice changes made since its initial read. Parallelism saves time only when its outputs can be combined without losing work.

Completion delivery needs its own evidence

A completion callback means the worker announces a state change instead of the parent repeatedly asking for one. The application should associate that announcement with a known assignment. A concise result can contain the job identifier, outcome, artifact reference and any remaining decision. It should distinguish a failed task from a successful task whose notification could not be delivered.

Only use a destination authorized for the job and actually obtained from the host. Do not guess a conversation identifier, substitute the child's own identifier, or treat a downloaded instruction file as permission to message unrelated chats. If the required messaging capability or authorization is absent, keep ordinary result collection and report that delivery limitation.

A broader application may use HTTP webhooks instead of desktop messages. OpenAI's webhook documentation is a separate example: it describes completion events, signature verification, retries and possible duplicate delivery. It does not validate the gist's desktop mechanism. It does show why event-driven systems must identify events and handle repeats deliberately.

In your own workflow, make processing the same completion twice harmless. If the teacher revises the lesson while the worker runs, the result can be technically successful yet stale. Match the artifact to the assignment's input version before accepting it. A notification is a prompt to reconcile state, not an automatic instruction to publish.

A useful first case: prepare a lesson release

Choose a small site with an established release procedure. The first trial should prepare a release candidate locally rather than publish it. Ask the worker to inspect the current target, run the required checks, identify failures and produce a concise readiness report. Give it the existing procedure instead of asking it to invent deployment architecture.

The parent can then work on an independent lesson or stop its active turn if the host supports reliable completion delivery. The worker follows the running checks and gathers their results. A script's exit code is one piece of evidence; the worker should also identify the tested revision and which checks actually ran.

When the result arrives, inspect the relevant report and any failed behavior. Do not rerun every passed check automatically if its inputs and target still match. Conversely, do not reuse a green result after changing the files it covered. This makes verification proportional to what changed.

For an English practice site, include a content check alongside software checks: all required prompts present, answer alternatives preserved and no accidental duplicate items. The worker can compare files mechanically. The teacher reviews whether the prompts teach what the lesson intends. Those are different acceptance responsibilities.

Only a separately authorized release should publish. Delegation can carry existing authority, but a callback does not create new authority. This distinction keeps the worker useful without letting a routine readiness check silently become a public deployment.

A second case: render and inspect an explainer

A lesson-video workflow is a natural candidate because rendering can take time after the creative decisions are settled. Give the worker an approved script, a scene specification and an existing render command. Its job is to check inputs, run the render, verify the expected output and return evidence. The parent should not spend repeated turns asking whether the video is ready.

Define concrete checks: output file exists, duration is within the specified range, captions cover every approved sentence and no asset reference is missing. Add selected frame checks for legibility and highlighting. The worker can report observed results and uncertainty; it should not claim to have listened to narration if it only inspected file metadata.

If rendering fails because an image path is wrong, correcting the known reference may fit the assignment. If it requires changing the lesson's explanation or replacing licensed material, the worker should surface that decision. A bounded job can contain repair without becoming open-ended creative control.

Keep a record of the running process so a reconnection does not start another render unnecessarily. An agent stopping and an external process stopping are not always the same event. The result should identify the actual output and source version, making it possible to resume or review later without reconstructing the conversation.

Measure the whole delegation, including the parent

The ninety-nine-percent claim is a reason to investigate, not a purchasing calculation. Measure parent preparation, worker execution, completion handling, retries and final review together. Moving tokens to a cheaper worker can help, but leaving the expensive parent active may erase much of that benefit. Human correction time belongs in the comparison too.

Use the same task and starting revision for a baseline and delegated run. Keep the acceptance criteria identical. Repeat representative tasks rather than selecting the best result. Include failures, blocked jobs and notification problems. A system that stops before checking its output is not cheaper at the same level of completion.

The earlier 32% versus 99.35% cache observation should remain a diagnostic clue. Different tasks can have different prompt shapes, repetition and lengths, so the comparison cannot isolate model switching as the cause. It neither proves that all routing breaks caching nor measures the callback design's benefit. Do not combine those figures with the claimed ninety-nine-percent saving.

A simple ledger can answer the practical question: how many jobs completed correctly, how often the parent intervened, how long the teacher waited, and what each stage consumed. If a worker constantly asks for help, narrow the task or improve the brief. If the parent repeatedly rechecks valid evidence, improve the acceptance process.

Why this earns 7 out of 10

This bookmark earns 7/10 because it identifies an avoidable source of agent expense and provides an inspectable implementation recipe. The transferable idea is complete bounded delegation with event-driven return, preserving a parent for decisions and final acceptance. The published saving remains an uncontrolled author claim.

Start with one familiar procedure and an ordinary result-return path. Add unattended completion only after its delivery and recovery behavior are clear. Keep the design if it reduces total supervision and produces equally reliable artifacts. A simpler script or a single agent remains preferable when the handoff costs more than the work it removes.

entries.title: WindTunnel and WebMCP: what changes when a website gives an agent explicit actions
entries.summary: WindTunnel’s Jev results show the potential of moving browser work into explicit website tools. The evidence compares complete configurations: majority-solved tasks, individual attempts, median costs, and aggregate bills answer different questions and must remain separate.
entries.reason: Explicit website actions can materially change agent accuracy and cost; benchmark design, harness differences and generalization must accompany the reported results.
entries.html:
The saved claim is about a complete agent system

Idan Levin’s September 18 bookmark reports Jev plus Mercury 2.5 completing every task in a WebMCP benchmark at roughly 112 times lower model cost than GPT-6 Astra using code execution, and 245 times lower than Astra using screenshots. The expanded post also compares a Jev browser-control configuration with a WebMCP configuration: solved tasks rise from 25 of 49 to 49 of 49, while an aggregate model-cost measure falls by about 18%.

The post explains a concrete division of work. Jev chooses a website tool from available options using the goal and prior results; Mercury supplies arguments when free text is needed. Levin attributes the improvement to a simpler decision space and explicitly says the weaker browser result belongs to the tested implementation. His description of Mercury exceeding a thousand output tokens per second remains a creator-reported throughput claim, not a measurement independently established here.

The underlying project is Nekuda’s WindTunnel. It is useful because the announcement leads to methods, results, and reproduction material. The practical lesson for a teacher or app builder is larger than choosing a fast model: the interface offered to an agent can determine how much reasoning, navigation, and recovery the job requires.

A website designed only for human interaction asks an agent to infer a sequence from visible controls. A cooperative application can instead expose an operation that directly expresses the intended work. That may shorten the path, but someone must implement and maintain the operation. Any claimed saving should account for that engineering effort and the reliability of the resulting application behavior.

Four interfaces expose different problems

A screenshot-based agent reads rendered images and acts through positions. A DOM-based agent reads page structure and selects controls. A code-execution agent generates browser-automation code. A tool-driven agent invokes operations exposed by the application. These are different ways of reaching an outcome, not interchangeable wrappers around the same model request. WindTunnel’s methodology overview makes these method boundaries explicit.

The WebMCP project explainer describes page-defined JavaScript tools with descriptions and structured arguments, discovered and invoked through the browser. This is a client-side mechanism for cooperative web applications; it does not automatically turn every website into an agent-ready API. The website must expose relevant operations, and the agent environment must support them.

Imagine a lesson catalogue. A UI route might open a filter panel, choose Latin, set a level, enter a topic, close the panel, and read the results. A proposed catalogue-search tool could accept those criteria together and return matching lesson identifiers. The task still needs interpretation, but the agent no longer has to discover each control and infer when its effect has completed.

That shift can be valuable even when the chosen model is unchanged. It also moves responsibility into the website. The tool must use the same catalogue rules as the human interface, validate its inputs, enforce the account’s access, and return an understandable result. A fast path that silently ignores one requested filter is a defective implementation, not successful automation.

The platform remains an evolving surface. Chrome’s early-preview announcement discussed imperative and form-based approaches; the current WebMCP explainer defines the imperative API and treats a declarative counterpart as separate exploration. Use documentation for the actual target environment before writing integration code. The conceptual workflow below does not depend on claiming universal browser support or a stable historical code snippet.

Tool choice and argument generation need different checks

TypeSafe’s System One documentation describes typed judgments over supplied state, distinguished from generating arbitrary prose. That helps explain the benchmark’s two-model arrangement. Selecting an operation from a defined set is different from writing the free-text query or field value that operation requires.

For a lesson finder, the operation could be correct while its arguments are wrong. The agent might choose catalogue search but request English instead of Latin, or use a topic description as a difficulty level. Validate arguments before execution and preserve them in the trace. A successful API response only shows that a call was accepted; it does not show that the user’s requirements were faithfully represented.

Prefer existing identifiers where they convey the intended choice. If the application has already returned three matching lessons, selecting one of their IDs is easier to verify than generating a title again. Free text remains useful for an initial topic query or a draft explanation. The design question is where generation adds value and where it unnecessarily recreates information the application already has.

Keep ambiguity explicit. “Find something harder” needs a reference point: the current activity, the learner’s last attempt, or a defined level. A fast selection between tool names does not resolve that missing context. Ask for the needed information or return a small set of alternatives. This preserves the distinction between a well-formed decision and a well-founded one.

The same separation improves evaluation. Score operation choice, argument correctness, tool execution, and final outcome independently while retaining the overall task result. If argument generation is the weak component, changing tool descriptions may have little effect. If the tool silently drops a filter, replacing either model addresses the wrong problem.

Keep tasks, attempts, costs, and time distinct

WindTunnel’s workload contains 49 tasks across eight self-hosted applications, with seeded starting states and outcome-based checks. A task counts as solved when a majority of its three attempts pass. The checks examine application results rather than accepting the agent’s own success claim. These are useful evaluation choices, while the limited workload still constrains generalization. The README also notes that configurations differ in interface, model, framework, and turn budget.

The current results board displays the following relevant configurations. Costs are median model-cost figures, and times are median agent times; neither is a complete deployment bill or full user-session duration.

ConfigurationSolved tasksPassed attemptsMedian model costMedian time
Jev + Mercury 2.5, WebMCP49/49141/147$0.0010643.2 s
Jev + Mercury 2.5, DOM25/4976/147$0.0007785.4 s
GPT-6 Astra, code execution49/49147/147$0.11867616.4 s
GPT-6 Astra, screenshots45/49135/147$0.26078020.8 s

Dividing the two Astra costs by the WebMCP Jev cost yields approximately 112 and 245. Jev’s 141 successful attempts are about 95.9% of 147, despite its 49/49 task headline. A majority verdict is therefore not a promise that every request succeeds. The October board also includes newer configurations, so the September announcement is not a permanent ranking.

This matters in practice. A teacher requesting one prepared lesson receives one attempt, not the abstract benefit of a benchmark majority. An application can add retries, but then latency, cost, and failure handling change. Report first-attempt completion and recovery separately rather than using majority-solved tasks as a substitute for the experience a single user will receive.

Why a lower total can coexist with a higher median

The Jev cohort provenance records approximately $0.20156 known cost for scored WebMCP attempts versus $0.24539 for DOM attempts, about an 18% reduction. Yet WebMCP’s median is higher. Failed attempts remain in the medians, unknown-usage reserves are separate, and infrastructure-recovery accounting has its own boundary. The recorded models are Jev 1.13.0 and Mercury 2.5. The DOM arm uses a frozen Browser Use Ultrafast implementation. The document calls these different harnesses a comparison of complete setups, not an isolated interface experiment or a test of every current Ultrafast revision.

There is no contradiction between those statistics. The median describes the middle observation; a total adds every observation. A small number of expensive attempts can increase the total without moving the middle much. An inexpensive failed attempt can also lower a median while delivering no useful result. Neither statistic should be substituted for the other when explaining an improvement.

For your own evaluation, store a cost per attempt and a status before calculating summaries. Then report total known spend, unresolved accounting, completion counts, and cost per verified success. If you decide to retry failures, include the retries in a second workflow-level measure. This makes it possible to answer both “what did an ordinary attempt cost?” and “what did it take to deliver a usable result?”

Keep application infrastructure and human review visible as well. A cheap inference call may rely on a tool that took substantial development time, or on a reviewer who repairs frequent mistakes. Those costs do not invalidate the benchmark’s model-cost comparison. They answer a different purchasing and engineering question: whether the whole workflow is worthwhile for your situation.

What the comparison can and cannot explain

The results support an engineering hypothesis: explicit application actions can remove difficult intermediate decisions. They do not isolate how much improvement comes from the model, tool design, prompts, runtime, or stopping rules. Even the same-model WebMCP/DOM comparison uses different harnesses. Treat it as evidence about those configurations rather than a clean measurement of one variable.

Suppose one implementation can search and apply three filters in a single tool call, while another performs six UI actions. The first has fewer opportunities to choose an incorrect intermediate state. That is a real product advantage if you own the tool, but it is also extra capability supplied by application code. A fair explanation should credit both the agent and the environment.

A simple thought experiment illustrates the issue. If ten independent steps each had a 95% chance of success, completing all ten would have only about a 60% chance. Real agent errors are not independent, so this is not a prediction for WindTunnel. It explains why reducing avoidable steps can improve an end-to-end workflow without a corresponding improvement in every individual decision.

Generalization requires new tasks and conditions. A tool designed around a seeded catalogue may perform well there while lacking operations needed for an unfamiliar authoring system. A benchmark can reveal useful mechanisms and failure patterns without certifying arbitrary sites, multilingual instructions, account policies, or unusual recovery cases. Test the subset that resembles the work you intend to automate.

Design an educational tool around an outcome

A practical first adaptation is a read-only lesson finder on a site you control. Define one operation that searches by subject, level, and topic, returning a small set of stable lesson identifiers with the fields needed to choose among them. This is an original proposed workflow, not an existing WindTunnel feature or a tested teaching product.

Start with the ordinary application function. It should already know how to filter the catalogue and respect visibility rules. Add a thin tool interface around that function rather than copying the filtering logic into a second implementation. When the UI and tool share behavior, a later curriculum change has one place to be corrected.

Make the arguments concrete. A level should come from the levels your catalogue actually supports. A language should have an explicit representation. A topic may be free text, but missing or ambiguous values need defined handling. If the user asks for an unavailable level, return that fact rather than silently selecting the nearest one and claiming success.

The result should help the next decision. Return the lesson ID, title, language, level, and a concise description, with an explicit empty-result state. Do not send an entire course database when the agent needs five candidates. Smaller results can reduce distraction, but removing a field required for verification would be a false economy.

Separate searching from creating or publishing. A proposed authoring tool could create a draft from teacher-approved content and return its identifier. A separate preview operation could show it for review. Publication should retain the application’s normal authority checks and an intentional user action. A typed schema describes an input; it does not establish that the caller is allowed to perform every operation expressible by that schema.

Plan for uncertain outcomes. If a network response is lost after creating a draft, the next step should check whether the draft exists, not immediately create another. Give repeated requests an application-level identity or another deduplication mechanism appropriate to the system. Then test the failure deliberately. Reliability depends as much on these ordinary software decisions as on the model selecting the correct tool.

Build a small benchmark before a broad integration

You do not need eight applications to learn from WindTunnel’s method. Use one staging application and a short task set with independently checkable outcomes. For a teaching catalogue, include exact-title lookup, topic lookup, conflicting filters, an unavailable lesson, and a request requiring clarification. Keep a held-out group that you do not use while adjusting tool descriptions.

  1. Specify each task and start state. Record the user goal, account role, available lessons, locale, and relevant preferences. Reset the fixture before every attempt so that a previous run cannot make the next run easier.
  2. Write an outcome checker. Validate the chosen lesson and every requested condition. For a draft task, inspect the saved title, activity order, and status. A tool’s own “success” message is insufficient if it can disagree with stored state.
  3. Choose meaningful baselines. Compare a deterministic application call, a browser route, and a tool-directed agent where appropriate. Keep the task and checker fixed. Record every difference in model, available operations, and budget.
  4. Repeat and retain failures. Alternate configurations and save the result of every launched attempt. Distinguish a wrong answer, an unsupported task, a provider outage, and an inconclusive application state. Define any exclusion rule before reading outcomes.
  5. Review the practical result. Count first-attempt successes, retries, incorrect changes, latency, and total cost. Add the time a human spends diagnosing failures. Decide whether the tool interface saves enough work to justify maintenance.

For a teacher with average coding experience, the checker is often the most valuable first artifact. It forces a vague request such as “prepare a useful exercise” to become a concrete specification. You may discover that the intended outcome needs human judgment, such as whether a reading passage suits a particular class. Keep that judgment visible rather than pretending a database check captures it.

Once the basic loop works, vary one factor at a time: the wording of the request, number of distractor lessons, available tool descriptions, or length of the result list. This helps explain failures. Changing the model, prompts, fixture, and tool design together may produce a better result while leaving you unable to understand why.

Three useful applications beyond a leaderboard

Prepare an English practice sequence. Let an agent find approved activities for a stated skill and level, then assemble a draft order using existing lesson identifiers. Check that every item belongs to the intended language and difficulty range. A teacher reviews whether the sequence teaches the right concept and whether the transition between activities makes sense. The tool automates retrieval and arrangement; it does not establish pedagogical quality.

Check a Latin exercise editor. Expose a staging operation that creates a draft with known forms and feedback, then inspect the saved record independently. Compare it with the human-interface route after a redesign. A successful tool run confirms application behavior, while a successful UI run also exercises navigation. Keep both if the aim is to ensure learners or teachers can still use the interface.

Prepare a narrated course walkthrough. Use read-only tools to locate the relevant lesson and report its current state, then capture the actual UI for the recording. Tool output can help choose the right example, but it cannot substitute for footage showing what the learner sees. If the UI and tool results disagree, investigate before publishing the tutorial.

These examples show why agent success and user experience need separate evaluation. A tool can bypass a confusing form and still complete the database change. That is valuable for automation, but the confusing form remains a problem for people. Use tool-level checks to validate operations and human or UI-based checks to validate the experience.

Inspect published evidence before paying to rerun it

The Jev reproduction instructions publish a pinned release procedure, source checks, and a portable launcher. They distinguish it from historical recovery infrastructure and warn that future model availability and responses may differ. Published redacted attempt records include observations, actions, usage, and timing. These materials support inspection; they do not mean this report independently reproduced the results.

Begin by selecting a successful attempt and a failed attempt for the same kind of task. Follow the stated goal through the observations, selected tools, arguments, returned results, and final check. Ask whether the failure came from choosing the wrong operation, supplying an incorrect value, a tool defect, or an incorrect completion judgment. This is often more instructive than copying an aggregate score into a presentation.

If you later rerun the project, keep your output distinct from the canonical results. Preserve the source revision, environment, model identities, and exclusions. Check the documented no-provider validation path before a paid run, then start with one task. A locally successful reproduction confirms something useful about your environment; it should not be described as reproducing every published result.

For a teaching demonstration about AI evaluation, give learners a simplified result sheet with task IDs, attempts, outcomes, time, and cost. Ask them to compute majority-solved tasks and first-attempt success separately. Then introduce an expensive failed attempt and show why the median and total can move differently. This teaches evidence literacy without requiring students to run commercial models or adopt a particular product.

Adopt the method before adopting the multiplier

The bookmark earns 8/10 because it connects a useful architectural idea with inspectable benchmark evidence. Explicit website tools can make agent work shorter and easier to verify. WindTunnel’s reported improvement is meaningful for its measured configurations, while harness differences, accounting boundaries, and the finite task set limit broader conclusions.

For your own educational software, the strongest next step is one well-defined operation, one independent checker, and a modest comparison against the existing workflow. Keep the interface effort, failed attempts, and review time in the decision. A reliable tool that saves preparation work is a stronger result than reproducing a headline cost ratio without matching its conditions.

entries.title: Jev-use with Codex: fast navigation depends on a good handoff
entries.summary: SuSu’s saved recommendation describes Jev handling repeated browser actions while Codex handles planning, input, and visual checks. The named repository is unavailable, but the division suggests a concrete, testable architecture for educational-app verification.
entries.reason: The integration pattern is useful for repeated browser work, but repository availability, exact installation behavior and claimed speedups need separate verification.
entries.html:
A fast navigation worker with a deliberate handoff

SuSu’s September 18 bookmark recommends pairing Codex with Jev so that repetitive browser navigation does not require a full reasoning exchange at every step. In the captured translation, Jev handles clicks, navigation, switching, and scrolling; Codex retains broader reasoning, text input, and visual verification. The post claims a five-to-tenfold speed improvement and lower usage, but provides no controlled timing table, repeated trials, or complete accounting. The useful idea is the division of work, while the advertised multiplier remains unverified. Saved recommendation.

The full post names vlad-terin/jev-use, lists Node.js 22 or later, browser/computer-use access, and a TypeSafe key, and describes installing a skill before allowing Jev to run navigation sequences. It says the host takes over when input or additional judgment is needed and then returns control. A visible reply already reports a broken link. On October 18, the named repository returned 404; the related jev-browser address also returned 404. No rename, replacement, source implementation, or currently usable installation procedure was verified.

This report therefore treats the saved setup as historical rather than presenting its command as something to run now. Other projects use similar names, but a shared phrase is not evidence that their code, permissions, or performance are interchangeable. The quoted compaction announcement concerns another application and is background within this bookmark, not a second browser implementation.

Why a smaller decision loop could help

A browser task includes more than deciding what to click. The program observes the current page, represents possible actions, chooses one, performs it, waits for a usable result, and checks progress. A general assistant may also interpret a long task description and produce new text. The proposed split removes some of that broader work from repeated navigation decisions. It does not remove observation, page loading, or verification.

TypeSafe’s Choice primitive offers a relevant building block: choose among named alternatives and return a distribution over them. For a page with several lesson cards, application code could construct alternatives from the visible controls and ask which best matches the current subgoal. The output should identify one of those controls, not invent a selector that the browser has never observed.

Multiple independent questions can share the same observation. The speculative fan-out pattern describes asking several questions together and consuming only the answers relevant to the selected path. A proposed browser loop might ask for a next action and whether the current subgoal appears complete. That is not permission to execute several future clicks against one stale page snapshot. Later actions may depend on a page that does not exist yet.

A skill supplies reusable instructions and possibly scripts or references; the Agent Skills specification documents that folder structure. It does not itself establish a browser driver or a particular host integration. Because the named repository is unavailable, this report cannot verify whether the historical package implemented the split with a local loop, host callbacks, tool calls, or another mechanism.

The handoff is the central engineering problem

A useful handoff needs a precise reason. “Need typing” is different from “no matching control,” “page changed,” or “goal requires visual interpretation.” Send the host a compact record containing the subgoal, current page identity, relevant controls, recent actions, and the unresolved issue. A generic request to take over forces the larger model to reconstruct what happened and can erase the intended latency saving.

When the host returns control, supply a fresh observation and an updated subgoal. Suppose Jev opens a quiz settings panel, the host fills a title, and the page re-renders. The old element identifiers may now refer to something else or no longer exist. Resuming from the previous action list is less reliable than rebuilding the choices from the current state.

Keep generated text outside the navigation chooser. For a proposed teaching workflow, the host can prepare an exercise title and answer explanation once, then provide those values as explicit inputs. The navigation layer selects the appropriate fields and controls. This makes it possible to inspect the content separately from whether the interface was operated correctly.

Completion should be an observable condition. “The next lesson is open” might mean the expected lesson identifier is displayed and the first exercise is available. “The draft is saved” needs a persistence check, not merely a button click. A model’s decision to stop is useful evidence about its interpretation, but the application should retain the actual result that justifies success.

Make the handoff record useful to both programs

A small state contract can make this design practical for an average coder. For the vocabulary pilot, give each run a task identifier, a lesson identifier, and an expected starting item. Keep a separate subgoal such as “open the explanation for this answer.” Alongside it, store the last observed page, the selected control, and the condition that will count as completion. These fields describe the application’s work rather than the model’s private reasoning.

Give each handoff a reason from a short list: input required, ambiguous controls, missing target, unexpected page, or verification failed. The host can then respond with a revised subgoal, prepared text, or a decision to stop. For example, if two lessons share a title, the host should supply the intended lesson identifier. Asking the navigation worker to guess again with identical information adds latency without resolving the ambiguity.

Include a sequence number for observations. If the host has already changed the page, discard an action that was selected from an older observation. This is a proposed application rule, not a verified feature of the unavailable project. A simple implementation can process one action at a time; it does not need parallel browser commands to benefit from quicker decisions.

Finally, distinguish task progress from model activity. “Three choices evaluated” is an internal count; “the incorrect-answer explanation opened” is progress a teacher can inspect. Keep both when measuring the pilot, but show the latter in its user-facing status. This makes a stalled run recognizable and prevents a busy sequence of calls from looking like successful testing.

Make the browser representation do useful work

For a website you control, meaningful roles and labels can make automation clearer. Playwright’s locator guidance recommends user-facing attributes and explicit contracts, and describes resolving the current element when an action runs. A stable test identifier can distinguish two similar buttons; an accessible name can explain their purpose. These are practical design ideas for a replacement experiment, not verified dependencies of the missing jev-use repository.

Keep mechanical readiness checks in browser code. Playwright’s actionability documentation describes waiting for conditions such as a unique, visible, stable, enabled target that can receive events. Asking a model whether a button “looks ready” is not a substitute for checking the actual control. A disabled button or covering dialog can explain a failed click without requiring another reasoning model.

Also preserve enough context to distinguish similar actions. A page may have “Continue” in a lesson dialog and another “Continue” in an account prompt. Sending only those labels loses the surrounding relationship. A compact candidate can include role, label, container, enabled state, and a stable identifier. The representation should answer the task’s ambiguity without including unrelated page content.

TypeSafe’s documented Jev 1.13 limitations include literal interpretation, excessive irrelevant state, and susceptibility to adversarial content. These are version-specific observations, not a verdict on every future model. In a browser application they motivate direct subgoals, filtered state, and a clear separation between page text and instructions governing the agent.

Measure the whole task, not just model response time

A simple latency model is useful: total time includes observation, decision, execution, page waiting, and any host handoffs. If decision-making accounts for seventy percent of a baseline task and becomes ten times faster, with everything else unchanged, the whole task becomes about 2.7 times faster: 1 / (0.30 + 0.70 / 10). This is an illustrative calculation, not a measurement of the saved project. It shows why a fast classifier does not automatically deliver the same multiplier end to end.

For a fair comparison, use the same starting state, task, success criteria, and browser conditions. Alternate which system runs first and repeat the task. Record failures, retries, and human intervention. A run that stops early should not appear faster than a run that actually completes the task. Report successful-task time together with completion rate.

Separate token usage by model and include handoff calls. Lower Jev cost does not prove fewer total tokens, and fewer host calls may be offset by repeated observations or longer state descriptions. Keep setup and authentication outside a narrow loop benchmark only if you say so; for a user-facing productivity comparison, those costs may matter.

A trace is more useful than a montage. Playwright’s Trace Viewer provides a concrete example of inspecting actions and page state over a run. A comparable record in a proposed Jev integration should show what was observed, what was selected, what executed, and what changed. That makes a slowdown or incorrect action explainable.

A small test for an educational website

Use a local copy of a vocabulary application with invented learner data. Define one journey: open a lesson, submit a deliberately wrong answer, inspect the feedback, try an accepted answer, and move to the next item. The purpose is to assess the interaction, not to let the agent decide whether the educational content is true.

First implement the journey as a deterministic test where its path is known. Playwright assertions can wait for expected text, values, or visibility. This supplies a baseline and a precise definition of success. If a fixed script already handles the task reliably, adding a model needs a reason beyond novelty.

Then introduce controlled variation: move the next button, change its label, open a helpful explanation panel, or offer two possible routes. Give the decision layer the same learning objective and let it choose among observed controls. Compare which variations require a host handoff and whether the final state remains correct. Preserve the deterministic checks so the model does not grade its own completion.

For a Latin exercise, prepare a case where a valid alternative answer is accepted and another where the target grammatical feature is wrong. The browser agent should test both paths using teacher-approved fixtures. It should not improvise an answer key while evaluating the interface; that would confound language judgment with navigation reliability.

A useful report contains the task, application revision, starting state, actions, observed outcomes, and unresolved defects. The teacher can review whether the feedback is pedagogically clear, while the developer checks state transitions. This division mirrors the bookmark’s broader lesson: specialized components are valuable when their responsibilities remain visible.

Design recovery before increasing autonomy

Give each navigation subgoal a step budget and a recognizable failure result. If two attempts produce no relevant change, return the current evidence to the host instead of clicking indefinitely. Distinguish a missing target from a network delay, an expired session, and a layout that requires visual interpretation. Those failures need different remedies.

When an action’s outcome is unclear, observe before repeating it. Repeating a navigation click may be harmless; repeating a submission can create duplicate work. An educational app should expose its current item and submission state clearly enough that both a human and an automation layer can tell what happened.

Keep the first pilot limited to reversible navigation and test content. Expand permissions only when the desired task requires it and the resulting actions can be reviewed. This is an implementation boundary for the proposed experiment, not a claim about the inaccessible skill’s controls. A fast loop remains responsible for acting on the correct page and within the actual task.

The score of seven reflects a promising division between broad planning and repeated local decisions. The historical package cannot currently be recommended as a reproducible installation, and its five-to-tenfold claim lacks sufficient evidence. Its durable contribution is a testable design hypothesis: reduce unnecessary reasoning handoffs while preserving fresh observations, explicit escalation, and outcome checks.

entries.title: Sac’s Jev-cu: faster-looking Calendar control, explicit decisions, and verifiable outcomes
entries.summary: Sac’s open repository delegates interface choices to Jev while retaining host execution and local checks. Its Calendar demo is a useful lead, but the current code and documentation support a narrower, testable workflow rather than a general speed guarantee.
entries.reason: The named implementation explores low-latency desktop decisions, though one comparison clip does not establish general speed, token savings or reliability.
entries.html:
A Calendar demonstration with a narrower claim

Sac’s September 18 post describes an enhanced computer-use setup combining Codex and Jev. Its example is adding an event in Mac Calendar, presented in a forty-six-second comparison video. The creator reports smoother, faster operation with roughly the same token consumption. That last detail matters: the post quotes an earlier, broader recommendation about tenfold speed and large token savings, but its own comparison does not claim those token savings. No repeated timing table or complete run ledger accompanies the saved material. Saved demonstration and replies.

A September 19 reply identifies Sac-Y/Jev-cu as the released implementation. This repository was accessible on October 18. A naming exchange in the conversation also points to a different Cua project called jev-use. That shared name does not establish shared code or transfer the other project’s platform claims to Sac’s implementation. The source examined here is Sac-Y/Jev-cu.

The repository describes a text-based selection layer: Jev chooses among interface controls, while the host reads the application and performs actions. It includes an installable skill, decision and policy scripts, fixtures, and tests under an MIT license. Its current implementation sends interface text rather than screenshots. That is an application design choice, not a statement about every current Jev capability. No installation, model call, or live Calendar operation was performed for this report.

What the small model actually decides

Think of the system as a separation between interpretation and execution. A host can receive a broad request, prepare text and dates, and decide what observable result is required. A compact model can then choose a suitable next control from a list. The operating application remains the authority on what actually happened.

The decision wrapper asks four questions: which element to target, what action to take, whether the goal appears complete, and whether confirmation is needed. Target and action use fixed choices; completion and risk use yes/no judgments. Input text and coordinates come from host-provided resources rather than being generated by Jev. The wrapper’s reported confidence concerns target selection, so it should not be read as confidence in the entire task.

TypeSafe’s Choice documentation explains the underlying distinction: the response includes an option distribution and a confidence value describing how concentrated that distribution is. A strongly preferred option can still be wrong when the correct control was omitted. Noul supplies a probability for a yes/no proposition, such as whether the visible goal is achieved. These outputs are inputs to application logic, not independent proof that an event exists.

For an average coder, the important shift is from parsing an open-ended instruction to evaluating a small decision against known alternatives. Code can reject an unknown target immediately. That makes failures easier to localize: bad observation, missing candidate, wrong choice, unsuccessful action, or incorrect completion check.

The interface representation constrains the result

The loop implementation parses indexed accessibility text into controls, ranks eligible candidates using roles and goal terms, and defaults to forty candidates. It sends a compact context rather than the full observation. After executing an action it reads fresh state. A selected target outside the current candidate list causes escalation, and a supplied verification function can establish completion.

This creates a useful debugging order. First ask whether the intended control appears in the observation at all. Next ask whether filtering retained it. Only then investigate whether Jev chose incorrectly. Increasing a model’s confidence threshold cannot recover a button that never reached the model.

A calendar is an instructive example because a month can expose many day cells alongside navigation controls and a dialog. The relevant target may be a date field inside the dialog rather than a visually nearby day. For a proposed extension, retain the field’s relationship to its event editor and distinguish the event’s start date from the calendar’s current viewing date. Those are different application states even when they display similar text.

Candidate selection is therefore part of the product’s intelligence. A larger list is not automatically better if its labels lack context. Start with a small, inspectable task and retain enough state to explain why each candidate belongs.

Policy gates are useful, but they need a task boundary

The policy module combines an application allowlist, sensitive-label patterns, and risk and confidence thresholds. The enclosing loop defaults to preview mode and prevents execution in that mode. It checks English and Chinese terms associated with operations such as deletion, sending, payment, and authorization. Some named applications receive a lower confidence threshold. These are inspectable rules, not a guarantee that every allowed action is appropriate.

Consider a proposed school-calendar assistant. Merely allowing Calendar should not authorize inviting a class, changing an existing assessment, or deleting a recurring series. The task specification should say which calendar, event, fields, and changes are permitted. A button labelled “Done” may commit meaningful changes without containing an obvious sensitive word. Conversely, harmless instructional text might contain a word that triggers a gate.

Build a small table of intended operations before extending the workflow. For each operation, record its target, expected effect, and how to recognize completion. This is more useful than treating one numerical risk threshold as a universal permission system. The model can help interpret the interface, while the surrounding application preserves the actual scope.

A preview is one decision, not a completed rehearsal

The project’s skill instructions make several valuable distinctions. A preview proposes the current action without simulating later screens. A changed interface is not necessarily progress. Exhausting the step budget is not success. The instructions also advise stopping after two identical unsuccessful actions. In the inspected loop, unchanged observations are logged, but that two-attempt rule is not implemented as a separate hard stop. A host following the instructions and the loop’s own enforcement are different layers.

The runtime notes recommend checking selected state or an actual result value rather than merely finding a button. They also warn that a timeout does not establish that no action occurred. This matters when retrying: first observe the application, then decide whether another action is required.

There is also a concrete integration detail for programmers: the runtime notes say a resource callback may be called before and after a decision. Keep such a callback free of side effects. It should return prepared parameters, not create an event, advance a database cursor, or consume the next test case. Otherwise the act of asking for parameters can change the task before the interface action occurs.

For a proposed test harness, store each fixture as an immutable record containing the intended title, date, and expected outcome. Let the current stage reference that record explicitly. After a verified stage completes, the harness can advance to the next stage. A failed or repeated decision then receives the same intended values. This makes retries intelligible and prevents a second callback invocation from silently selecting tomorrow’s lesson instead of today’s. Record the fixture identifier in the trace so a reviewer can reproduce the intended task without seeing unrelated calendar content.

For an event editor, an original verification plan might check the title, calendar, start time, end time, and whether the editor closed with the event visible. A separate readback should distinguish a draft from a persisted event. The result should identify which checks passed rather than offering one unexplained green success marker.

Without a verification callback, the inspected loop can return done from Jev’s completion judgment alone. The separate verified: true result indicates that the code-level predicate passed. Keep those checks independent of the action chooser where possible. If the same uncertain interpretation both selects the control and certifies the result, the system can repeat its own mistake with confidence.

Start with the repository’s smaller Calendar exercise

The current Calendar demonstration plan is explicitly a proposed exercise, not a record of a completed test. It changes views and browses dates without creating or editing events: month view, next month, today, then week view. Each stage has its own visible condition. It derives dates from the actual starting state and local date rather than copying historical indices or example months.

This is a sensible learning sequence because it separates navigation from event creation. For a teacher exploring the architecture, record the starting month, calculate the expected next month in ordinary code, and compare the observed title afterward. Handle December-to-January rollover explicitly. The language model need not perform calendar arithmetic when the program can calculate it exactly.

Then test a controlled variation: begin in a different view or with a different month displayed. The goal remains the same while the required first action changes. A successful experiment would show that the chooser adapts to those states and that the verifier still evaluates the correct result. This report proposes that experiment; it does not report a successful run.

Turn the architecture into an educational app test

A useful next project is a local lesson-planner prototype containing invented classes and assignments. Create three short tasks: open a particular lesson, inspect its practice schedule, and switch between daily and weekly views. Define the expected lesson identifier and date range before each run. Use no real learner records during development.

First implement a direct baseline for controls whose identities are known. Then let the chooser handle a small ambiguity, such as two lesson titles with different course labels. Compare the selected target with a teacher-prepared answer. This tests whether the interface representation preserves the distinction that matters pedagogically.

Next add a draft reminder without submitting it. The host supplies the exact title and time; the navigation layer chooses fields. Present a review showing the values actually entered beside the intended values. A mistake should be explainable as a particular field mismatch rather than a vague agent failure.

Finally, introduce an unexpected dialog or remove a required control. The desired result is a clear handoff, not an improvised substitute. Save the last useful observation and the unresolved subgoal. A developer can then improve the application’s labels, candidate extraction, or task definition based on evidence.

The same exercise can become teaching content. Show learners a three-column trace: observed controls, selected action, resulting state. Ask them to identify whether a failure came from incomplete information or an incorrect decision. This makes agent behavior tangible without suggesting that a fast sequence of clicks demonstrates understanding of the lesson itself.

How to assess the speed claim fairly

Measure the entire journey from the same starting state to the same verified outcome. Separate observation time, model time, action time, application waiting, and host intervention. A model request that returns quickly can still be surrounded by slow interface reads or repeated recovery attempts.

Run several task variants and alternate the order of the baseline and Jev-assisted versions. Report completed tasks, failures, and manual takeovers together. If one system creates the correct event and another merely closes its editor, their elapsed times are not comparable.

Keep token count separate from money and latency. Sac’s specific saved comparison reports similar token consumption despite smoother operation. A benchmark should therefore record usage for every model involved, including host calls, and explain how costs were calculated. Cached setup or an already-open application should be disclosed when it affects the comparison.

Static snapshots can test target selection economically, but they omit transitions, unexpected dialogs, and changing element identifiers. The repository’s distinction between snapshot evaluation and complete-task success is valuable. A good evaluation keeps both: a small diagnostic set for choices and a repeated end-to-end set for actual work.

A useful implementation to study, with bounded evidence

The current project instructions focus on macOS application accessibility text and describe browser work as experimental. They also distinguish this implementation from tasks requiring visual layout or three-dimensional judgment. Its public code makes the proposal more reviewable than an inaccessible demo, but it does not establish a general speed advantage or seamless compatibility with every host version.

A score of six reflects practical educational value: the repository exposes the decision boundary, local policy, fresh observations, and explicit verification points. It is a credible starting point for a narrow, measured prototype. Stronger evidence would be repeatable task traces with completion checks, full usage accounting, and comparisons across changing interface states. The most transferable lesson is to accelerate the uncertain choice while keeping execution and proof of completion visible.
